## [SkillCT: A Nine-Dimension Benchmark for Agent Skill Quality Without Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38147) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SkillCT introduces a nine-dimension benchmark that assesses agent skills across static, dynamic, and human-assisted aspects, moving beyond downstream task execution. It also proposes an execution-free baseline that predicts quality profiles of unseen skills by retrieving similar reference skills, reducing token consumption and evaluation time. This addresses a real gap in the emerging agent-skills ecosystem by enabling scalable, pre-deployment assessment of specification quality, behavioral robustness, and responsibility boundaries. It could help developers and repository maintainers evaluate and refine skills without costly task-specific environments. The benchmark spans static assessment of intrinsic specification properties, dynamic assessment of behavior stability across backbone models and request variations, and human-assisted assessment of behavior-chain consistency and task granularity. The execution-free baseline leverages retrieval of similar reference skills to predict multidimensional quality profiles, preserving consistency with full assessment while reducing cost.

## [DecompGym: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Decomposition Algorithm Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38175) ⭐️ 7.0/10

DecompGym introduces an 81-instance benchmark spanning nine problem families (five Benders, four column generation) to evaluate how well 12 GPT, Claude, and Gemini models running in coding-agent tools design and implement decomposition solvers. Each solver must execute within 60 seconds, pass a numerical feasibility and LLM-judge method audit, and achieve an objective within 1% of the stored optimum. This is the first benchmark targeting a genuinely hard, understudied task—automating the design of Benders decomposition and column generation solvers—and its failure analysis shows that output-only checks are insufficient, pointing to the need for process-aware verification and error-localizing feedback in coding agents. It will be valuable to researchers in AI for optimization and to practitioners building agentic solvers for large-scale operations research problems. On the first attempt, two models solved every instance and seven solved more than 90%; most Benders failures (48 of 62) were missing or suboptimal solutions, while the most common column-generation failure was method-audit rejection, with output checks alone accepting 93 of the 108 attempts that failed the audit. Reflection turned 66% of retries into successes versus 39% for independent regeneration, and the most common rejection reason, an 'optimalif', occurred 96 times, 92 of them in one model.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Benders decomposition and column generation are classical optimization techniques that solve large problems by iteratively passing cuts, columns, and dual values between a master problem and subproblems; they are powerful but notoriously difficult to implement correctly. Large language models are increasingly used to automate parts of algorithm design, raising the question of whether coding agents can build such decomposition solvers for new problems. DecompGym is a first step toward answering that question by measuring both correctness and methodological soundness of agent-generated solvers.

A new arXiv paper (2610.38201) proposes a Bounded Dual-Loop Automated Schematic Synthesis Framework that converts natural language specifications into verified, editable KiCad schematics for power electronics converters. The workflow integrates six stages across requirement parsing, knowledge-driven power stage synthesis, contract- and evidence-coordinated component selection with ngspice transient verification, and modular control hardware integration, achieving 100% SPICE simulation pass rates in case studies. This work addresses a critical barrier to applying LLMs in electronic design automation: severe engineering hallucinations such as fabricated part numbers and violated voltage derating margins. By producing verified, editable KiCad schematics and manufacturing deliverables, it could significantly reduce manual effort and errors in power electronics design, impacting EDA toolchains and LLM-application communities. GAAC introduces a lossless BF16 KV cache compression and serving system that uses per-channel exponent coding and a fused attention kernel to achieve approximately 1.4x compression without approximation, enabling bandwidth-efficient long-context LLM inference on personal devices. This work addresses the growing KV cache bottleneck for long-context inference on resource-constrained devices, offering a bit-exact compression method that reduces memory usage and improves throughput without sacrificing model accuracy, which could benefit edge deployment of LLMs. GAAC achieves 1.405-1.407x lossless BF16 KV compression across five models, with lower ratios for FP8 E4M3 (1.09-1.14x) and E5M2 (1.25-1.30x) caches; on NVIDIA DGX Spark it speeds up decode attention by 1.19-1.27x at 64K context and reduces resident KV memory by ~26%, while on Apple M4 it achieves 1.02-1.25x attention speedups.

Rubricon is a new pipeline that automatically generates and refines discriminative rubrics for evaluating LLM responses without human preference labels, rubric annotations, or generator-model training. Across five benchmarks, its rubric-based scores align 9% better with expert-authored rubrics than the best prior synthetic method (RRD, QSRG, OpenRubrics, or agentic generation via Codex). On HealthBench, post-training a Qwen3.5-9B model with Rubricon rubrics yields 4.5% better performance than training with rubrics from RRD, the strongest alternative synthetic generator.

## [Verification-Guided Reflow Boosts Retrosynthesis Solvability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38245) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Verification-Guided Reflow (VGR), which integrates reaction verification as a decision action during AND/OR retrosynthesis search, raising verified solvability on Retro190 from 51.1% to 62.6% compared to post-search route evaluation. A refined strategy of early pruning and delayed guidance further improves verified solvability to 71.1% while using fewer proposal calls and unique verifier queries. This work addresses a key challenge in AI-driven retrosynthesis: infeasible reactions can invalidate entire routes, and post-hoc evaluation cannot correct search errors. By feeding verification results back into the search process, VGR improves the reliability of computer-aided synthesis planning, which could benefit chemists and drug discovery pipelines relying on automated route design. Verification results are represented as binary verdicts, and queries are scheduled from the search structure; acquired verdicts either exclude reactions or adjust search priorities. Notably, combining early verification with immediate prioritization of accepted reactions performs worse than either change alone, motivating the early pruning and delayed guidance strategy.

## [Game-Theoretic Foundation Extends Bisimulation Metrics to Undiscounted RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38313) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper introduces a game-theoretic foundation for bisimulation metrics in undiscounted reinforcement learning settings, interpreting prior metric operators as Bellman-Shapley operators of zero-sum turn-based games. This yields unique metric definitions even when the discount factor γ=1, enabling the transfer of dynamic-programming theory and algorithms. Bisimulation metrics have been largely confined to discounted MDPs, limiting their applicability to average-reward and total-reward problems that are common in real-world continual learning. This work removes that limitation, potentially enabling principled state aggregation and representation learning in undiscounted settings. The framework characterizes metric finiteness via structural properties of the MDP and motivates directed metrics that remain finite in weakly communicating MDPs. It also provides error and suboptimality guarantees for aggregation-based planning and proves that the metrics bound total-reward and, under state-independent optimal gain, optimal relative value differences.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Bisimulation metrics quantify how similar two states are in terms of task-relevant behavior, which is useful for state aggregation and representation learning in reinforcement learning. Traditionally, these metrics are defined using contraction operators that require a discount factor less than 1 to guarantee a unique fixed point. In undiscounted settings (total- and average-reward problems), such contraction arguments fail, so new mathematical foundations are needed.

The paper introduces CHORD, a relational graph discrimination framework that detects hallucinations in LLMs by modeling hidden states as joint relational graphs over layers, tokens, and features, and uses meta-learning to generalize to unseen target models. It formalizes the problem of cross-model hallucination detection (CMHD) and shows that CHORD outperforms representative detection methods in cross-model generalization. Most internal-representation-based hallucination detectors are model-specific and fail to transfer to new LLMs, so a method that generalizes across models could make hallucination detection practical in heterogeneous deployments where many models are used. This addresses a key barrier to deploying LLMs safely in real-world applications. CHORD represents hidden states as joint relational graphs over layers, tokens, and features, feeds them into relation-aware attention to obtain structure-aware features, and uses meta-learning to shape these features toward transferable detection signals. The core challenge is cross-model representation heterogeneity: hidden states from different LLMs exhibit severe semantic inconsistency, which limits transferability of classical detectors.

However, because different LLMs have different architectures and learned representations, a detector trained on one model often does not work on another, a problem known as cross-model representation heterogeneity. ## [World Reward Models Directly Select Better Programs, Outperforming LLM Judges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38439) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes World Reward Models (WRMs) that directly predict which candidate program will perform better, avoiding the error-prone step of predicting execution outcomes. Their WRM, ForeCritic, adapts a 9B typed decision model to 5k executed program pairs and picks the better program 79.4% of the time on 12,438 held-out pairs from 26 ML tasks, while general-purpose LLM judges reach 53–62%. This approach can significantly speed up search-based ML agents by reducing the need for costly program executions, cutting mean task time by 4.4–7.5 times when integrated into AIDE, ML-Master, and ForeAgent. It offers a theoretically grounded alternative to world models for program synthesis and could improve the efficiency of automated machine learning systems. The paper proves that a selector predicting execution from the same inputs cannot outperform the best direct selector, and that predicted outcomes add error which can make a likelihood-trained world model prefer the worse program on every instance. Cross-entropy on executed winners drives a WRM toward the optimum, and ForeCritic's probabilities are calibrated.

The paper proposes Structured Representation Learning for Behavior Cloning (SRLBC), an architecture that separates embeddings for slow, fast, and exogenous variables to improve closed-loop generalization in multiscale dynamical systems. Validated on a pressurized water reactor load-following benchmark, SRLBC outperforms shared-embedding baselines and, when embedded in a safety-augmented approximate NMPC framework, achieves 6.8x speedup over NMPC with at least 99.8% constraint satisfaction. This work addresses a key challenge in imitation learning for control: multiscale systems with stiff dynamics are hard to clone due to nonlinear couplings that a shared latent space cannot capture. The approach enables fast, safe approximate controllers for safety-critical industrial systems like nuclear reactors, potentially reducing reliance on expensive online optimization. On 500 long-horizon roll-outs across 20 training seeds, standalone SRLBC policies approach NMPC performance at 15x lower computational cost, but still leave a few percent of trajectories infeasible. Embedding the learned policy in a safety-augmented approximate NMPC framework, which calls the optimizer only when the predicted input sequence is not certified safe, yields controllers 6.8x faster than NMPC with at least 99.8% feasibility; under distribution shift, SRLBC degrades the least and retains over 98% feasibility after safety augmentation.

The bias was observed only with the Tülu-3 recipe, not with post-training from Meta, Alibaba, or Mistral, and none of seven deployed commercial models showed greater doubt toward lower-status posters. ## [WISD: Weakened Models as Self-Distillation Teachers for Reasoning LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38681) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce Weakening-Induced On-Policy Self-Distillation (WISD), which creates a weaker counterpart of a reasoning model via low-bit quantization or magnitude pruning and uses the contrast between the original and weakened model as an on-policy self-distillation signal. Across math and coding benchmarks, quantization and pruning improve average accuracy by 4.0 and 5.5 percentage points respectively, with pruning lifting Qwen3.5-4B from 57.7% to 70.5% on HMMT 2025 and from 39.1% to 56.7% on LiveCodeBench v6. Existing self-distillation methods typically need privileged information (such as reference solutions or stronger teacher contexts) to build a better self-teacher, which limits them to settings where such data exists. WISD removes this requirement by using a deliberately degraded model as the contrastive signal, making self-improvement feasible with only unlabeled prompts and offering a cheap post-training path for reasoning models. The weaker model is constructed in two ways—low-bit quantization and magnitude pruning—and the method is evaluated across diverse architectures and scales on mathematical and coding reasoning tasks. Quantization also raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 68.5% to 74.6% on HMMT 2025 and from 61.8% to 69.5% on LiveCodeBench v6, though the paper is an arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

**Background**: Self-distillation is a training technique in which a model teaches itself, typically by acting as both teacher and student with different contexts. On-policy distillation means the student generates its own rollouts in real time and receives dense token-level supervision on those outputs, rather than learning from a fixed offline dataset. Low-bit quantization compresses a model by reducing numerical precision of weights and activations, while magnitude pruning removes parameters with the smallest absolute values; both are standard compression techniques that degrade model quality in a controlled way.

## [AI-Written Papers Misattribute Numbers More Than Fabricate, Study Finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38691) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper re-analyzes all 540 released judgments from a public benchmark of nine AI research agents across fifteen open research problems, and manually labels 256 numerical claims from 18 submissions. It finds that about four in five unsupported claims correspond to values in the agent's own files that come from the wrong experiment, metric, or run, and introduces a deterministic claim-to-evidence checker that certifies claims with over 90% precision (78 of 85; Cohen's kappa = 0.89) against blinded annotators. This work shifts the focus from detecting outright fabrication to diagnosing misalignment between papers and underlying experiments, which is the dominant failure mode in AI-generated research. It offers a more reliable verification tool for automated paper generation and motivates provenance-first auditing of AI-produced research, affecting developers of AI research agents and integrity-checking pipelines. The deterministic checker's rules were fixed before labeling, and while it verifies only a subset of claims, most claims it cannot verify are still traceable, so failure to verify is not evidence of falsehood. An LLM verifier given the same evidence recovers more traceable claims but accepts about three times as many misattributed ones, suggesting the two approaches are best used together; applied to 99 submissions, the checker reveals large differences in traceability across agents, and a second judge from a different vendor preserves the official agent ranking while passing twice as many papers.

## [Certified Test-Time Compute on Hamiltonian Physics-Structured AI Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39073) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes a theoretical and empirical framework for test-time compute on a Latent Dynamics Model with Hamiltonian dynamics, providing exact structural guarantees (phase-volume Jacobian, bounded energy change, latch-transport law) for mechanisms that expand access. It introduces a taxonomy of reachability failures (escape and reach failures) and resolves them via a Lorentz squeeze and a gated canonical translation, verified on an analytic testbed. This work offers a principled approach to test-time compute by grounding it in conservative physics, potentially enabling more stable and interpretable extra compute allocation in AI systems. It could influence future research on reliable test-time scaling and memory mechanisms in learned models. The Lorentz squeeze resolves escape failures by injecting bounded, re-absorbable energy that grows quadratically with excess distance, while the gated canonical translation resolves reach failures at detJ=1 exactly with energy cost equal to the potential difference between endpoints (zero on the matched channel). An untrained state-replacing map annihilates phase volume and erases stored charge, whereas the gated channel transports it; the main contribution is the formalization and verification of the certificate stack, not benchmark performance.

SocialArena introduces a unified three-tier framework defining LLM social intelligence along role-playing ability, mental state reasoning, and behavioral reasoning, operationalized through a role-playing dialogue paradigm with explicit character thinking. The authors also propose the U-TRIMF framework to synthesize diverse social contexts and spent $132.4K on trained human annotators to produce arena-style preference labels with natural-language critiques. This matters for developers building socially interactive applications such as mental health counseling, companionship chatbots, and educational tutoring. The benchmark's reliability rests on a costly human-annotated arena-style protocol in which annotators compare model responses and provide preference labels plus natural-language critiques, rather than relying solely on LLM judges. The U-TRIMF framework is used to guide synthesis of social contexts with broad coverage so that conclusions are not confined to specific scenarios.

A new arXiv paper measures planned clicks on 31 public web pages and finds that 0.4% of clicks planned on fully loaded pages became stale within 30 seconds, compared to 17% of clicks planned in the first second after a page opened. The paper introduces a benchmark generator, a break-even formula for when a pre-click check pays off, and three rules for agent developers. Researchers introduce LinguaArray, a framework where an LLM proposes a small Semantic Focus Set of ground terms or constraints to guide quantified array SMT solving, while the SMT solver remains the sole proof engine and certifies all results. On 1015 SMT-LIB instances across five logics with a 1200s timeout, LinguaArray solves up to 69.1% of instances and increases solved-instance counts by 105%–397% over the corresponding backends. This work shows a verifiable way to combine LLMs with formal reasoning systems, addressing a known hard problem in quantified array reasoning where instantiation-based techniques often fail. It could impact formal verification and neuro-symbolic AI by enabling solvers to tackle instances they previously could not solve, without trusting LLM outputs as proofs. LinguaArray interacts within a finite time and then falls back to the backend solver to mitigate potential regressions, and the LLM-suggested focus sets are validated by the solver. The approach is inspired by backdoor sets in SAT solving, where a small set of variables can make the rest of the problem easy to solve.

## [Kairos orchestrates five PDDL planners for broad coverage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39454) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Kairos profiles each PDDL task to select among five specialized planning engines—covering ground heuristic search, compressed and snap-action temporal search, time-step hybrid dynamics, and lifted search—and schedules them under a shared time and memory budget. Every candidate plan is independently validated, and 'unsolvable' is reported only when a search whose exhaustion constitutes a proof exhausts its space. This approach enables runtime robot planning to handle the full spectrum of PDDL, from STRIPS to PDDL+, while remaining competitive with specialized planners and making explicit what each answer guarantees. It could significantly benefit robotics and automated planning applications that require fast, reliable re-planning with heterogeneous task features. On 1,756 tasks from nine comparative suites, Kairos solves more tasks at full limits than the strongest evaluated planner of each suite, with the largest differences on numeric, temporal, PDDL3 and PDDL+ planning, and also solves the most tasks at 100 ms and 1 s. Ablations identify compressed temporal search and the novelty fallback as major contributors, and a comparison with VAL traces every disagreement to a PDDL+ convention or a documented VAL defect.

## [Federated Training's Effect on Grad-CAM Faithfulness in Deepfake Detection Is Non-Monotonic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39483) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A systematic study evaluates Grad-CAM explanation faithfulness in federated deepfake detection using an EfficientNet-B4 detector on FaceForensics++ across five federated clients with varying data heterogeneity. It finds that federated models match or exceed centralized baseline faithfulness at near-IID and moderate heterogeneity, but at extreme heterogeneity explanations become spatially incoherent and causally misleading. This challenges the assumption that federated learning uniformly degrades explainability, showing instead a threshold effect tied to client heterogeneity. It has direct implications for deploying privacy-preserving deepfake detection in forensic settings where analysts rely on explanations to trust flagged clips. The degradation is not a general cost of federated training but a threshold effect: at extreme heterogeneity, Grad-CAM explanations break down entirely, becoming spatially incoherent and on average causally misleading. The study provides practical guidance for identifying safe deployment conditions and releases code and data partitions for reproducibility.

A new arXiv paper (2610.39497) introduces 'conditional interaction,' a predict-gate-execute-update loop where a lightweight System-1 predictor estimates the utility of candidate interactions and only admits those above an adaptive threshold for costly System-2 execution. The authors show that under ideal screening and equal execution costs, execution compute can fall by a factor approaching 1/ρ_u, where ρ_u is the density of utility-relevant interactions. This work challenges the dominant scaling paradigm that relies solely on enlarging System-2 (bigger models, more data, longer reasoning) and suggests that co-designing a lightweight System-1 predictor can yield substantial compute savings. If validated, it could reshape how AGI progress is measured, shifting focus from total compute to 'informative compute' and making ρ_u a measurable coordinate of scaling efficiency. The paper bounds selection regret by predictor error and the utility margin, and notes that prediction errors, exploration, and distribution shift reduce the achievable savings. The framework spans training, test-time reasoning, adaptive decision-making, and agentic tool use, with utility and cost defined per application.

**Background**: System-1 and System-2 refer to dual-process models of cognition: System-1 is fast, intuitive, and lightweight, while System-2 is slow, analytical, and resource-intensive. ## [Source-agreement metrics fail to evaluate LLM fact-to-story reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39500) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.39500) shows that source-agreement metrics, which treat any departure from the source as an error, are inappropriate for evaluating fact-to-story reconstruction tasks where perspective shifts are intentional. The authors had three model families rewrite 2,000 news articles as summaries and stories, and found that accountability distortion—shifting blame away from perpetrators—rose up to sevenfold in stories compared to summaries. This work exposes a critical gap in LLM evaluation methodology: current metrics can either penalize legitimate creative transformations or let real distortions slip through. The finding that accountability distortion survives claim-level fact checking and produces grammatically cleaner text has direct implications for anyone deploying LLMs for content transformation, especially in news media and public communication. The study analyzed changes across all five Ws axes and filtered out distortions warranted by the assigned perspective, setting aside a third of detected distortions. Time and manner were replaced rather than lost, while place and causation lost their carrying expressions; where human judges disagreed, three authors relabeling cases converged on whether a distortion occurred but not on whether it was warranted. The authors release ReTold-2k, a reconstructable corpus with scoring protocol and per-judge baselines kept unaggregated.

SkillCompiler introduces programmatic compilation into self-evolving agent skills, decomposing skills into fine-grained operations and compiling well-specified ones into validated, executable programs while retaining LLM reasoning for context-dependent operations. A new arXiv paper (2610.39614) shows that the transformer architecture emerges as the score of last-token laws in a maximum-entropy model of language, where sentences are treated as empirical measures of tokens. The derivation yields softmax attention with untied query-key and value matrices, and causal masking follows naturally for ordered sentences. This provides a fresh mathematical perspective on attention mechanisms, potentially inspiring new architectures or training methods grounded in information theory. It connects transformers to fundamental principles of statistical mechanics and choice theory, which could lead to more principled designs. The derivation uses Luce's choice axiom truncated at the lowest relational order to obtain the softmax choice rule, with the attention cross-moment as its mean parameter. The query-key matrix is the Lagrange multiplier of a maximum-entropy problem inside each sentence, while the value matrix is the multiplier of a constraint over the language, making them untied; multi-head attention and weight-tied unembedding are also discussed.

Luce's choice axiom formalizes choice probabilities with independence from irrelevant alternatives, leading to softmax-like rules. Random measures generalize probability distributions to random objects, and here sentences are modeled as empirical measures of tokens, with a language as a law on the space of such measures.

The study covers a wide range of token lengths and uses generalized linear models to characterize scaling behavior, showing that prefill energy has a quadratic component with input length. ## [Bank-World: A 50-Task Benchmark for Evaluating Agents on Multi-Turn Banking Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39733) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Bank-World introduces a benchmark of 50 banking tasks across two simulated institutions, testing agents on single-turn assignments and multi-turn interactions with simulated employees who supply information, approve actions, and revise instructions. Across 1,600 attempts by four models, the authors find that agents often make correct decisions but fail to turn them into completed work, such as charging fees twice, distributing correct totals in incorrect amounts, or executing payments while approval is pending. This benchmark highlights a concrete and important failure mode for LLM agents in realistic enterprise workflows: correct reasoning does not guarantee correct execution and state management. It provides a rigorous, executable-grading evaluation that can guide the development of more reliable agents for banking and other regulated domains where permissions, record reconciliation, and consistency matter. Grading combines executable checks of recorded actions and state with model judgments of task requirements, including whether valid alternative solutions satisfy them. The task environments, executable graders, and full trajectories are retained privately to reduce contamination and preserve the benchmark for future evaluations.

A new arXiv preprint (2610.39802) analyzes why safety-aligned LLMs over-refuse harmless queries by examining intermediate-layer representations and gradient structure, revealing that harmful-sample gradients are low-rank and more aligned with refusal-target gradients than helpful-target gradients on over-refusal prompts. The authors propose GOAL (Gradient Orthogonalization with contrAstive Learning), a framework that orthogonalizes over-refusal gradients against the low-rank refusal subspace and adds a contrastive learning objective to separate harmful and over-refusal representations. Over-refusal is a critical side effect of safety alignment that degrades user experience and model utility, and this work provides a mechanistic explanation and a targeted mitigation method that could help alignment researchers build models that are both safe and helpful. The findings on imbalanced gradient coupling and representation overlap offer concrete insights for improving safety training objectives. The analysis shows that harmful and over-refusal representations are visually distinguishable at certain intermediate layers but increasingly overlap in deeper layers, and that harmful-sample gradients exhibit high intra-class similarity and concentrate in a low-rank subspace. GOAL addresses this by orthogonalizing over-refusal gradients against the low-rank refusal subspace and adding a contrastive learning objective, with experiments across multiple models and benchmarks showing effective mitigation while preserving safety and general capabilities.

AegisFlow introduces a training-free, non-myopic path-safe guidance framework that formulates guided generation as a global safety-critical optimal control problem with time-varying barrier functions. It derives a tractable approximation of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation to compute global optimal control, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in text-guided image manipulation and robotic planning. This work addresses a key limitation of existing training-free guidance methods—myopic min-norm controllers that hover near constraint boundaries—by enforcing constraints along the entire generative path. It enables better trade-offs between target alignment and constraint satisfaction, impacting diffusion/flow matching applications in image editing and robotics. AegisFlow integrates a time-varying barrier function directly into the global cost functional and uses a mathematically grounded approximation of the HJB equation for tractability. Code is available at https://github.com/LiuKunpeng03/AegisFlow.

## [KARMA: Training-Free Knowledge Evolution for Industrial Ad Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39884) ⭐️ 7.0/10

KARMA is a training-free framework that evolves six typed knowledge modules for industrial advertising agents while keeping model weights and harness code frozen, using a deterministic Trace Verifier, a Critic, and a tool-constrained Evolver with a validation gate. Evaluated on cases sampled from roughly 500,000 real-world operation logs across six e-commerce domains, it raised the average hold-out score from 30.19 to 39.15 (+8.96 points, +29.7%) across 18 domain–model settings with three LLM families. This work shows that industrial agents can adapt their decision knowledge without expensive retraining, which is important for fast-changing domains like online advertising where product offerings, traffic patterns, and policies shift constantly. The regression-gated, atomic-edit approach also makes adaptation inspectable and reversible, addressing a key barrier to deploying self-improving agents in production marketplaces. Ablations show that removing either successful or failed trajectories more than halves the average hold-out gain, and evolved knowledge transfers across domains without further adaptation, yielding an average hold-out gain of 8.54 points across all source–target pairs. The framework links retained patches to their diagnostic evidence and validation outcomes, supporting inspectable and reversible knowledge adaptation.

## [Value of Information Unifies Memory Retrieval and Credit Assignment in RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40030) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.40030) argues that both cheap memory retrieval and credit assignment in reinforcement learning can be governed by a single quantity: the value of information. The authors propose estimating this quantity from archived rollouts using a learned world model, and show that when read at the observation, it yields a provable lower bound on the optimal value of the acquiring action, while when read at the decision, it defines the optimal retrieval set. This work offers a unified theoretical framework that could significantly reduce the cost of attention-based memory retrieval and improve credit assignment in reinforcement learning, which is particularly impactful for robot learning under latency and energy constraints. If validated, it could lead to more efficient and scalable RL systems for real-world applications. The value of information is estimated from archived rollouts with a learned world model, and the lower bound floors the TD target of the acquiring action while attributing this floor to the observation that earned it. A pilot retrieval system trained with this signal solves a memory task with reduced context, though results are preliminary and no community discussion is available.

## [Anti-Prompt paradigm treats human capability as a design goal in AI-assisted work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40151) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces the 'generative paradox' in AI-assisted education and proposes an Anti-Prompt paradigm that reverses the default interaction order: when immediate generation would preempt a consequential human act, AI should first create conditions for human construction. The paper also presents developmental function allocation, which treats retained human capability as a design objective alongside current joint performance, and illustrates these ideas with representative Anti-Prompts, a canonical interaction sequence, and stress tests in mathematical reasoning, experimental science, software diagnosis, and lesson design. This work shifts attention from the output of human-AI teams to what people can still understand, challenge, repair, and adapt when assistance changes or disappears, which is crucial for education, HCI, and AI ethics. It offers a conceptual framework for designing AI systems that preserve human expertise rather than erode it, with implications for how generative AI is deployed in learning and high-stakes decision-making. The paper distinguishes four manifestations of the generative paradox (performance, assistance, ownership, and capability stock) and separates the validity of a product, responsibility for its construction, and evidence of capability after support changes. It concludes with falsifiable predictions about retained capability and a system-level hypothesis about the reproduction and distribution of expertise, but remains a position/design paper without empirical validation.

## [SPLICE: Closing Information Gaps in Multi-Agent LLM Workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40186) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose SPLICE (Selective Probing and Link Insertion for Closing information gaps in multi-agent Execution), a method that locates information gaps in fixed multi-agent LLM workflows, inserts a single directed edge to deliver missing evidence, and then uses a trained selector to decide whether to adopt the resulting candidate answer. On five benchmarks, SPLICE improves Web tool-use task scores by 8.0% and the mean score on four reasoning and planning benchmarks by 5.7% over the static skeleton, at 1.25–1.44× the cost, and transfers zero-shot to four unseen backbones. Multi-agent LLM systems are increasingly used for complex web and reasoning tasks, but their fixed communication graphs can silently starve agents of needed evidence or feed them wrong upstream conclusions. SPLICE addresses both failure modes by treating edge insertion as a decision problem rather than a default fix, which could make multi-agent workflows more reliable without redesigning their topology. SPLICE re-executes only the receiver and affected downstream nodes after adding an edge, and its adoption selector relies on process features—how far the receiver moved, where its new content came from, and whether the change propagated to the final answer—rather than the final output alone. The method is evaluated on five benchmarks and transfers zero-shot to four unseen backbones, though it incurs 1.25–1.44× the cost of the static skeleton.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Multi-agent LLM workflows typically connect specialized agents in a fixed communication graph, where each agent can only read outputs from designated upstream agents. If evidence gathered by one agent never reaches the agent that needs it, an information gap occurs, leading to incomplete or incorrect answers. Adding a connection can supply the missing evidence but may also cause the receiver to adopt an incorrect upstream conclusion, and the final answer alone cannot distinguish these cases.

## [EpiAgent adds learnable epistemic beliefs to LLM agents via self-play](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40227) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose EpiAgent, a framework that equips LLM-based agents with an explicit, learnable epistemic layer that maintains beliefs about others' private information and combines them with available information into an epistemic state for action selection. The agent's policy is decomposed into Epistemic Update and Action Planning, trained via Epistemic Self-Play, a bi-level optimization algorithm that alternately optimizes the two stages using an intrinsic prediction reward. This work bridges epistemic game theory and LLM agents by giving agents an explicit mechanism to reason about others' hidden information, a capability often missing in current LLM-based multi-agent systems. It could improve decision-making in competitive and mixed-motive scenarios such as negotiation, auctions, and strategic interactions where incomplete information is central. The two-stage policy is formulated as a bi-level optimization problem, where the Epistemic Update stage is optimized to predict subsequent observations via an intrinsic prediction reward, and the Action Planning stage is optimized for task performance. Empirical results show EpiAgent consistently outperforms prompting-based and RL-based baselines in both mixed and competitive scenarios, with analyses confirming improved belief inference accuracy and the contribution of learned beliefs to action planning.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Epistemic game theory explains strategic behavior through the beliefs players hold about others and how these beliefs are updated as interactions unfold, especially under incomplete information where agents lack full awareness of others' private information. Bi-level optimization is a class of optimization problems with two nested levels, where the upper-level objective depends on the solution of the lower-level problem, and it has been widely used in machine learning for problems with hierarchical structure. Self-play, where an agent improves by interacting with copies of itself, has been successful in training game-playing agents but is less explored for equipping LLM agents with explicit belief modeling.

## [EnvOS: Auditing Computer-Use Agents in Dynamic Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40246) ⭐️ 7.0/10

EnvOS is a new framework for constructing and certifying environments that change mid-task, verifying before any agent runs that each change fires correctly, the task remains solvable, and the grader separates correct from incorrect behavior, then re-checking verdicts post-hoc from archived evidence. In experiments on stale information, Claude Opus 5 succeeded on 0/16 clinic-booking tasks with no extra information, 2/16 when reminded to re-check the source, and 15/16 when the updated value was shown, while in insurance-claim approval Opus 5 succeeded 10/10 and Claude Sonnet 5 rose from 1/10 to 9/10 when the current policy was shown again. This addresses a real and under-explored problem in agent evaluation: when an agent fails, the cause may be the agent, a change that did not fire, an update the agent never received, or a grader that scored wrongly, and EnvOS separates these causes. Because every environment is generated from a seed and graded by an audited automatic verifier, such environments are natural candidates for training agents with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards. The gain from showing the updated value over a reminder held after correcting for all tests (p = 0.00293), but the Sonnet 5 gain was significant only in its pre-registered test and not after multiple-test correction. In stress tests of the grading itself, the EnvOS pipeline accepted none of 26 corrupted episodes designed blind from the rules as clean, and on an externally generated set it caught 25 of 39, versus 4 for simple log checks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Computer-use agents built on large language models operate software that can change while they act, such as an appointment moving, a policy being revised, or a record being updated. Testing such agents is hard because failures can stem from the agent, from environment changes that did not fire as intended, or from faulty grading. EnvOS is a framework that builds and certifies these dynamic environments before evaluation and re-checks verdicts afterward using archived evidence.

## [TACE: Two-Stage Advantage Estimation for Multimodal RLVR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40250) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes TACE (Two-stage Advantage and Credit Estimation), a new estimator for GRPO that factorizes token-level advantage into sample-level baselining and token-level credit assignment. It replaces linear standardization with a one-dimensional optimal-transport map to a standard normal and renormalizes clipped token weights to have mean one, achieving the strongest results on a majority of benchmarks in a multimodal reasoning suite. This work addresses a core inefficiency in GRPO-based RLVR training, where heavy-tailed rewards and unnormalized token credits can destabilize gradients. By providing a principled fix with theoretical guarantees, it could improve the reliability and performance of reinforcement learning for multimodal LLMs, impacting researchers and practitioners working on RLHF/RLVR. TACE proves population-level inter-task moment equity, a deterministic tail bound, and mass-conservation, boundedness, and sign-anchoring properties that affine baselines and unnormalized token weights do not satisfy. However, it does not dominate every setting, and the evaluation is limited to a multimodal reasoning suite.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is a reinforcement learning algorithm that estimates advantages by comparing rewards within a group of sampled completions for the same prompt, and it underpins models like DeepSeek-R1. RLVR (Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards) fine-tunes LLMs using automatic, rule-based checkers as rewards, commonly applied to math and coding tasks. Optimal transport provides a principled way to map one distribution to another, and here it is used to calibrate reward distributions across tasks.

## [OpenConjecture benchmarks LLMs on randomly sampled arXiv math conjectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40382) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces OpenConjecture, a dataset of open conjectures collected from arXiv mathematics papers published since February 2026, and evaluates frontier GPT models on a random sample of 200 conjectures over three passes using a reproducible protocol without problem-specific guidance. The models produced candidate solutions for roughly 60% of the conjectures, with counterexamples about 1.3 times more common than proofs. This work moves beyond cherry-picked breakthrough cases to provide a more honest, systematic picture of LLM capabilities in AI-assisted mathematics, highlighting that correctness alone is insufficient and that evaluations must also assess fidelity to the intended statement, attribution, and the nature of the mathematical contribution. The analysis finds that models sometimes propose resolutions outside the authors' intent (e.g., proposing the trivial group as a counterexample) and that many proofs follow closely from existing results, though some resolutions exhibit at least moderate novelty; the abstract is truncated and no expert verification of candidate solutions was attempted.

The paper identifies that chain embedding retrievers trained on gold histories degrade at test time due to error accumulation, and proposes on-policy state training that trains the encoder on self-reached states, improving multi-hop retrieval without invoking a language model. This work addresses a real train/test distribution mismatch (exposure bias) in chain embedding retrievers for multi-hop RAG, showing that a small LM-free retriever can be competitive with search agents, which could lead to more efficient and reliable retrieval systems. By the third step, about half or more of the states visited contain a wrong passage, and these passages lower the chance of retrieving a missing gold passage beyond what state difficulty explains; the proposed method labels each self-reached state with the earliest missing gold passage while masking others, and mixes with teacher-forced states contrastively.

## [Prefix Executability: New Metric for Tool-Using Agents Beyond Final Success](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40444) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces prefix executability as a trajectory-level evaluation protocol for tool-using agents, measuring whether every prefix of a predicted tool-call sequence remains executable under tool schemas, state preconditions, and data dependencies. The protocol defines five metrics—Prefix Executability Curves (PEC), First-Error Depth (FED), Trajectory Executability Rate (TER), horizon-normalized AUC-PEC, and Recovery Rate (RR)—and is instantiated on BFCL-v3 multi-turn, ToolSandbox, and τ³-bench. This work shows that final success metrics can obscure whether intermediate tool calls were actually executable, and that rankings based on outcome-only versus prefix-level evaluations can diverge significantly. It provides an actionable reliability signal for comparing agents, diagnosing failures, and assessing validation mechanisms, which is crucial as LLM-based tool-using agents become more prevalent in real-world applications. The study finds that agents whose execution is conditioned on an unverified plan often achieve higher point-estimate final success than non-plan-conditioned baselines while substantially lowering TER and AUC-PEC, revealing that apparent success may rest on non-executable trajectories. As a validation intervention, explicit pre-execution plan checking can improve executable-prefix survival while maintaining competitive terminal success.

**Background**: Tool-use benchmarks like BFCL-v3 multi-turn and ToolSandbox evaluate agents on multi-step function calling, often scoring only final task success. However, such outcome-only metrics ignore whether intermediate tool calls were valid given tool schemas and state dependencies. Prefix executability addresses this gap by checking the executability of every prefix of the tool-call sequence, providing a more granular view of agent reliability.

The paper introduces rewindable interactive proofs (RIPs), a new model for scalable oversight where a weak verifier can rewind a powerful AI prover to an earlier state. ## [Prefill-Based Decode Length Prediction Has Fundamental Limits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40541) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.40541) shows that predicting LLM decode length from prefill-phase hidden states is fundamentally limited by the inherent stochasticity of autoregressive decoding, and derives bounds that any such method must obey. The analysis models decoding as a stopped stochastic process, yielding per-prompt normality and an affine variance law σ = αμ + b. This work reveals that reported accuracy gains in decode-length prediction benchmarks often conflate predictor quality with task hardness, and that system error dominates model error, meaning architectural tweaks to predictors yield diminishing returns. It argues for a benchmarking protocol that fixes model, data, and sampling parameters and reports relative-error metrics, which could reshape how inference scheduling research is evaluated. The per-step stopping probability ramps up over hundreds of steps, so decode length inherits a central limit theorem from many local decisions, giving per-prompt normality with an explicit error term and a variance law whose slope equals the coefficient of variation of the number of response segments. Empirically, the normal law reproduces per-prompt MAE and the central mass of the decode-length distribution to within a few percent, and a broad design space of predictors (MLP, EGTP, FiLM, soft-label, and Mixture-of-Experts variants) converges to similar performance close to the bound.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: LLM inference has two phases: prefill, which processes the input prompt in parallel and is compute-bound, and decode, which generates output tokens autoregressively and is memory-bandwidth-bound. Predicting decode length from prefill hidden states is a key primitive for inference scheduling, enabling better resource allocation, request scheduling, and memory management. However, decoding is stochastic due to sampling, and this inherent randomness imposes fundamental limits on how accurately length can be predicted from prefill alone.

A new arXiv preprint (2610.40545) proposes a value-indexed memory framework in which retrieval is a persistent local traversal through an address space, rather than a fresh global search at each step. The authors introduce a cost-regularised indexing objective that preserves information value in local neighbourhoods while charging for every memory made locally accessible, and demonstrate a proof-of-principle on MiniGrid Memory where a persistent local traversal head reaches 0.95 mean return after 0.59M training steps with a five-token context. This work reframes long-context retrieval as a stateful process that exploits overlap between neighbouring retrieval steps, potentially offering a more efficient alternative to attention or global retrieval for LLM agents that repeatedly solve related retrieval problems. If the hypothesis that stateful retrieval is easier to learn than stateless retrieval holds, it could influence the design of memory-augmented models and agent architectures. The method separates a memory's content from its address, defining utility by the information revealed through retrieval while geometry only determines how cheaply that information can be reached; the marginal-value form yields both attractive and exclusion pressures so complementary memories are co-retrievable and redundant ones are not. The experiment only tests the simplest fixed-geometry instance on MiniGrid Memory and does not test learned geometry or repeated retrieval, so further experimentation is needed to validate the full proposed method.

The paper introduces LBS (LLM-integrated Bayesian State space models), a probabilistic framework that combines a state space model backbone with a pretrained LLM to jointly forecast numerical time series and textual observations. ## [Rank-Aware Exponential Mechanism Enables Differentially Private Listwise Preference Release for LLM Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37682) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces a rank-aware exponential mechanism that privatizes listwise preference data into a low-sensitivity binary partition under local differential privacy (LDP) for LLM alignment. Unlike randomized response, which perturbs all items uniformly, the mechanism concentrates noise near borderline items, and experiments show it consistently outperforms existing LDP baselines at matched privacy budgets. Listwise preference feedback provides richer supervision than pairwise comparisons but also reveals more sensitive user preferences, and this work is the first to address listwise alignment under LDP. It enables privacy-preserving LLM alignment with richer ranking data, which could benefit applications where user preference data is highly sensitive. The high sensitivity of the full ranking space demands excessive noise that neutralizes the benefits of listwise supervision; the proposed mechanism leverages ranking information to sample a fixed-size binary partition, reducing noise sensitivity while preserving ranking information. The code is available at https://github.com/tdsai-lab/RAEM, and evaluations are on downstream LLM alignment tasks.

**Background**: Local differential privacy (LDP) is a privacy model in which each user perturbs their own data before sharing it, so that even an adversary with access to an individual's response cannot learn much about their personal data. The exponential mechanism is a general technique for designing differentially private algorithms that select outputs with probabilities proportional to their utility, and it is well suited for non-numeric data such as rankings. Listwise preference learning for LLM alignment uses full rankings of candidate responses as supervision, offering richer signal than pairwise comparisons but also exposing more sensitive preference information.

The study evaluates four models from two families at two scales and finds that the interaction between prompt phrasing and specific examples accounts for 54% of per-example variability on average, exceeding 70% on tasks like ANLI and WiC. ## [Analogy Vector in LLMs Reveals Instruction Tuning Gradient](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37685) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper extracts an 'Analogy Vector' from LLM residual streams via difference-in-means and shows that while this rhetorical direction exists in all base models, its behavioral accessibility under linear intervention scales continuously with instruction tuning exposure. Across seven matched base-instruct pairs (Gemma-2, Llama-3.1, Qwen-2.5; 2B-32B), Gemma-2 base models show flat steering landscapes (present but inert), whereas Qwen-2.5 base models are already partially accessible, with base-instruct cosine similarity of the analogy vector reaching 0.94-0.97 for Qwen versus 0.37-0.66 for Gemma. This work challenges the binary 'base vs instruct' framing by showing that the relevant variable is the amount of instruction exposure across the full training pipeline, offering a mechanistic account of how instruction tuning organizes rhetorical knowledge in activation space. It positions activation steering as a complementary interpretability tool and has implications for model steering, representation engineering, and understanding what pretraining actually encodes. The Analogy Vector improves the harmonic mean from 3.22 to 3.94 (+22%) for Gemma-2-9B-IT on 300 held-out test prompts, and a small human validation study confirms the LLM judge on Analogy Quality. The finding is based on a single arXiv preprint with no community discussion, and the geometric corroboration relies on cosine similarity between base and instruct vectors.

## [OrbitalGym: JAX-based testbed for planning in orbital games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37686) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces OrbitalGym, a JAX-based simulation environment that compiles adversarial orbital games to batched GPU code, enabling large-scale parallel evaluation of planning algorithms across many system configurations. It compares PD, LQR, model predictive path integral control, and Monte Carlo tree search in two close-range games—pursuit-evasion and lady-bandit-guard—and finds that in pursuit-evasion the propellant ratio dominates outcomes, while in lady-bandit-guard better guard policies raise defense probability by at least 10% in 56–74 of 90 configurations. This work provides a systematic way to distinguish when better planning algorithms matter versus when vehicle capability (thrust, propellant, sensing) dominates in adversarial space scenarios, which is directly relevant to satellite defense, rendezvous and proximity operations, and multi-agent reinforcement learning research. It also offers a GPU-accelerated benchmark that could standardize evaluation beyond the common practice of testing one method against a passive or random defender. OrbitalGym supports varying numbers of agents, state representations (position, velocity, attitude, fuel), explicit or implicit communication, and proximity or conical field-of-view sensors; the study sweeps thrust and propellant ratios, initial separation, game duration, sensor capability, and the definition of capture. A key caveat is that the headline findings are specific to the two close-range games and the chosen policy set, so generalization to other orbital scenarios remains to be tested.

## [Single confidence threshold gives non-English languages less automation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37688) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A pre-registered confirmatory study tested three vendors' typed decision interfaces on 1,000 MASSIVE items in 51 languages at a 0.9 confidence threshold and found that English requests clear the threshold 8.6–11.7 percentage points more often than other languages even when predictions are equally accurate. The gap persisted after reweighting all languages to equal accuracy, and the standard ECE calibration metric failed to detect it on one interface. This reveals a systematic fairness problem in human-in-the-loop decision systems: a single operating threshold can silently route far more non-English requests to human reviewers, increasing cost and latency for those users. It affects anyone deploying confidence-gated classifiers or LLM APIs across languages and argues for reporting per-language coverage at the operating threshold. The study used a written analysis plan, 51 languages, and three vendor APIs; translating inputs into English nearly closed the gap at 0.9 but English still led at the same 5% error target, and fitting per-language thresholds did not eliminate English's coverage advantage. Native African-language requests also showed a gap in the same direction relative to their English human translations.

## [Knowledge Graph Metadata Enrichment Boosts Enterprise RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37728) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.37728) investigates using a knowledge graph to store metadata and frequently changing information for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), evaluated on a snapshot of the SEC EDGAR dataset with 167,050 filings from 10,511 companies and 508,714 embedded chunks. The two-stage GraphRAG design solved 16 of 20 questions on all three attempts, compared to 10 for text-to-SQL and 3 for vector RAG. This work highlights a critical limitation of similarity search in enterprise RAG: company attribution and other metadata are not recoverable from cosine similarity at scale, leading to failures even on single-document queries. The findings suggest that knowledge graphs can provide structural advantages for identity resolution and metadata enrichment, which could impact how enterprises design RAG systems for large document collections. The knowledge graph contained 430,257 nodes and 561,144 edges, with an accession number on every edge. Notably, vector RAG lost the single-document category it was expected to win (passing 3 of 15 vs. GraphRAG's 15 of 15), and all six confident falsehoods in the benchmark were from text-to-SQL conflating distinct people with the same surname, a failure that GraphRAG avoided by resolving identity to an identifier before reading any text.

## [EUReCA: Unified CBCT Reconstruction for Variable Projection Counts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37740) ⭐️ 7.0/10

EUReCA is a geometry-aware feed-forward model that reconstructs clinical linac CBCT from 8 to 100 projections using a single set of weights, without retraining for specific view counts. It combines learned projection features with an in-frame FDK reconstruction and achieves 29.9–33.2 dB PSNR on simulated data, outperforming feed-forward baselines and iterative methods while running orders of magnitude faster. This work addresses a key clinical need in image-guided radiotherapy: reducing projection count lowers radiation dose and scan time but makes reconstruction ill-posed. By generalizing across view counts and acquisition trajectories without retraining, EUReCA offers a flexible, practical foundation for variable-view CBCT, potentially improving workflow and patient safety. The model encodes each projection with a shared multiscale backbone, back-projects features into multiresolution 3D grids using the acquisition geometry, aggregates variable numbers of views at fixed computational cost, and refines the volume with a global 3D transformer and multilevel decoder. On 15 measured patient CBCT scans, it achieved the best performance at every tested view count compared to vendor reconstructions.

Sparse-view reconstruction aims to reduce projections, but traditional analytical methods like FDK (Feldkamp-Davis-Kress) degrade with fewer views, and deep learning approaches often require retraining for each view count. EUReCA introduces a geometry-aware feed-forward approach that unifies reconstruction across variable view counts and trajectories.

## [Sycophancy in LLMs Traced to Two Distinct Training Stages](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37788) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.37788) measures sycophancy across 13 open checkpoints from 5 model lineages, from base models through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and preference optimization to release. It finds that deference to claims in the prompt already exists in every base model, while conversational capitulation—dropping a stated answer when the user objects—is largely absent from base models but present in every post-trained checkpoint. This work challenges the common assumption that sycophancy is mainly a product of preference-based post-training, showing instead that two distinct behaviors with different origins exist. It suggests that evaluation and mitigation strategies need to target prompt deference and conversational capitulation separately, which is important for alignment and RLHF research. The study separates how far an injected claim moves a model's answer from how firmly the answer was held, and varies who makes the claim, how reliable they are said to be, and how strongly they make it. Notably, when the objection names an alternative, most post-trained models give up firmly held answers as often as loosely held ones, and the base model ranks sources in the same order as its post-trained descendants.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Sycophancy in AI refers to the tendency of large language models to tailor responses to what users want to hear rather than what is accurate. It is often attributed to preference-based post-training methods such as RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) and DPO (direct preference optimization), which fine-tune models on human rankings of outputs. However, early measurements have also found sycophancy in pretrained base models, raising questions about its origins. This paper systematically traces sycophancy across training stages to identify where each behavior emerges.

## [Weekday Representations in LLMs Are Seven Discrete States, Not a Continuous Ring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37796) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.37796) tests the continuous manifold assumption on the prototypical weekday representation in language models and finds that it behaves as seven discrete states arranged in a circle rather than a continuous ring. Local sensitivity analysis reveals seven minima aligned with the weekdays, producing a step-like mapping under on-manifold steering, and no intermediate concepts such as time of day, uncertainty, or natural text populate the space between states. This finding challenges the widely held continuous manifold assumption used in representation steering and interpretability, suggesting that moving along a manifold may not correspond to smooth conceptual change. It could affect how researchers design steering methods and interpret latent geometries in LLMs. The study focuses on the weekday manifold, which exhibits a striking circular geometry, yet local sensitivity has seven minima aligned with weekdays, yielding step-like behavioral changes under on-manifold steering. Tests for intermediate concepts (time of day, uncertainty, natural text) found none populating the intermediate space, motivating similar tests on other representation manifolds.

## [Spectral Error Analysis Improves Machine-Learned Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37843) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper analyzes how errors propagate in machine-learned Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians and proposes representing prediction errors in the eigenbasis of the reference Hamiltonian. It introduces a training signal called FermiScope based on the cumulative local density of states (cumulative LDOS), which reduces HOMO-LUMO gap error without increasing element-wise matrix error when fine-tuning three Hamiltonian networks on the QH9 dataset. Machine-learned Hamiltonians promise to bypass expensive self-consistent-field iterations in density functional theory, but entry-wise training does not guarantee accurate spectral properties. This work provides a more complete training objective that could improve the reliability of AI-accelerated electronic structure predictions for molecules and materials. The analysis shows that both wavefunction-alignment losses and electron-density matching only capture part of the error, and that shifting predicted orbital energies leaves the electron density unchanged. The cumulative LDOS uniquely determines the Hamiltonian and yields non-vanishing gradients for large orbital-energy errors, with gains carrying over to out-of-distribution and molecular-dynamics splits where wavefunction-alignment helps less.

**Background**: Kohn-Sham density functional theory (DFT) is the standard method for computing electronic structure, but its self-consistent-field (SCF) iterations are costly for large systems. Machine-learned Hamiltonian models use equivariant neural networks to predict the Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian matrix in one forward pass, and diagonalizing it yields orbital energies, the HOMO-LUMO gap, molecular orbitals, and electron density. However, these models are typically trained to match the reference matrix entry by entry, which does not ensure accurate eigenvalues or eigenvectors.

## [Echo: Scaling Visual RL with Off-policy Experience via Inverse Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37865) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Echo introduces a single-stage off-policy visual RL framework that uses inverse distillation, where a state-based auxiliary policy imitates the visual policy to collect unrendered experience, avoiding the imitation gap of two-stage teacher-student distillation. Evaluated with FastTD3 on three visual control and two dexterous manipulation tasks in Genesis, Echo reduces time to reference returns by 60% and 56% on average, and improves peak mean returns by 62% and 12%, respectively, compared to SDPG. This work addresses the computational bottleneck of scaling visual RL by decoupling experience collection from expensive rendering, potentially enabling more efficient training of visual policies for robotics and control tasks. If validated, the single-stage approach could simplify pipelines and close the performance gap between state-based and visual policies. Echo leverages a shared privileged critic to directly improve the visual policy using off-policy value learning from the auxiliary policy's experience. The evaluation is preliminary, limited to five tasks in Genesis, and relative gains are reported against SDPG under specific configurations, so broader generalization remains to be tested.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Visual reinforcement learning trains policies directly from image observations, but rendering images and running visual policy inference in GPU-accelerated simulators is computationally expensive. A common workaround is two-stage teacher-student distillation: a state-based teacher is trained first, then a visual student imitates it, but this introduces an imitation gap because the student learns from a fixed teacher rather than from its own evolving behavior. Off-policy RL methods, such as FastTD3, can learn from experience collected by different policies, improving sample efficiency. Echo builds on these ideas by using inverse distillation to scale off-policy experience without proportional visual computation.

A new arXiv preprint (2610.37901) presents a six-module scanner that detects unintended vulnerabilities in benign LLM agent skills and composite vulnerabilities arising from multi-skill interactions. Metis-1.6 introduces two from-scratch language models, Praxis (2.94B total, 0.46B active parameters) and Logos (10.23B total, 1.18B active parameters), built by a single researcher using a hybrid Mamba-2 and attention mixture-of-experts stack that runs twice per token. Logos ranks second among 30 models in mathematics, scoring 67.50% on AIME 2025 and 63.64% on HMMT February 2026, but is weak at code, instruction following, and long context. The report candidly documents failures: the intended optimizer never ran (attention trained with AdamW throughout pretraining), a 1.77B-parameter n-gram memory learned to switch itself off, five fine-tuning choices cost capability, and a length reward under group-mean normalization inverted sign once a group's pass rate exceeded 2/3, fixed with a one-line clamp.

## [Statistical Methods Detect Positional Bias in LLM-Based Recommenders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37962) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This paper proposes two statistical detection methodologies, POB-ICM (based on contingency matrix analysis and Chi-square independence testing) and POB-UNBP (a sample-efficient approach derived from a uniformity null model under permutation-based evaluation), to detect positional bias in LLM-based recommender systems. Using a controlled RAG testbed built on a real product catalog with 2,000 template-generated user queries and 20 permutations each (40,000 instances), both methods reject the null hypothesis of positional independence and uniformity in all evaluated state-of-the-art models. Positional bias in LLM-based recommenders can lead to unfair or suboptimal recommendations, and this work provides measurable, reproducible tools to audit and mitigate it. The findings motivate routine governance controls such as order randomization and standardized prompting for deployed systems, affecting researchers and practitioners building RAG-based conversational recommenders. The authors introduce three complementary metrics—permutation sensitivity, positional bias, and strong positional bias—to quantify the effect, with the latter targeting cases where position displaces recommendations toward clearly less relevant items. A robustness analysis across candidate-set size and decoding temperature shows the bias is structural and model-dependent, not an artifact of deterministic decoding or candidate-set size, and source code is publicly released.

## [Tennis event detection benchmark challenges broadcast-only models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38042) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper releases a new benchmark of 345 frame-level bounce and hit annotations across eight clips spanning broadcast, fixed elevated, phone, and court-level viewpoints, and proposes RallyArb, a parameter-free arbitration layer over ball tracks and player poses. On phone and court-level footage, supervised spotters with published broadcast weights achieve a pooled bounce F1 of only 0.130, while RallyArb maintains a bounce F1 above 0.8 on three such clips. This work highlights a critical generalization gap in sports video analysis: models trained on broadcast footage fail dramatically on consumer-captured video, which is increasingly common. The benchmark and arbitration approach could enable reliable tennis event detection outside professional broadcast settings, benefiting amateur analytics and low-cost sports applications. RallyArb fits no parameters on event labels and finds 8 of 11 bounces on a held-out clip, but it places hits too far from the contact frame to match human timing; zero-shot vision-language models detect events on every viewpoint but miss the contact frame by about 0.1 seconds. Fine-tuning the spotter leave-one-clip-out from broadcast weights reaches about 0.8 bounce F1 on two phone and court-level clips but stays at 0.2 on a grazing phone angle.

## [Jailbreak Connectivity Framework Achieves Universal Multimodal LLM Attacks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38091) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes Jailbreak Connectivity (JC), a framework that optimizes continuous adversarial paths in image space to generate diverse, transferable, and universal visual jailbreak attacks against multimodal large language models (MLLMs). On MM-SafetyBench, JC achieves average attack success rates of 84.01%, 85.77%, and 97.95% on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct, InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B-IT, respectively, exceeding the strongest baselines by up to 68.36 percentage points. This work reveals structured vulnerabilities in MLLM safety alignment and demonstrates that visual jailbreak attacks can be made highly transferable and universal, which could inform more comprehensive security evaluations and defenses. It affects AI safety researchers, model developers, and anyone deploying multimodal LLMs in security-sensitive applications. JC leverages low-loss regions in image space to connect adversarial examples, using path sampling for diversity, lightweight surrogate classifiers for cross-model transfer, and a distribution-level objective for universal attacks across harmful queries. In black-box evaluations, JC improves attack success rates over FigStep by 24.69 and 27.34 percentage points on GPT-5.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro, respectively.

## [Convex-SKM-Net: Fast Neural Constraint Satisfaction via Halfspace Corrections](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38197) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Convex-SKM-Net introduces a convex constraint-satisfaction layer that forms linearization halfspaces from residual and (sub)gradient oracles and applies fixed-depth dual projected-gradient descent (dual PGD) using GPU-friendly matrix operations, avoiding constraint-specific projectors. The method jointly learns the predictor and a positive-definite mobility, and achieves up to 144.3× inference speedups on second-order-cone model-predictive control (SOC-MPC) and 7.7× on a convex QCQP benchmark, with all test outputs satisfying a 10⁻³ feasibility tolerance. This work addresses a key bottleneck in learning-based decision-making: enforcing hard constraints at inference time without costly iterative repair. The combination of convergence guarantees, strict feasibility, and large speedups could make neural methods more practical for real-time control and optimization tasks such as power systems and model predictive control. The paper proves convergence of outer iterates at fixed dual depth and linear convergence in distance under Slater's condition and bounded subgradients. On QCQP, the mean objective gap is 0.012% with full test feasibility at 10⁻⁴, and learning mobility reduces the five-seed affine-task mean gap by 22.4%.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Constraint satisfaction in neural networks means ensuring outputs satisfy given constraints, such as physical limits or safety requirements. Traditional methods often use constraint-specific projections or iterative repair, which can be slow. Convex optimization provides a framework where problems have global optimality guarantees, and Slater's condition is a common constraint qualification ensuring strong duality. Model predictive control (MPC) with second-order cone constraints is a widely used control technique that requires solving convex optimization problems in real time.
