## [Role Grounding Attack exploits LLM agent memory via nested social interactions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38209) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.38209) formalizes the Role Grounding Attack (RGA), a vulnerability in which an attacker-designed nested conversation, shared as an experience-sharing post, causes a victim LLM agent to misattribute the attacker's preferences to its own user. The authors demonstrate two instantiations—tool selection manipulation and privacy leakage—and report high attack success rates across five mainstream memory systems and six language models. This work highlights a subtle but serious threat to LLM agents that learn from social platforms and persist memories, showing that memory poisoning can occur without explicit malicious instructions. As agents increasingly share experiences and make tool-calling decisions, such misattribution could lead to unauthorized tool use and sensitive data leakage, affecting both developers and end users. The attack works in two stages: during memory formation, the victim agent loses context binding when remembering preferences from a nested conversation and grounds the attacker's preference to its user; during retrieval, the misattributed preference persists and influences decisions. The privacy leakage variant combines a tool-call preference with a task-requirement preference, causing the victim to select the attacker's tool and include sensitive information in its arguments.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: LLM-based agents increasingly maintain long-term memory, often in vector databases, to recall past interactions and improve performance; this persistent memory introduces the risk of memory poisoning, where a single adversarial write can influence future behavior. Prompt injection and multi-agent prompt infection are related threats, but RGA specifically targets role-to-principal attribution—the mapping of whose preferences are being recorded—rather than injecting explicit instructions.

## [Skeleton Coding: Specify Program Structure First for AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38214) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv position paper (2610.38214) by Perona, Soatto, and Van den Broeck argues that behavioral specifications for coding agents cannot be determined a priori because they depend on the agent-chosen program structure, and proposes 'Skeleton Coding', where developers specify the structure in a high-level code-like format alongside behavioral specs. The authors model AI-assisted coding as a control problem and show theoretically that skeletons can exponentially reduce the number of tests needed, and empirically across four models and three benchmarks, the best skeletons reduce mean test error by 48.4% relative to the best end-to-end behavioral specifications. This work challenges the common practice of giving coding agents only end-to-end tests and I/O examples, showing that specification completeness is fundamentally tied to implementation structure. It could change how developers interact with AI coding tools, potentially reducing test-writing burden, narrowing the performance gap between small and large models, and lowering implementation cost by 15–26x. The paper reports that even when the agent can query a complete reference implementation, adding a skeleton reduces mean test error relatively by up to 27.0%, and skeletons narrow the average gap between small and large models by about 52.4% while reducing code erosion by 24.7% on average. As a position paper, it lacks empirical validation beyond the reported benchmarks and does not provide a formal user study.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Coding agents are AI systems that generate code from specifications such as tests and input-output examples. Program synthesis is the task of automatically deriving a program that satisfies a given specification, and a specification is complete if it uniquely determines the intended program. The paper argues that because agents first choose a program structure (decomposition into data types, modules, and functions), the same set of tests may be sufficient for one structure but leave another underdetermined, requiring different edge cases or exponentially more examples.

## [Coding agents follow repository precedent over new task intent, study finds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38244) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.38244) reports that across 5,625 controlled trials with four coding agents and six implementation pairs, agents overwhelmingly followed existing repository precedent when it conflicted with their own default choices (359/360 trials). The study also found that written priority rules were far more effective than code examples at overriding precedent, raising joint success from 38/60 to 59/60 in controlled settings and from 0/120 to 117/120 in real open-source repositories. This matters because coding agents are increasingly used to evolve existing codebases, and their tendency to mimic past patterns can silently override a developer's explicit intent, leading to unintended architectural drift. The findings suggest that teams should encode priorities and rationale as written rules, not just examples, to steer agents reliably in agentic software engineering workflows. Not all precedents carry equal weight: three supporting local files yielded 96% adoption versus only 4% for sibling-resource files, and merely changing file placement shifted adoption from 0% to 100% at a fixed example count. The study validated results in four open-source repositories across three programming languages, and the rule-based steering was effective when loaded via a harness.

Amazon Science researchers released Vendster, an evaluation arena that measures how a forecaster's bias and prediction-interval width affect a buyer-vendor discount negotiation between two LLM agents. Under-prediction bias significantly improves outcomes for more forecast-reactive agents (dose-response slopes -0.387 and -0.416, p<0.001), while interval width has no significant effect at zero bias; Vendster is released under CC BY-NC 4.0 on GitHub.

EPSBench introduces a benchmark of 149 firm-quarters across 86 US companies to evaluate LLM agents' ability to forecast quarterly earnings per share (EPS) from filings, transcripts, and news. ## [LLM-PowerTrace: Open Dataset of 100ms GPU Power Traces for AI Workloads](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38315) ⭐️ 7.0/10

LLM-PowerTrace introduces an open dataset of time-resolved, per-GPU power traces sampled every 100ms for LLM fine-tuning and inference across various NVIDIA platforms, paired with complete workload and system metadata. The dataset includes controlled sweeps over parameters such as batch size, sequence length, precision, parallelism, concurrency, GPU frequency, and quantization, and defines power-grid-facing metrics and scaling laws for extrapolation. This dataset addresses a critical gap in understanding sub-second power dynamics of AI compute, which are essential for data center infrastructure planning and power grid stability as AI workloads grow. It enables researchers and engineers to model, forecast, and manage the fast-changing electrical behavior of large-scale AI systems, potentially influencing energy-aware AI system design and grid integration strategies. The traces are sampled at 100ms resolution on varying NVIDIA platforms, capturing peaks, ramps, and synchronized fluctuations across accelerators. The dataset covers open model families across a wide range of sizes and includes fine-tuning methods with sweeps over batch size, sequence length, precision, parallelism, and checkpointing, as well as inference variations in concurrency, GPU frequency, KV-cache and weight quantization, prompt and output lengths, and request-arrival patterns.

## [Structured Memory Boosts Zero-Shot Vision-Language Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38318) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.38318) presents an 8B-scale zero-shot vision-language navigation agent that organizes memory into task, temporal, and spatial components, achieving the highest success rate among evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines on the R2R-CE val-unseen benchmark. Ablations show that removing temporal memory drops success rate and increases average path length from 16.9m to 39.1m, while removing the spatial-map and planning component also reduces success rate. This work provides concrete evidence that structured memory organization—rather than simply scaling model size—is critical for zero-shot navigation with smaller open models, which could make embodied AI more accessible and transferable to real-world robots. The real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 showing better transfer than a post-trained baseline suggest practical viability beyond simulation. The system uses an 8B observer to summarize observations and an 8B reasoner to select waypoint intents or request additional views, with a geometric controller executing targets; a semantic information perspective motivates distinguishing between retaining evidence, making it accessible, and acquiring new observations. The paper also introduces LAW2, a complementary evaluation using paired instruction interventions to assess instruction-following behavior beyond endpoint success.

The paper introduces a pose-aware diffusion prior learned from a single 2D projection per training sample, enabling extremely sparse-view CT reconstruction without dense 3D training volumes. This addresses the train-sparse/infer-sparse gap in medical imaging, where both scanning and dataset construction are limited by time, motion, or radiation constraints. The method learns from one 2D projection per training sample and uses three guidance terms during diffusion sampling: measured-view fidelity, shared-volume reprojection, and projection-physics consistency. Evaluated on two public CT datasets across 1-, 4-, and 8-view settings, it outperforms or matches baselines that use dense-volume supervision.

MUSE introduces a memory management framework that builds global, approach-level, and implementation-level memory from historical trajectories, injecting global and problem-matched approach memory at initialization and retrieving implementation-level lessons during execution via an LLM gate. Across four benchmarks covering numerical problem solving, kernel optimization, and scientific software repair, MUSE outperforms retrieval and memory baselines on all metrics, with ablations confirming the value of the multi-level design and gated injection. This work shows that task-level retrieval alone misses implementation lessons that become relevant mid-execution, and that selective runtime injection can yield consistent gains across diverse scientific coding tasks. It offers a practical blueprint for agent memory design that could improve LLM-based coding assistants in domains where procedural knowledge matters. The framework uses an LLM gate to select relevant experience and generate specific review advice or skip injection entirely, and transfer experiments show memory remains useful across kernel benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/hr-jin/MUSE, though the abstract does not report specific performance numbers or discuss overhead from the gating mechanism.

## [SpaceAct: New Benchmark Tests MLLMs on Closed-Loop 3D Spatiotemporal Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38405) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced SpaceAct, an interactive benchmark with 108 verified instances across 36 task families built on interlocking bricks and mechanical puzzles, alongside SAPA, a Spatiotemporal Active-Probing Agent framework. Unlike prior passive VQA benchmarks, SpaceAct requires models to rotate cameras to resolve occlusion, read in-scene rulers, output 6-DoF poses under collision and statics checks, and self-correct via split-screen rollback feedback. This benchmark shifts evaluation from static image description to closed-loop physical interaction, addressing a real gap in how multimodal LLMs are assessed for embodied AI. Results show that even with a valid plan, frontier models remain bottlenecked by 3D visual grounding and action refinement, highlighting where future research must focus. Across 10 frontier MLLMs on the 44 hardest instances, scores span 4.8–79.1, with seven models solving at most 27.3% of 6-DoF tasks; adding a reference plan (+plan) closes 44% of the gap for top models but leaves 5.2 collisions per episode, while adding exact 3D state (+state) closes 90% and cuts collisions to 0.5. Notably, 46% of failures are collision or observation loops, and the benchmark includes diagnostic modes such as no-camera, blind, and L7 levers.

## [RoleFUZZER: Fuzzing User Behavior to Test LLM Role Adherence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38438) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced RoleFUZZER, a framework that adapts coverage-guided fuzzing from software testing to search over plausible user behaviors that pressure LLMs into violating their system-prompt role specifications across multi-turn interactions. In 15 campaigns across five roles (tutor, financial advisor, AI interviewer, antagonistic roleplay character, and web agent), it achieved at least 89% coverage of a 64-cell behavior grid, while a free-form LLM baseline reached only 39–69% coverage with fewer violation types. This work addresses an understudied safety and alignment problem: whether role-conditioned LLMs actually adhere to their system-prompt specifications under realistic, potentially adversarial multi-turn user behavior. By providing a systematic, coverage-guided evaluation method, it could influence how role-based LLM applications are tested and hardened before deployment. The framework uses a user-behavior coverage grid that crosses a grounded taxonomy of user interaction types with the role specification under pressure, and it reveals that the same specification can fail in opposite directions—for example, open-weight target models override the player's safety signals on the antagonist role, while Claude Haiku 4.5 breaks character instead. The study is an early arXiv preprint with limited validation and no community discussion provided.

## [AtomSteer: Test-Time Constraint Steering for Atomistic Generative Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38517) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AtomSteer introduces a test-time inference framework that steers pretrained atomistic generative models with structural constraints via bounded local projections, graph-rigid stereochemical transformations, and periodic symmetry projections, accepting updates that improve constraint satisfaction while limiting changes to the rest of the structure. It is demonstrated across three pretrained backbones—FlowMM, ET-Flow, and Boltz-2—spanning de novo crystal generation, crystal structure prediction, molecular conformer generation, and protein-ligand complex structure prediction. This work provides a unified, retraining-free way to add chemical and crystallographic control to existing atomistic generative models, which could make them more practical for materials discovery and drug design where strict symmetry and stereochemistry requirements are critical. It affects researchers using diffusion and flow matching models for scientific discovery, as it improves constraint satisfaction without architectural changes. AtomSteer improves space-group distribution coverage in de novo crystal generation, target space-group recovery in crystal structure prediction, molecular validity and E/Z stereochemical accuracy while retaining conformer ensemble fidelity, and reduces ligand E/Z errors in protein-ligand complexes with competitive docking success and PoseBusters validity. The approach relies on bounded local projections and symmetry-aware corrections during sampling, accepting updates only when they improve constraint satisfaction while limiting changes to the rest of the structure.

This matters for organizations adopting generative AI, for policymakers concerned with workforce skills, and for AI/ML researchers studying human-AI interaction, because it offers a multilevel frame for governing adoption and a research agenda centered on longitudinal, multilevel measurement. The paper is an integrative narrative review rather than an empirical study, so its seven principles and five proposed organizational design levers are explicitly framed as proposals to be validated rather than established practice. ## [TERRA: Targeted Exploration for Efficient Rover Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38657) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TERRA is an online adaptation framework that guides exploration toward task-relevant model errors to efficiently adapt simulation-trained rover world models for deformable-terrain deployment. In simulation, it reaches approximately 90% slope-climbing success within five trials under severe out-of-distribution pretraining, and on the ERNEST rover it recovers coordinated active-suspension locomotion on a deformable Mars-simulant slope within three to five real-world trials. This work addresses the sim-to-real gap for planetary rovers operating on steep, deformable terrain where trial-and-error is costly, offering a sample-efficient adaptation method that could improve rover mobility and autonomy in future space missions. It also demonstrates a general approach for targeted exploration in model-based reinforcement learning that may transfer to other robotic systems with limited deployment data. ## [PACK3D fixes positional encoding failure in packed 3D attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38694) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PACK3D introduces a local-global attention operator that decouples memory layout from geometric structure by applying axial RoPE on true token-grid coordinates instead of packed sequence positions. Experiments show that standard packed-sequence RoPE collapses under Morton, block-contiguous, and random repacking, while axial grid-coordinate RoPE remains exact and improves performance on Allen WTC-11 hiPSC microscopy. This work identifies a general failure mode in attention over packed geometric data, where positional mechanisms learn memory layout rather than object geometry, and offers a principled fix that is trainable at scale. It is relevant to 3D vision and efficient transformer research, potentially enabling more robust and spatially interpretable models for volumetric data. PACK3D keeps local neighborhood attention exact, compresses only distant context into contiguous 3D block summaries, and applies axial RoPE before block summarization so that query-to-summary logits remain weighted sums of query-relative 3D displacements. A fused Triton implementation matches windowed-attention latency at 65k tokens while providing long-range context that windowing cannot.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Packing a 3D volume into a token sequence is a common technique for efficient attention, but it destroys the correspondence between sequence order and spatial geometry. Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE) encode position by rotating query and key vectors, and axial RoPE extends this to multiple dimensions by applying rotations per axis. PACK3D builds on local-global attention, which combines exact local attention with compressed global context, to address the geometry mismatch introduced by packing.

The paper introduces GUIDER, a method that jointly optimizes a decision flow controller and a reasoning policy to train models on clinical guidelines. On the MedGUIDE benchmark, GUIDER with Qwen3-14B achieves 82.5 weighted accuracy and 73.5 guideline adherence, outperforming the strongest clinical reinforcement learning baseline by 3.3 and 3.1 points respectively. This work addresses two key challenges in using clinical guidelines for process supervision: the path-answer gap and path multiplicity. By enabling more accurate and guideline-adherent clinical reasoning, GUIDER could improve the reliability of AI systems in healthcare decision support. GUIDER computes process rewards over multiple controller-generated flows to account for path multiplicity, and gates these rewards on answer correctness to address the path-answer gap. It also improves over CRPO, MRPO, and FaithMed on out-of-domain benchmarks AMEGA-LLM, RealMedQA, and CancerGUIDE with Qwen3-14B and Gemma4-12B backbones.

## [AtomTree: Hierarchical LLM Framework for State-Aware Embodied Instruction Following](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38744) ⭐️ 7.0/10

AtomTree is a hierarchical framework that incrementally builds a tree of subgoals and actions, with the LLM deciding at each step from the current symbolic state whether to decompose further or output a grounded low-level action. It includes a lightweight memory module and triggers hierarchical backtracking replanning when actions stall, and in zero-shot evaluation on the ALFRED benchmark it outperforms prior LLM-based planners. This work addresses key limitations of existing LLM planners—single-pass planning, commitment to initial plans, and failure-driven updates—by introducing state-aware incremental decision-making and backtracking, which could improve robustness for long-horizon embodied tasks. It offers a valuable technical contribution to the embodied AI and robotics communities, though it is not a fundamental breakthrough. The LLM makes decisions based on the current symbolic state, and a lightweight memory module summarizes past outcomes for reuse; when a low-level action stalls, hierarchical backtracking returns to the parent node and regenerates the subtree plan from the latest state to prevent drift. Evaluation is zero-shot on the ALFRED benchmark, and a project page is available at https://zhaihaotian.github.io/atomtree-website/.

**Background**: Embodied instruction following requires an agent to interpret natural language commands and execute long-horizon tasks in interactive environments, which is a core challenge in robotics and AI. ## [CopyLoop: Training-Free Decoding Speedup for Looped Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38822) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CopyLoop is a training-free decoding algorithm that proposes multi-token suffixes by copying from repeated context and screens them early at a shallow recurrent depth, achieving 2.98x–10.70x speedups over full-depth autoregressive decoding on Base models and 2.74x–3.52x on Thinking models across six checkpoints from the Ouro, Raven, and Huginn families. Looped Transformers trade memory for recurrent computation, but their sequential full-depth decoding is a major latency bottleneck; CopyLoop shows that substantial inference speedups are possible without retraining or a separate draft model, making looped architectures more practical for deployment in code generation and multi-step reasoning tasks. The method combines low-cost context-copy proposals with shallow screening and continuous recurrent scheduling, processing newer blocks concurrently while earlier blocks progress toward full-depth verification; ablations confirm strong synergy between shallow screening and continuous scheduling, and speedups grow on longer generations with reusable contexts, though only lightweight model calibration is required.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Looped Transformers (also called recurrent-depth models) repeatedly apply a shared block of layers, increasing computation per token without adding parameters; examples include ByteDance's Ouro, which loops the entire 48-layer stack, and Huginn, which loops only a 4-layer core. Because each loop depends on the previous one, decoding latency scales with recurrent depth. Speculative decoding is a related inference optimization where a smaller draft model proposes multiple tokens that a larger model verifies in one pass, preserving output quality while cutting latency.

The paper introduces Curriculum of Models (CoM), a reinforcement learning method that trains an investigator model against a sequence of progressively less compliant versions of a target model, starting from one that rarely refuses harmful requests and advancing to the original safety-trained target. When trained on multiple behaviors simultaneously, the CoM-trained investigator can elicit held-out behaviors, but PRBO-trained investigators achieve higher success rates. FlipJev introduces a fast black-box, query-based red-teaming attack that finds short universal adversarial suffixes flipping confident answers of Jev, a representative typed decision model, within minutes. A new arXiv paper trains hundreds of introspectors across three low-level signal types and eight language models, finding that standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) leads to 'causal bypass' where self-reports rely on spuriously correlated signals rather than the actual internal state. The study focuses on lower-level signals, such as a single neuron activation, because they allow precise interventions, serving as a minimal prerequisite before understanding more complex introspection. This theoretical insight connects two-player game dynamics with single-policy training and could lead to more efficient exploration in GFlowNets, impacting researchers in generative modeling and reinforcement learning who rely on diverse high-reward sampling. The paper shows that standard semi-gradient updates treat the sampling distribution as fixed, while the full gradient reduces observed balance errors by avoiding high-error regions, which is anti-exploratory; NRD ties the parameters of an adversarial game to recover a single-policy dynamic that extends exploration without a separate teacher or auxiliary policy.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Generative Flow Networks (GFlowNets) are generative models that learn to sample discrete objects proportionally to a target reward, making them useful for scientific discovery where diverse high-reward candidates are desired. They are trained by minimizing balance errors over sampled trajectories, so correctness depends on exploration: if a region is never visited, balance cannot be enforced there. Standard training uses a semi-gradient update that ignores the effect of parameter changes on the sampling distribution, and this paper analyzes the full gradient to reveal a previously overlooked anti-exploratory mechanism.

## [Aligning Facts with Second-Hop Retrieval Closes Compositionality Gap in GPT-2-like Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39016) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.39016) shows that a GPT-2-like transformer trained from scratch on a two-hop reasoning task can transfer compositional behavior to out-of-distribution (OOD) atomic facts if the training distribution is modified so that both in-distribution (ID) and OOD facts are positionally aligned with the second-hop retrieval step of a learned compositional circuit. This intervention requires no architectural changes or additional OOD compositional supervision, and it closes the observed compositionality gap in the controlled setting. This work provides evidence that the compositionality gap is not a fundamental architectural limitation of transformers and can be addressed through mechanistically informed training data design, which could influence how future models are trained for better out-of-distribution generalization without increasing model size or adding supervision. The study is limited to a controlled two-hop reasoning setting with a GPT-2-like model trained from scratch, so it remains to be seen whether the findings generalize to larger models and more complex, naturalistic reasoning tasks. The intervention specifically targets the positional alignment of atomic facts with the second-hop retrieval step of a previously identified compositional circuit.

In transformer language models, compositional generalization refers to the ability to combine known facts in novel ways, and a persistent challenge is that models often fail to apply learned compositions to out-of-distribution knowledge. ## [Entropy Shape Correlation Reveals What On-Policy Distillation Learns](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39020) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces the entropy shape (the sequence of next-token entropies) and Entropy Shape Correlation (ESC) to measure student-teacher agreement in entropy shape, showing that on-policy distillation (OPD) transfers not only which tokens to consider ('how to branch') but also where to keep reasoning paths open ('where to branch'). By intervening on a teacher's entropy while preserving its token preferences, the authors demonstrate that 'where to branch' causally drives OPD gains independently of 'how to branch', and that pre-OPD ESC can select the best teacher for both students, outperforming existing predictors. This work provides a novel mechanistic understanding of why stronger teachers sometimes fail to improve students in OPD, offering a practical metric (ESC) for teacher selection and outcome prediction that could improve post-training efficiency for large language models. It is valuable for ML researchers working on knowledge distillation and LLM post-training. The existing token-overlap metric only captures 'how to branch', while ESC captures 'where to branch'; the authors track ESC throughout training and show it causally drives gains via controlled interventions on teacher entropy. The code is available at https://github.com/maybenotime/opd-esc, and the evaluation protocol formulates OPD outcome prediction as a teacher selection task.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a post-training technique where a student model learns from a teacher's dense token-level supervision on trajectories generated by the student's own evolving policy, addressing the mismatch between fixed demonstrations and deployment histories. Next-token entropy measures a model's uncertainty at each position, and its sequence over a generation forms an 'entropy shape' that reflects where the model is confident or uncertain. Prior work noted that a stronger teacher may fail to improve the student, attributing it to a lack of new knowledge, but the nature of that knowledge was unclear.

## [Overparameterization Needed to Make Targets Detectable via Gradients](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39027) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces an oracle model of neural network learning and uses Kolmogorov n-widths to quantify effective representation complexity, proving a task-agnostic lower bound on the initial effective width required for target-dependent gradient information to become detectable. For k-sparse parity in D dimensions, it shows a polynomial separation between the width needed to represent the target and the width needed to discover it, with a sharper unsigned critical scale of Θ̃_k(D^{k-1}τ²). This work provides a theoretical explanation for why overparameterization is necessary during training, not just for final representation, and connects representation complexity to gradient-based discovery. It offers ML theory researchers a new framework for understanding transient complexity and width-time trade-offs in learning. The analysis combines complexity bounds transferred from forward representations to gradient-query features with statistical-query lower bounds, and interprets precision through accumulation over fresh samples to yield a width-time frontier. Experiments support the predicted dimension dependence but show that optimization and generalization depart from the idealized frontier.

## [CGSE: Critic-Guided Synthetic Experience in Latent World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39100) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes Critic-Guided Synthetic Experience (CGSE), a method that augments an offline dataset by sampling candidate actions from an offline policy, refining each action to maximize a first-order approximation of the Q-function within a trust region, and then using a frozen latent world model to imagine the next state for each refined action. The critic selects the best synthetic transition, which is appended to the replay buffer, and on three OGBench manipulation tasks CGSE improves an offline policy by a relative 7.1% on average success rate. This work addresses the compounding error problem in latent world model rollouts by using the world model only as a local transition generator rather than for long-horizon imagination, which could make offline reinforcement learning more scalable without costly or unsafe real-world interaction. The approach is relevant to practitioners working on offline RL, model-based RL, and data augmentation for robotics and control tasks. CGSE requires no additional real-environment interaction or test-time planner, as it generates synthetic experience entirely offline using the world model. The action refinement is performed within a trust region to avoid deviating too far from the offline policy, and the method is evaluated on three OGBench manipulation tasks with a relative improvement of 7.1% in average success rate.

**Background**: Offline reinforcement learning aims to learn policies from fixed datasets without online interaction, but collecting new experience can be costly or unsafe. World models learn a dynamics model that can generate imagined experience, yet rolling out these models over long horizons suffers from compounding errors that degrade policy learning. Trust regions constrain policy updates to stay close to the behavior policy, and Q-functions estimate the value of actions; CGSE combines these ideas to refine actions locally within a world model.

## [PCM: Proof-Carrying Messages to Secure Multi-Agent AI Communication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39109) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose Proof-Carrying Messages (PCM), a protocol where each claim from an AI agent must be backed by cryptographically verifiable evidence from an append-only Merkle log and signed attestations. On a benchmark of 926 messages containing 712 lies, PCM accepted only 10 (1.4%), all stale evidence, while plain A2A accepted all 712 and six deployed protocol models accepted 504–712. This addresses a critical security gap in multi-agent systems: prompt-injected agents can fabricate facts and authority that propagate unchecked through agent networks. PCM's offline verification and three-valued claim results could become a foundation for trustworthy agent-to-agent communication as A2A and MCP adoption grows. PCM uses Merkle log inclusion proofs, signed attestations from signers the agent cannot control, and narrowing grant chains rooted in recorded human approvals; claims resting only on the agent's own report are never proven. Verification is offline, takes about 1 ms, and two independent verifiers agreed on all 926 verdicts, though the work is an arXiv preprint with no adoption yet.

**Background**: Multi-agent AI systems let agents delegate tasks and share results, but protocols like A2A and MCP authenticate only the communication channel, not the truth of the sender's claims. Merkle logs are append-only, hash-chained data structures that provide tamper-evident inclusion proofs, commonly used in Certificate Transparency.

LatentDiff is a new framework that reformulates triple set prediction (TSP) in knowledge graphs as latent space graph generation, using a relation-aware residual-quantized autoencoder and an observation-anchored latent diffusion model. It outperforms state-of-the-art methods by an average of 5.4 percentage points in F_tsp on three benchmark datasets. This work addresses key limitations of the dominant subgraph-based paradigm, such as fragmented structural reasoning and missing cross-subgraph dependencies, by enabling unified global reasoning over the entire graph. It could significantly improve knowledge graph completion, benefiting applications like question answering and recommendation systems. The autoencoder encodes the whole graph into relation-aware latent embeddings, quantizes them with chunked residual codebooks, and reconstructs triples via a factorized decoder. The diffusion model perturbs the target latent toward the observed latent and recovers missing triples through progressive denoising.

## [REALM: Dependency-Graph Method Enforces Least Privilege for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39155) ⭐️ 7.0/10

REALM (Required Execution Assets Linked to a Mission) is a new arXiv preprint that represents a task's required assets as dependency-graph nodes, resolves prerequisite relationships, and admits newly discovered assets through source-scoped selection, separating asset discovery from authorization. Evaluated on 60 clean tasks and 560 injected cases in AgentDyn with qwen3.5-flash, it completes 40.0% and 36.4% of tasks respectively while reducing attack success rate from 16.6% to 0.2%. LLM agents are routinely granted broader access to files, accounts, and services than a task requires, and prompt injection exploits this excess access to redirect execution toward unrelated resources. REALM's approach shows that enforcing least privilege at the asset level can sharply cut injection success while preserving the agent's freedom to choose its computation, which is directly relevant to enterprise agent deployments. The design splits responsibilities: the REALM Builder maintains selected grants and projects Asset Files, while the Partial API Manager exposes resource-bound Partial APIs to the agent inside a Task Container. Notably, task completion rates of 40.0% and 36.4% indicate a substantial utility cost, and the evaluation is limited to a single base model and the AgentDyn benchmark.

**Background**: Prompt injection is a class of attack in which malicious instructions embedded in content the model reads cause it to take unintended actions; against agents, the damage extends to every system the agent can reach. The least privilege principle, long standard in information security, holds that a process should receive only the access needed for its specific task, and researchers are now adapting it to LLM agents through frameworks like MiniScope. ## [PRISM: Personalized Item Embeddings in User History for Sequential Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39175) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PRISM introduces personalized item representations in user history by generating user-relative item embeddings via an autoencoder that compresses layer states from a user tower, a user-item tower, and same-request candidate mixing into one embedding per scored pair. Offline evaluation on Surface 1, a billion-scale recommendation surface, shows an average downstream normalized entropy (NE) change of -0.15%, compared to -0.07% for VISTA at similar history lengths. This work makes personalization a property of the history inputs themselves, supplying richer evidence for sequence modeling and potentially improving recommendation quality at scale. It also identifies a sequence-length scaling law, suggesting that personalized item representations provide a new scaling dimension for sequential recommenders. The autoencoder jointly compresses all layer states from multiple towers into one embedding per scored pair for downstream replay, reusing upstream ranking computation. Over history lengths of 26–240 events, the NE gain follows a fitted power law with exponent 0.468, increasing from 0.06% to 0.17%.

**Background**: Sequential recommenders typically build user history from item identifiers or content features using a shared embedding map, so the same item gets the same initial embedding for all users. Item embeddings are dense vector representations learned from user-item interactions or metadata, and autoencoders are neural networks that learn compressed representations by encoding and reconstructing data. PRISM changes this by making item embeddings user-relative within the history, so the same item can have different representations depending on the user's relationship to it.

EmbodiExp introduces outcome-grounded subgoal experiences, each specifying a subgoal, applicability conditions, an adaptable policy, and a verifiable outcome, and composes them online during task execution. The framework uses subgoal-level outcome attribution to extract verified local successes and condition-specific guidance from failed trajectories, and verified outcomes can establish preconditions for subsequent experiences, enabling online composition. ## [Textual Personas Fail to Make Vision-Language Models See Like Described Individuals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39331) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.39331) shows that prompting vision-language models with textual personas such as 'You have low vision' does not replicate the perceptual effects of actual visual impairments. Across 14 models, describing blur left recognition unchanged, while actually blurring the image lowered performance as it does for people. This finding challenges the growing practice of using persona-prompted VLMs as stand-ins for people with disabilities in user studies and accessibility research. It suggests such simulations may erase real differences between groups and individuals, undermining the validity of accessibility evaluations built on them. The persona never outperformed simple rules based only on the facts stated in the persona, and inside open models the description changed neither the image information nor the answer probabilities. Yet the models could correctly estimate how blur and illusions affect people, indicating they know the effects they fail to exhibit.

A new arXiv paper identifies a critical evaluation flaw in Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) called semantic mismapping, where global Hungarian matching reassigns anchored old-category indices, leading to overestimation of new-category accuracy by up to 25.63 points. The authors propose a permutation-cycle condition to characterize when this occurs and introduce Semantics-Preserving Evaluation (SPE) and Mismapping-Mitigating Optimization (MMO) to address the issue. The proposed solutions could lead to more reliable benchmarks and fairer comparisons in open-world recognition research. The paper theoretically derives a permutation-cycle condition that explains when semantic mismapping can artificially inflate the global matching score, and shows that minimizing the proposed region-balance loss (RBL) and novel-diversity loss (NDL) tightens an upper bound on spurious accuracy gains with controllable residual terms. Empirical results under both global Hungarian matching and the new SPE protocol demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

## [SymKL: A Unified Representation-Space Measure of Signal Degradation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39403) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SymKL introduces a modality-agnostic full-reference degradation measure that fits an implicit neural representation (INR) to a pristine signal and compares the diagonal Fisher information profiles of the reference and degraded observation via symmetric KL divergence. The authors derive an exact closed-form expression for the diagonal Fisher of SIREN, enabling efficient computation, and demonstrate on image, speech, and volumetric 3D benchmarks that SymKL tracks degradation severity monotonically where conventional metrics saturate or fail. Existing full-reference measures such as PSNR, SSIM, or their audio counterparts are inherently modality-specific, forcing practitioners to use different metrics for images, audio, and 3D data. A single unified measure could simplify benchmarking and quality assessment across signal processing and representation learning, and the Fisher-information formulation opens a new connection between degradation quantification and the information geometry of learned representations. SymKL requires only the reference and degraded observation, with no knowledge of the corruption process or degradation severity, and it relies on the diagonal (not full) Fisher information matrix to keep computation tractable. The code is promised to be released after the review process, so results are not yet independently reproducible.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Implicit neural representations (INRs) encode a signal as the weights of a neural network that maps coordinates to signal values, yielding continuous, differentiable, and resolution-independent representations; SIREN is a popular INR variant using sinusoidal activation functions. The Fisher information matrix characterizes the local geometry of a model's parameter space, and its diagonal entries measure the sensitivity of individual parameters; because the full matrix is expensive, practitioners often use only the diagonal. The Kullback–Leibler divergence measures the difference between two probability distributions but is asymmetric, so a symmetric version (the sum of both directions) is often used as a distance-like measure.

The paper presents safe multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) algorithms that guarantee zero constraint violation throughout learning for both cumulative and stepwise constraints. By combining optimistic reward estimates with pessimistic cost bounds, the algorithms achieve an O~(1/√T) suboptimality gap under smooth Tchebycheff scalarization, and a preference-free variant attains O~(1/√T + 1/√K) with the same safety guarantee. This is the first sample-efficient MORL algorithm that guarantees safety for every executed policy, addressing a critical gap in deploying RL to real-world systems where constraint violations during learning are unacceptable. It impacts safety-critical applications such as robotics and autonomous systems that must balance conflicting objectives under strict safety requirements. The algorithms require knowledge of a strictly feasible policy and its costs, but the authors relax this requirement at the cost of at most constant cumulative violation. The analysis relies on averaged occupancy measures and smooth Tchebycheff scalarization to derive the convergence rates.

The paper identifies that standard test-time batch normalization in intermediate-fusion cooperative perception mixes statistics from clean and corrupted agents, degrading even the clean ego vehicle's detection by 3.58 to 6.68 AP@0.5 points. AgentNorm requires no gradients or labels, is independent of test-frame order, and runs locally on each agent without changing transmitted features; it outperforms pooled normalization by 5.53-12.94 points under fog and motion blur and beats pooled normalization in all ten infrastructure-corruption settings on the real-world DAIR-V2X-C dataset. ## [Intrinsic Distribution Matching Adds Gaussian Moment Constraints to DMD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39633) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Intrinsic Distribution Matching (IDM), which augments distribution matching distillation (DMD) with explicit Gaussian moment constraints on feature means and per-coordinate standard deviations, using the generator's EMA copy instead of an external feature encoder. Experiments on Z-Image-Turbo 6B and Qwen-Image 20B show IDM reaches 94.25% and 90.20% on Chinese and English LongText-Bench at two network evaluations, the highest among compared methods at that budget. This work offers a principled way to improve one-step and few-step text-to-image generation by adding moment matching to DMD, potentially leading to faster and more faithful image synthesis. It could benefit researchers and practitioners working on diffusion distillation and efficient generative models. The method decomposes the reverse-KL field into a Gaussian moment component and a non-Gaussian residual, constraining only the statistics that can be explicitly matched. Ablations show the added moment loss yields gains, and generator EMA features perform competitively with an external DINOv2 encoder across five reported metrics.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Distribution matching distillation (DMD) is a technique that distills a multi-step diffusion model into a one-step or few-step generator by minimizing the reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence between the generated and reference distributions, typically using score differences. The reverse KL divergence is mode-seeking and can be decomposed into moment and residual components. Exponential moving average (EMA) of generator weights is a standard practice in generative models to stabilize training and improve sample quality.

A new arXiv paper proposes representing a research field's open problems as structured, provenance-linked data in a two-layer knowledge graph, using an LLM constrained to candidate sets to extract, ground, and assess problem status across curated catalogs in database and AI research. This work demonstrates a practical approach to turning prose problem lists into queryable data, which could significantly improve research tooling and knowledge management by enabling queries about recent workers, untouched problems, and methods tried. ## [ZEST-Search: Zero-Label Co-Evolution Training for Tool-Efficient Search Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39682) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ZEST-Search introduces a zero-label, tool-efficient framework for training search agents via heterogeneous co-evolution, where a proposer adaptively generates validated search tasks online around the solver's evolving capability boundary while the solver learns search-augmented reasoning through reinforcement learning. Experiments on seven general-domain and multi-hop QA benchmarks show consistent performance gains and higher tool efficiency without any labeled search-training data or expert search trajectories. This work addresses two key challenges in search-agent training: the inability of fixed or labeled task collections to adapt as agents improve, and the tension between answer accuracy and tool efficiency in outcome-only reinforcement learning. By eliminating the need for labeled data and expert trajectories, ZEST-Search could make training deep search agents more scalable and cost-effective, impacting researchers and practitioners building LLM-based retrieval-augmented agents. The framework uses an answer-first and evidence-path-guided generation process to construct validated tasks from unlabeled reference questions, and employs an intermediate-difficulty reward for the proposer and a task-local tool-aware reward for the solver to jointly optimize task difficulty and search efficiency. The approach is evaluated on seven benchmarks, but as an arXiv preprint, it has not yet undergone peer review.

## [InferD: A Honeypot Framework for AI Inference Infrastructure](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39807) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers present InferD, a low-interaction honeypot framework that faithfully emulates AI inference services—including model inventories, token formats, tool-call protocols, and authorization flows—while never performing actual model inference or tool execution. The framework is organized around a principle called 'deception without inference,' answering every observable request from static response pools and decomposing emulation into four deception planes plus a provenance plane. LLM serving stacks, commercial inference APIs, vector databases, and agent orchestration gateways are now exposed on the public internet and indexed by scanners within hours, yet existing honeypot frameworks were designed for conventional network services. InferD provides a principled way to measure threats against this emerging AI infrastructure surface, which is valuable to both security and ML systems practitioners. InferD decomposes emulation into four deception planes—transport, service protocol, vulnerability surface, and agentic session—and adds a provenance plane that links a planted credential to evidence of downstream model-mediated processing. As a low-interaction honeypot, it offers limited interaction and does not expose real components, and it is an academic framework without community discussion provided.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: A low-interaction honeypot is a software system that emulates one or more services to attract scans and opportunistic probes without exposing real components of the underlying operating system. LLM serving stacks are multi-layer systems that handle requests and stream tokens back, and tool-call protocols such as MCP and UTCP define how tools are presented to models and how calls are returned. InferD adapts the honeypot concept to this AI-specific surface, where faithful emulation of model inventories, token formats, and agentic sessions is required without running any real computation.

## [MedCBR Aligns Medical Vision-Language Models at Capability Boundary](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39835) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MedCBR introduces a two-stage alignment framework that combines Difficulty Weighted Boundary Preference Optimization (DBPO) with Entropy Gated Grounded Policy Optimization (EGPO) to improve medical vision-language models at their capability frontier. Experiments on six medical benchmarks show consistent gains over strong general, specialized, and reinforcement learning baselines, reaching 61.2% average accuracy with the largest improvements on challenging differential diagnosis tasks. Current medical vision-language models are often aligned with objectives that reward the wrong behavior, such as letting easy cases dominate updates or allowing answer shortcuts through sparse final-answer rewards. MedCBR's focus on clinically critical boundary cases and verifiable anatomical grounding could lead to more trustworthy diagnostic reasoning, affecting medical AI developers and clinicians who rely on such models. The framework constructs counterfactual boundary preferences using empirical pass rates and preference pairs that share reasoning prefixes but diverge at decisive diagnostic branches, while EGPO rewards answer correctness, anatomical grounding, and reasoning fidelity according to prediction entropy. Ablations show super-additive gains, with the combined two stages exceeding the sum of their individual improvements.

## [MASCAL: Calibrated Confidence for Multi-Agent Collaboration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39927) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MASCAL enables each agent in a multi-agent system to learn a calibrated correctness probability for its answers by jointly optimizing task performance and confidence calibration via reinforcement learning. The upstream agent passes this probability at handoff, giving downstream agents a quantitative basis for trust decisions, and the final answer also carries a calibrated probability. This work addresses a key gap in multi-agent systems where upstream answers vary in correctness and downstream agents lack quantitative signals to decide whether to trust or verify them. By improving both accuracy and calibration across three collaboration architectures, MASCAL enhances the reliability and interpretability of multi-agent decision-making for complex tasks like multi-hop question answering. MASCAL introduces confidence-aware weighting, which increases the learning weight at positions responsive to the upstream probability, so the downstream agent learns more from decisions where it actively uses the signal. The method generalizes to deeper collaboration chains and different model scales, and intervention analysis confirms that upstream confidence affects downstream decision behavior, supporting selective answering and targeted rechecking.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Confidence calibration in machine learning refers to the property that a model's predicted probability matches the empirical frequency of correctness—for example, predictions made with 80% confidence should be correct about 80% of the time. Multi-hop question answering is a complex NLP task that requires integrating scattered evidence across multiple documents through sequential reasoning steps. Multi-agent systems tackle such tasks by dividing work among specialized agents, but without calibrated confidence, downstream agents must judge the reliability of upstream answers based solely on textual evidence.

## [Optimal Privacy Budget Allocation for DP-SGD via Control Theory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39954) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper formulates the allocation of a fixed privacy budget across DP-SGD iterations as an open-loop optimal control problem under composed zCDP and introduces Privacy-Budget Adjoint Mirror Descent (PB-AMD). It proves that every local minimizer exhausts the certified budget, yielding an exact-budget simplex formulation, and establishes budget stability and stationarity guarantees. This work bridges certified privacy accounting and optimization by showing how to schedule noise variance to maximize utility under a fixed privacy budget, which could improve model accuracy for privacy-preserving machine learning in domains like healthcare and finance. It provides a principled alternative to heuristic allocation rules such as uniform or square-root schedules. PB-AMD combines pathwise adjoint gradients with entropic mirror updates to preserve positivity and enforce the budget exactly at each iteration, and a linear-quadratic reduction yields an explicit square-root allocation law. Experiments show tracking improvements over several allocation rules and lower schedule-optimization times than projected gradient descent, though the guarantees rely on regularity and coercivity assumptions.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD) trains models by clipping per-sample gradients and adding Gaussian noise at each step, with privacy accounting bounding the total privacy cost. Zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) is a variant that composes cleanly, making it convenient for tracking cumulative privacy loss across iterations. However, standard accounting does not specify how to distribute a fixed budget over training to maximize utility.

## [New Exact Polynomial-Space Algorithms for Max 2-SAT via Accumulated Pruning Constraints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39992) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces deterministic polynomial-space algorithms that solve Max 2-SAT exactly in time O*(2^{(1-γ)n}) for a fixed γ>0 on several classes of instances, including formulas with many biased variables, semirandom 2-CNF formulas, and Max-Cut on regular expander graphs and stochastic block model graphs. The key technique extends the classic DPLL branching algorithm by accumulating pruning constraints derived from comparing the two values of a variable when the search assigns it its less promising value. This provides the first polynomial-space algorithms with such running times for nontrivial classes of dense Max 2-SAT instances, improving exponential time bounds and potentially impacting exact algorithm design for NP-hard optimization problems. The pruning constraints are general and can be added to any branching algorithm for Max 2-SAT, suggesting practical relevance beyond the studied classes. For semirandom formulas and block-model graphs, the algorithms remain exact on every input while the time bound holds with high probability over the input; the clause density may grow with n. The pruning constraints are expected to be particularly useful for sparse formulas where each constraint involves only a few variables.

DPLL is a classic complete backtracking-based search algorithm for SAT that branches on variables and propagates assignments. The paper builds on DPLL by adding learned constraints that prune the search space, achieving improved exponential-time bounds for exact solving.

## [EpiCoach: LLM agent runs auditable N-of-1 training experiments for one athlete](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40370) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers present EpiCoach, an LLM-agent system that treats a single cross-country mountain biker as the subject of accountable N-of-1 science, storing claims in an evidence-gated hypothesis registry where each claim must issue a probabilistic prediction before a session and only updates through computed evidence from logged statistical fits. The agent prescribes each training week as a constrained experiment maximizing information gain around two instrument rides, using a mechanistic digital twin built from heart rate, GPS and barometric altitude data, and in a live three-week phase the ledger sealed 20 predictions, scored 14, and the safety officer vetoed the agent twice. This work shows how agentic AI can make personal health personalization auditable and falsifiable rather than opaque, which matters for digital health because wearable-based coaching currently offers recommendations that cannot be checked or corrected. It also demonstrates a practical template for combining Bayesian experimental design with LLM agents in a safety-constrained loop, relevant to researchers and developers building personalized health tools. The digital twin combines a lagged heart-rate response model, a fitness-fatigue model with learned time constants, and a latent technical-descending skill state measured on discovered trail segments; in an eighteen-month rolling-origin replay the twin beat standard forecasters on heart rate but not segment time, and the agentic loop matched a static model. The study is limited to a single subject, and the live prospective phase covered only three weeks, with the climb forecast remaining pessimistic as the athlete improved.

## [SCARL aligns LLM confidence with rewards in RLVR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40407) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SCARL (Sequence Confidence-Aligned Reinforcement Learning) reshapes each advantage in RLVR using the alignment gap between a response's group-relative confidence and its certified outcome, without changing the advantage's sign. On Qwen3-4B-Base it improves average Pass@32 by 2.4 points over DAPO and outperforms nine compute-matched methods on coverage and per-draw accuracy. This addresses a fundamental misalignment in RLVR where a policy's confidence is not tied to its reward, causing barely-found successes and confident errors to receive inappropriate updates. The method also mitigates entropy collapse, potentially improving exploration and reasoning reliability for LLM post-training. SCARL provably reduces to its base estimator when confidences within a class agree, adds no extra forward passes and only one hyperparameter. Applied unchanged across four estimators and four backbones, it improves 14 of 16 settings while preserving policy entropy and widening the confidence-correctness separation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains language models by scoring sampled responses with a rule-based verifier and reinforcing those that pass, and has been used in models like DeepSeek-R1. Group-relative methods such as DAPO compute advantages by comparing responses within a group, but the advantage signal ignores the model's confidence in each response. SCARL introduces a confidence-alignment term to reshape advantages so that responses with the same advantage are driven toward equal confidence.

## [TextSeal2: Distortion-Free LLM Watermarking with Copula Mixing and Memoryless Races](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40613) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TextSeal2 introduces a distortion-free watermark for large language models that merges multiple keys into a single virtual key via a Gaussian copula and uses memoryless exponential races to preserve the watermark under speculative decoding. It detects 8 to 22 percentage points more 100-token answers than its predecessor TextSeal at equal diversity and a false-positive rate of 10^-3, and 18 to 22 percentage points more 200-token answers under speculative decoding. This work addresses a key practical barrier to deploying watermarks in production LLM serving: compatibility with speculative decoding, which is widely used to reduce inference latency. By preserving detection strength without sacrificing output diversity or adding latency, TextSeal2 makes robust watermarking more viable for AI safety and content provenance at scale. TextSeal2 verifies keyed drafts with one additional exponential race run on the leftovers of the draft races; by memorylessness, this reproduces block verification so the output follows the target model exactly. It requires no post-logits optimization and is comparable to textGrain, and any number of keys, including publicly shared keys, can be merged without diluting detection.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Watermarking LLMs embeds a detectable statistical signal in generated text to identify machine-generated content. The Gumbel-max (exponential) watermark is a popular decoding-based scheme with strong detectability, but it can reduce output diversity; TextSeal addressed this by routing tokens to one of two keys via a coin flip, though the detector then averages scores without knowing which key was used. Speculative decoding accelerates inference by having a draft model propose tokens that the target model verifies in parallel, and watermarks must survive this process without changing the acceptance rate. A Gaussian copula is a statistical tool for coupling random variables while preserving their marginal distributions, used here to mix keys with fresh noise.

## [Probing Visual Foundation Models for Persistent Spatial State](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40636) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper probes ten visual foundation model representations via frozen-feature probes to test whether they encode a persistent spatial state supporting object persistence, predictive updates, and actionability under egocentric streaming observations. It introduces a four-level capability framework—spatial structure, object persistence, predictive spatial update, and actionability—and finds that strong readout of the visible scene does not ensure accurate object persistence or future-feature retrieval. This work challenges the assumption that strong scene recognition implies spatial understanding, which is critical for embodied AI and robotics where agents must track objects beyond the current view. It suggests that current visual foundation models may lack the persistent, predictive spatial representations needed for reliable goal-directed action. The study uses matched controls to separate readout accuracy from reliance on visual history and motion, and finds that object persistence and actionability build on camera-pose readout, whereas feature prediction builds on visible-scene readout. Native future prediction retains recoverable spatial structure, but a spatial reader trained on real features does not transfer unchanged to predicted features.

## [SpecSlot: Role-Coupled Tokenization Cuts Global Attention Cost in Pixel-Space Generative Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40647) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SpecSlot introduces a role-coupled tokenization scheme that expands each spatial anchor into multiple DCT-band slots, keeping only the lowest-frequency slot in global attention while modeling high-frequency detail locally. On ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over a FLOPs-matched JiT control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and on text-to-image generation it surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost. This work decouples output detail from global attention sequence length, offering a way to scale pixel-space generative Transformers to finer detail without quadratic attention cost. It could influence efficient attention design and tokenization strategies in diffusion and rectified-flow models for high-resolution image synthesis. The method uses a rectified-flow Transformer with a spatial head that adds local correction to spectral predictions, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, it achieves comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control but converges faster, and on ImageNet-512 it comes within 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Pixel-space generative Transformers typically tokenize each image patch as one token, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. The discrete cosine transform (DCT) is a widely used transform in image compression (e.g., JPEG) that decomposes signals into frequency bands, and rectified-flow Transformers are a class of generative models that learn straight ODE paths for efficient sampling. Global attention allows all tokens to interact, while local attention restricts interactions to nearby tokens, and this work exploits the insight that low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally.

## [DERL: Dual-Evolving RL Learns to Design Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13399) ⭐️ 7.0/10

DERL is a dual-training framework where an outer-loop reward proposer learns via policy gradient from the inner policy's validation performance, autonomously discovering effective reward structures. It outperforms strong baselines on embodied (ALFWorld), scientific (ScienceWorld), and mathematical (GSM8K, MATH) reasoning tasks, with significant gains on out-of-distribution tasks. This work addresses the costly and often manual process of reward design in RL by learning the reward proposer itself, turning past trials into a meta-gradient signal. It could reduce human effort in crafting rewards for complex reasoning and agent tasks, and the strong out-of-distribution results suggest better generalization. The proposer composes rewards from task primitives and is updated by policy gradient based on the inner policy's validation performance, effectively capturing an empirical meta-gradient of task success. In mathematics, DERL improves on the outcome reward where directly added primitives hurt, and analyses under matched compute confirm the proposer discovers useful reward signals.

**Background**: Reinforcement learning (RL) trains agents to maximize a reward signal, but designing that reward is notoriously difficult and often requires manual engineering. Meta-gradient RL adapts the learning objective itself via gradient-based meta-learning, and benchmarks like ALFWorld (text-based embodied tasks) and GSM8K (grade-school math word problems) test reasoning and agent capabilities. DERL builds on these ideas by learning a reward proposer through validation feedback.

## [PRISM: Cost-Sensitive Gating for Proactive AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.01532) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PRISM introduces a cost-sensitive selective intervention framework that combines a calibrated decision-theoretic gate with a dual-process reasoning architecture, intervening only when the probability of user acceptance exceeds a threshold derived from asymmetric costs. On ProactiveBench, it reduces false alarms by 22.78% and improves F1 by 20.14% over strong baselines. This work addresses a core challenge for proactive agents: balancing the benefit of timely help against the burden of unwanted interruptions. The decision-theoretic approach enables tunable, auditable control over intervention behavior, which is crucial for deploying agents in real-world settings where false alarms erode user trust. The framework uses a calibrated probability threshold derived from asymmetric costs of missed help versus false alarms, and invokes a resource-intensive Slow mode with counterfactual checks only near the decision boundary. Training employs gate-aligned, schema-locked distillation from a teacher running the full pipeline, with the student's response policy explicitly decoupled from the intervention gate.

The simplest model achieves system-level SRCC of 0.957 and utterance-level SRCC of 0.838 with human mean opinion scores. It enables personalized quality evaluators from small amounts of listener annotations and runs in real time on a single consumer GPU. A systematic ablation shows that no addition meaningfully improves the frozen baseline, indicating that frozen MuQ representations already capture quality-relevant information, and encoder choice is the dominant design factor. LoRA-adapted models trained on as few as 150 clips already achieve usable correlation, but the metric is selectively sensitive to signal-level artifacts and insensitive to musical-structural distortions.

## [Hedge-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents on Real-World Financial Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.03918) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Hedge-Bench introduces a benchmark of 92 real-world environments derived from hedge fund analysts' reasoning traces, where agents must forecast discrete market events from frozen information snapshots. Across 11 frontier models, joint success rates (correct forecast plus over 60% research coverage) range from 2.54% to 31.52%, and GRPO training with turn-level credit assignment improves coverage on held-out environments from 17.17% to 33.36% at low reasoning effort. This benchmark fills a gap in evaluating AI agents on realistic, incomplete-information forecasting tasks that mirror professional analyst workflows, moving beyond routine document retrieval. The results show that even frontier models struggle with joint accuracy and coverage, while targeted reinforcement learning can substantially improve research coverage and generalize to out-of-distribution financial tasks. The benchmark uses frozen point-in-time information snapshots and evaluates forecasts against real-world outcomes, with three trials per environment. The trained Muse-Glimmer model at low effort exceeds the base model's extra-high-effort coverage while using 47.9% fewer tokens, and shows generalization with a 10.06 percentage point improvement in held-out forecasting accuracy at high effort and gains on GDPval, GDP_pdf, Harvey LAB, and Frontier Finance.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Financial analysts routinely make discrete predictions (e.g., whether a company will beat earnings) using only information available at that time, but evaluating AI on this is hard because future outcomes are unknown at test time. Hedge-Bench addresses this by freezing information snapshots and pairing them with subsequently resolved questions, creating a realistic testbed. GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is a reinforcement learning algorithm that drops PPO's value network and uses the average reward of a group of sampled answers as a baseline, making RL for LLMs more efficient. Turn-level credit assignment assigns rewards to specific turns in a multi-turn interaction rather than broadcasting a single trajectory-level score to all tokens, which improves learning in long-horizon agent tasks.

## [INFRAMIND: Infrastructure-Aware Multi-Agent LLM Orchestration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11440) ⭐️ 7.0/10

INFRAMIND introduces a hierarchical policy for multi-agent LLM systems that jointly plans collaboration graphs and selects models/reasoning strategies based on real-time serving conditions to meet deadlines and improve accuracy. Across five benchmarks on a shared five-model deployment, it improves low-load accuracy by up to 7.6 percentage points and increases correct, on-time answers from 20.4% to 33.8% on 500 MATH questions with 10-300s deadlines. This work addresses a practical coupling in multi-agent LLM systems: the reasoning workflow determines load, while changing load determines which reasoning choices remain affordable. By adapting reasoning decisions to serving capacity, it enables more efficient deployment of multi-agent systems under real-world latency constraints, potentially benefiting cloud providers and applications requiring deadline-aware reasoning. The hierarchical policy consists of a planner that selects the collaboration graph at arrival and an executor that jointly selects model and reasoning strategy before each agent call, connected by a shared latency penalty. With 15 models and Azure timings replayed, the fraction of correct, on-time answers rises from 11.6% to 54.8% over MasRouter, though results are benchmark-specific and depend on telemetry accuracy.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Multi-agent LLM systems use multiple language model instances that collaborate through structured workflows, such as graphs, to solve complex tasks. However, these systems share serving queues, and congestion can delay responses beyond deadlines. INFRAMIND builds on hierarchical reinforcement learning and infrastructure-aware AI, where orchestration decisions consider real-time load and latency to balance accuracy and timeliness.

## [GLASS: Training-Free Personalized Text Generation via Sparse Autoencoder Steering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.21620) ⭐️ 7.0/10

GLASS is a training-free framework that uses sparse autoencoders to extract a global user-style prior from historical responses and constructs local contrastive style vectors over clustered interaction scenarios. During inference, it jointly injects these global and local vectors into different model layers, enabling context-aware personalization without retrieval or parameter updates. This approach avoids the inference and storage overhead of retrieval-based methods and the computational cost of fine-tuning, while better disentangling stylistic signals from semantic content. It could benefit applications requiring efficient personalization and offers interpretability insights through SAE-based representations. GLASS outperforms retrieval-, fine-tuning-, and steering-based baselines on LaMP and LongLaMP benchmarks across ROUGE metrics and LLM-as-judge evaluations. Analyses show that SAE-based representations are more robust to topic and length shifts, suggesting better disentanglement of stylistic information from semantic residue.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Personalized text generation aims to capture a user's writing style from historical data. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are neural network components that learn sparse, interpretable feature representations from model activations, often used in mechanistic interpretability research. Activation steering is an inference-time technique that modifies a model's internal activations by adding directional vectors to control its behavior without retraining. LaMP and LongLaMP are benchmarks for personalized text generation, with LongLaMP focusing on long-form outputs.

## [WNM-3D adds 3D scene conditioning to world-action models for closed-loop VLN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07267) ⭐️ 7.0/10

WNM-3D introduces a generative World Navigation Model that conditions joint future-view and action prediction on 3D scene representations extracted from monocular RGB history for continuous vision-language navigation. A frozen feed-forward geometry encoder produces cross-view representations that a trainable 3D Scene-to-Token Adapter converts into a fixed-length scene prefix, kept visible to every future video-action block via block-causal attention during joint denoising. Existing world-action models for continuous VLN do not condition joint future-view and action generation on geometry-aware representations from observation history, so adding persistent 3D context could improve spatial reasoning and closed-loop robustness. WNM-3D consistently outperforms its backbone-matched WNM-2D counterpart on GN-Bench and VLN-CE and demonstrates closed-loop deployment on a physical robot, suggesting a practical path toward more reliable embodied navigation policies. The model is trained with supervised world-action learning, DAgger-style adaptation on policy-visited states, and Counterfactual DanceGRPO refinement, with component and stage-wise ablations supporting the Adapter design and the complementary roles of DAgger-SFT and reward-guided refinement. Results are reported on GN-Bench and VLN-CE, and the work is an arXiv preprint without community discussion provided.

Vision-language-action (VLA) policies map egocentric observations and instructions directly to actions, while world-action models (WAMs) additionally predict how observations will evolve under predicted motion, typically as future RGB frames.
