## [Paper Proposes Process-Based Criterion for Human-Machine Cognitive Equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.16213) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2608.16213v3) argues that intelligence is constituted by iterative process rather than output, and defines 'strong equivalence' across seven process features to compare human and machine cognition. It concludes that current generative AI is only weakly equivalent to human cognition, matching outputs while the underlying process remains absent or opaque. The framework shifts AI evaluation away from output-matching benchmarks toward process audits, which could reshape how researchers assess reasoning and creativity in models. It also warns of a symmetric risk: GenAI tools that outsource human generative processes may leave critical cognitive capacities unbuilt, affecting education and human-AI interaction design. The paper specifies seven process features for assessing strong equivalence and proposes design principles for GenAI that instantiate more process while preserving human judgment and creativity. It also outlines 'process audits' intended to make strong equivalence empirically testable, though the work remains a theoretical preprint without experimental validation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: In cognitive science, weak equivalence (sometimes called Turing equivalence) means two systems produce the same outputs, while strong equivalence requires them to share the underlying computational or causal process. Generative AI is trained on traces—textual and visual residues of human cognition—and reproduces samples from that distribution, which can mimic reasoning without performing it. Cognitive offloading research similarly examines how delegating mental work to external tools alters internal cognitive processes.

A new arXiv paper (2608.24069v2) presents the first systematic empirical study of how adversarial signals injected via web data or compromised agents propagate through LLM-based multi-agent trading systems. Testing four agent roles (Analyst, Researcher, Trader, Risk Manager) and four communication topologies on post-cutoff data across five assets, the authors find that no architecture is inherently robust. As LLM-based multi-agent trading systems move from research prototypes to live deployments controlling real assets, a single corrupted signal can reach the final decision and cause financial loss. The role-by-architecture analysis provides actionable insights for designing defenses in deployed financial AI. The study considers two low-barrier adversaries without model internals access: a data adversary planting manipulated web content and a compromised-agent adversary tampering with prompts. It introduces a parameter-free heuristic called the Adversarial Signal Preservation Score, and finds majority voting offers only conditional protection depending on benign-agent agreement, while compromising a terminal decision node can bypass upstream safeguards.

## [RePolicy jointly learns safety policy selection and agent behavior assessment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24275) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RePolicy introduces a safeguard that jointly learns to select the relevant safety policy from a library and assess whether an agent's behavior is safe, supported by the new PolicyTraj-20K dataset of over 20,000 annotated agent trajectories. Trained with supervised demonstrations followed by reinforcement learning, RePolicy-4B achieves leading overall safety-detection performance across six agent-safety benchmarks and 19 baselines. Existing policy-aware safeguards assume the correct policy is already known, but in real deployments the applicable rules vary by task, environment, and user, and an incorrect policy choice can lead to an incorrect safety judgment. By learning which safety requirements to apply, RePolicy addresses a practical gap in agent safeguards as LLM agents are increasingly deployed in open-ended, tool-using settings. The method randomizes policy order, identifiers, and distractors during training to reduce shortcut learning, and the dataset annotates trajectories with applicable policies, safety labels, and explanations. RePolicy-4B is built on the Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 backbone, and the work is an arXiv preprint (2608.24275v3) with no peer review or community discussion yet.

## [NovGauge Benchmark Diagnoses LLM Novelty Assessment with Fine-Grained Dimensions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11234) ⭐️ 7.0/10

NovGauge is a human-anchored benchmark containing 619 paper pairs and 50 multi-paper sets, drawn from ICLR reviewer overlap claims and survey co-citations, that labels instances along task, problem, and method dimensions. Evaluating 18 LLMs with a cascading diagnostic pipeline, it finds hallucination rates of 0–39% and that over 70% of non-hallucinated correct-positive judgments cite evidence that fails to logically support the stated reason. As LLMs are increasingly used in peer review at major AI conferences, this benchmark exposes that novelty assessment remains unreliable, especially when correctness is conditioned on faithful evidence grounding. It provides a diagnostic tool to pinpoint which dimensions models misjudge and whether their evidence is faithful, which could inform better evaluation and deployment of LLM-assisted reviewing. The cascading pipeline verifies per-dimension correctness, evidence grounding, and logical support; the best model, GPT-5.5, achieves only 43–72% Verified F1 across dimensions, and most models retain less than half of their raw F1 after faithfulness verification. These results highlight that high raw accuracy can mask unfaithful reasoning in novelty judgments.

## [GAI Framework Unifies Policy Iteration and Recursive Self-Improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13406) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Generalized Agent Iteration (GAI), a formal framework that models iterative policy improvement and recursive self-improvement (RSI) as two cases of a single learning paradigm. GAI defines the agent as a configuration of modifiable components and uses two dials—whether the improving mechanism is part of the agent and whether the evaluation standard is externally grounded—to distinguish GPI from RSI and classify systems as anchored, goal drift, or fully self-referential. RSI is a central concern in AI safety and capability research, but lacked a unified formal treatment; GAI provides a principled basis for comparing existing systems and analyzing failure modes one condition at a time. This could help researchers and policymakers reason more rigorously about claims of self-improving AI and design safer systems. The framework builds on generalized policy iteration (GPI), where policy evaluation and improvement alternate, but extends it to cases where the update principle and evaluation base lie inside the agent. The two dials yield coordinates that place existing systems on the same axes and make RSI defects statable condition by condition; the paper is a preprint without peer review.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Generalized policy iteration (GPI) is a classical reinforcement learning framework in which policy evaluation and policy improvement interact to converge to an optimal policy, but it assumes the update rule and evaluation standard are external to the agent. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) refers to an AI system iteratively designing a more capable successor, potentially leading to an intelligence explosion; as of 2026, RSI-related projects are ongoing and raise significant safety concerns. GAI aims to bridge these two concepts by formalizing RSI in terms of the classical GPI account.

## [World Model Science: Criticality and Chaos in Long-Horizon LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17419) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.17419v2) studies long-horizon LLM agent world-model dynamics through self-organized criticality, weak chaos, and metastable belief dynamics, finding that externally increased task pressure sharply raises collapse probability while natural pressure is only a modest predictor of later failure. Experiments span controlled puzzles, tool-use tasks, embodied environments, multi-hop retrieval, general-assistant reasoning, and Game of Life. This work offers a physics-inspired framework for understanding why long-horizon agents fail, showing that errors are temporally correlated rather than independent and that locally valid actions can continue after the overall task state is already wrong. These insights could inform reliability engineering, error-detection, and evaluation design for agentic systems. The paper reports power-law behavior, bounded divergence consistent with weak chaos, and metastable belief dynamics, with error propagation changing with dependency depth but remaining bounded in finite tasks. Belief states in embodied tasks appear shallow rather than strongly trapped in incorrect states, and larger horizons allow larger error cascades whose scale is constrained by task and model capability.

**Background**: Self-organized criticality is a property of dynamical systems that naturally evolve toward a critical point, producing scale-invariant behavior such as power-law distributions without external tuning. Weak chaos describes dynamics with bounded but non-trivial divergence, often studied in statistical physics. ## [ManifoldCache: Training-Free Diffusion Acceleration via Constraint Manifold Caching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.04510) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ManifoldCache introduces a training-free, data-free caching method for Constraint-Manifold Diffusion Models (CMDMs), unifying eight scientific generation models under a single abstraction. It proves that the noise-schedule midpoint is a safe-caching boundary and that deeper network blocks allow larger certified cache strides. Existing acceleration techniques fail on constrained diffusion models due to memory, fidelity, or mode confusion issues, so this method could significantly speed up inference for structured scientific generation in domains like protein design and crystal prediction. It offers a principled, calibration-free solution that may enable practical deployment of these models. The method exploits the orthogonal decomposition of the conditional score into normal (constraint-enforcing) and tangential (manifold-navigating) components, requiring no calibration data or training overhead. Caching before the noise-schedule midpoint incurs provably bounded error, while caching after it guarantees a positive fraction of trajectories suffer mode confusion.

Constraint-manifold diffusion models extend this to structured scientific data that must satisfy hard geometric constraints from physics, chemistry, or biology, making acceleration even more challenging. Feature caching, which reuses intermediate computations across denoising steps, is a popular training-free acceleration approach for standard diffusion models but has not been adapted to constrained settings.

## [LLM Judges Show 'Anchor Bias' in Entity Alignment Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.09554) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper presents the first systematic benchmarking study of LLM-as-judge reliability for entity alignment (EA), testing three frontier models, three datasets, and four EA systems. It identifies 'anchor bias,' a failure mode where exposing the system's decision label causes judges to invert discrimination, while a label-free protocol restores near-ceiling performance. This work reveals a critical flaw in using LLM judges for structured prediction tasks like EA, showing that stronger models are paradoxically more label-sensitive. It provides a reproducible auditing framework and the first biomedical EA benchmark, impacting anyone relying on LLM-as-judge for scalable evaluation. Judge discrimination collapses under label-exposing prompts (J-ROC-AUC 0.12–0.87), but a label-free protocol recovers 0.98–1.00 on distinctive-name datasets and 0.93–0.95 on biomedical pairs. Counterfactual label flips shift scores by more than 2 points in 53–99% of pairs, with sensitivity growing with model capability—a pattern termed the 'frontier model paradox.'

However, its reliability for structured prediction tasks like EA had not been systematically studied before this work.

## [AnyGoal benchmark tests world model generalization beyond expert rollouts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.26844) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces AnyGoal, a benchmark and open-source library of goal-shifted task variants built from widely used world-model environments to test whether world models can compositionally generalize their learned dynamics beyond expert rollout data. Across multiple environments and world model families, current models consistently fail when familiar state and action factors are recombined in ways underrepresented in expert trajectories. This work addresses an underexplored but critical gap in model-based reinforcement learning: the reliability of world models for planning depends on dynamics generalizing beyond the narrow state-action combinations seen in expert data. The benchmark and systematic analysis provide the research community with a standardized way to measure progress toward world models that generalize to new planning tasks. Each AnyGoal task is designed so that individual state factors and actions remain within their training support, but their combinations are underrepresented in expert trajectories, isolating compositional generalization from simple out-of-distribution detection. The study examines dynamics and representation failures across model families, interaction regimes, and evaluation metrics to map where current world models generalize and where challenges remain.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: World models are learned simulators that capture environment dynamics, allowing agents to plan and evaluate actions in imagination before acting in the real environment, which is central to model-based reinforcement learning. Expert rollouts—trajectories from skilled policies—are a common data source for training these models, but they cover only a narrow slice of possible state-action combinations. Compositional generalization refers to the ability to recombine familiar factors into novel but valid combinations, a hallmark of human learning that has proven difficult for machine learning models.

## [ARCANA benchmark exposes LLM struggles with far analogical reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29271) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced ARCANA, a new benchmark that tests far analogical reasoning by requiring models to map real-world objects or physical phenomena onto abstract grid-based transformations. A human study confirmed that people solve these tasks reliably, while evaluations across a range of large language models revealed a distinct performance gap and systematic failure modes. Far analogical reasoning—drawing deep structural parallels between superficially dissimilar domains—is a core component of human intelligence that remains under-tested in AI evaluation. ARCANA's human-validated tasks and demonstrated LLM failure modes make it a useful new probe for measuring abstraction and generalization in current models. Unlike the well-known ARC-AGI benchmark, which primarily emphasizes innate human priors, ARCANA focuses on far analogical mappings from real-world phenomena to grid transformations. The authors also propose ConceptSIR, a reasoning framework based on concept slippage, introspection, and reflection, which enables standard LLMs to solve several challenging ARCANA tasks that direct prompting failed on; all data, code, and the benchmark are publicly released.

## [CauProphet: LLM agents learn persistent causal cognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32477) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce CauProphet, an LLM agent that builds and refines persistent causal knowledge in a 'Causal Cognition' store and constructs structured 'Causal Beliefs' for each task to guide decisions. In financial research it achieves a 25.4% improvement in mean rank correlation with next-day returns over a baseline agent and raises prediction accuracy from 21.3% to 28.6% in dynamic real-world settings. Most LLM agents rely on retrieving past records or summaries, which limits their ability to reason about cause and effect over long horizons. CauProphet's persistent causal knowledge and demonstrated transfer to future tasks point toward next-generation agents that learn from experience more like humans, affecting areas such as scientific discovery, finance, and everyday planning. For each task, CauProphet combines relevant knowledge from its Causal Cognition with current evidence to form a Causal Belief capturing causal factors and the effects of possible actions, then updates both the belief and the cognition as new observations arrive. The project repository is available at github.com/OpenCausaLab/CauProphet, and experiments cover financial research, scientific tasks, and everyday action selection.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: LLM agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks by using external memory, but context windows remain insufficient and existing memory systems mainly retrieve records or summaries rather than causal understanding. Causal cognition, studied in humans and animals, refers to the ability to learn and reason about cause-and-effect relationships, which supports prediction, explanation, and planning. Causal inference frameworks such as structural equation models and directed acyclic graphs formalize how causal factors and action effects can be represented, which is the kind of structure CauProphet's Causal Belief aims to capture.

It emphasizes calibration challenges such as IIA violations, ordinal-scale bias, and few-shot recalibration under distribution shift, and describes how System 1 models integrate into agentic workflows and System 1 + System 2 cascades that route based on calibrated confidence.

## [Population-Centered Evolution Boosts Self-Improving Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36660) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Population-Centered Evolution (PCE), a method that improves self-modifying agents by distilling population-wide patterns of success, failure, and modification history into a 'population block' that guides improvements to a selected parent agent's harness. Under matched conditions, PCE achieves 72.1% success on SWE-bench Verified and 96.7% on Polyglot, improving over a strong group-evolution baseline by 3.2 and 5.9 percentage points, respectively. This work identifies a substantial gap between population coverage (tasks solved by at least one evolved variant) and the performance of the best individual agent, showing that useful capabilities emerge across the population but are not consolidated into leading agents. By treating the population as evidence rather than merely as candidates for selection, PCE offers a complementary principle for agent evolution that could lead to more effective self-improving AI systems. PCE reduces the gap between population coverage and best-agent performance by one-third on SWE-bench and closes it on Polyglot. The method is evaluated under matched models, initial harnesses, and evolution schedules, ensuring fair comparison with the group-evolution baseline.

The paper introduces CauTrace, a white-box diagnostic framework that characterizes both ordinary and adversarially induced LLM failures by analyzing functional states, representation propagation, and temporal-state coordination along reasoning trajectories. It defines seven functional states to represent support and constraint processing, and evaluates the framework on Qwen and LLaMA-family models using clean reasoning failures and paired adversarial perturbations. This work offers a unified diagnostic approach that moves beyond final-output correctness to reveal how failures develop internally, which could significantly advance AI safety and interpretability research. By identifying consistent operational signals across models, it may enable more targeted interventions and repairs for LLM reasoning errors. The framework measures how changes among the seven functional states persist across subsequent Transformer blocks, and characterizes when commitment and verification occur relative to support. Results show that failed traces exhibit weaker Attention-MLP agreement on support-state updates and less verification activity relative to commitment, with representation-level signatures and timing shifts varying by architecture.

White-box interpretability involves inspecting a model's internal activations, attention patterns, and intermediate representations to understand how outputs are formed. CauTrace builds on this by defining functional states and tracking their propagation across Transformer blocks, which are the fundamental building blocks that process and transform input data in LLMs.

The paper introduces Aligned Delta-Triplane Transformer (ADTT), a compact 4D occupancy world model that explicitly aligns historical triplanes using ego-motion compensation and predicts only future scene changes via a query-conditioned Transformer. ADTT uses ego-motion queries to guide controllable future motion and learnable external queries to capture scene changes beyond ego motion; the predicted residual changes are added to the aligned triplane prior and decoded into future occupancy. The framework is validated on a dataset of social engineering chat scenarios and compared against a Dual LLM baseline. This work addresses a key limitation in fraud detection: traditional static anomaly detection often misinterprets benign topic transitions (concept drift) as fraudulent behavior, leading to false alarms or missed threats. The framework uses a One Class Drift Detector (OCDD) with a sliding window to detect concept drift in flagged dialogues; when drift is detected, an LLM assesses whether the shift is fraudulent or legitimate, and if no drift is found, the behavior is inferred to be spam-like. The authors compare their modular approach against a Dual LLM baseline that uses different language models for detection and judgment, highlighting trade-offs in performance and interpretability.

## [DRIFT framework mitigates diversity collapse in RL fine-tuning for image generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.12401) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces DRIFT (DiveRsity-Incentivized Reinforcement Fine-Tuning), a framework that addresses diversity collapse in reinforcement learning fine-tuning of diffusion and flow models for image generation. It tackles the issue through three strategies: sampling a reward-concentrated subset to filter outliers, prompting with stochastic variations, and optimizing intra-group diversity with potential-based reward shaping. Diversity collapse is a fundamental limitation in RL fine-tuning of generative models, causing outputs to converge to a narrow set of high-reward samples. DRIFT achieves Pareto dominance in task alignment and generation diversity, improving diversity by 3.88% to 81.42% at matched alignment and alignment by 14.38% to 56.45% at matched diversity, which is crucial for applications requiring diverse candidate generations. The framework operates during on-policy fine-tuning and includes a potential-based reward shaping mechanism to optimize intra-group diversity. Code is available at https://github.com/NJU-RL/DRIFT, and the paper is a NeurIPS 2026 poster.

## [Jacobian Scopes: Unified Geometric Framework for Token-Level LLM Attribution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16407) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Jacobian Scopes, a suite of gradient-based token-level causal attribution methods grounded in perturbation theory and information geometry, which quantify how input tokens influence logits, the full predictive distribution, and model uncertainty (effective temperature). On token-ablation faithfulness benchmarks (LAMBADA and IWSLT2017) across six LLMs, the distribution-level Fisher and Temperature Scopes significantly outperform established gradient-based attribution methods in 10 of 12 model-dataset settings. This work provides interpretability researchers with a unified, theoretically grounded framework for attributing LLM predictions to specific input tokens, which could improve bias detection, translation analysis, and understanding of in-context learning mechanisms. Its strong empirical results and open-source implementation with an interactive demo lower the barrier for practical adoption. The framework includes semantic, Fisher, and Temperature variants that measure contributions to different output aspects, with the Fisher and Temperature Scopes showing particular strength on faithfulness benchmarks. The paper demonstrates case studies revealing implicit political biases, word- and phrase-level translation strategies, and mechanisms in in-context time-series forecasting, and provides a Hugging Face demo for custom text exploration.

## [JoBS: Bayesian Optimization for LLM Fine-Tuning Without Full Training Runs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.08351) ⭐️ 7.0/10

JoBS is a Bayesian optimization method that co-optimizes data and model configurations for LLM fine-tuning without requiring a full training run at each iteration. It allocates part of the budget to learn a scaling-law-inspired performance predictor from short training runs, then uses this predictor to guide Bayesian optimization over many more configurations. This approach significantly reduces the computational cost of hyperparameter optimization for LLM fine-tuning, making it feasible to explore a larger joint data-model space within a fixed budget. It could benefit AI practitioners who need to efficiently tune LLMs for downstream tasks without expensive full training runs. JoBS analyzes average regret and derives the optimal budget allocation between predictor learning and BO iterations. Empirically, it outperforms independent data and model optimization methods and existing multi-fidelity BO baselines across diverse downstream tasks, with code available on GitHub.

## [Training-free entropy method fixes flow-based OOD detection paradox](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09581) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Semantic Proportional Entropy Manipulation (SPEM), a training-free procedure that perturbs inputs more strongly when they are less similar to an in-distribution memory bank, thereby realigning likelihood ordering in normalizing flows. Theoretical lower bounds show that this entropy gap increases the expected log-likelihood difference in favor of in-distribution data, and experiments confirm the realignment even when the flow receives only noise instead of the original input. This work addresses the well-known likelihood paradox that undermines normalizing flows for out-of-distribution detection, offering a simple post-hoc fix that could make flow-based detectors more reliable in safety-critical applications. The surprising finding that realignment persists with noise-only inputs challenges assumptions about how flows use input information and may inspire new detection strategies. SPEM uses a pretrained encoder and a memory bank to scale noise by semantic similarity, then performs detection with the original flow model; a noise-only variant (SPEM-noise) isolates the effect of the original image. The method is training-free and comes with theoretical analysis characterizing when the realignment occurs, though the abstract does not specify benchmark details or computational overhead.

**Background**: Normalizing flows are deep generative models that can compute exact likelihoods for inputs, but they often assign higher likelihood to out-of-distribution (OOD) data than to in-distribution (ID) data—a phenomenon known as the likelihood paradox. SPEM takes an entropic perspective, manipulating input entropy via semantic-similarity-scaled perturbations to correct the likelihood ordering.

The paper proposes a robust Taylor-Lagrange Control (rTLC) method that addresses the feasibility preservation problem in safety-critical control, overcoming limitations of Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) and the original Taylor-Lagrange Control (TLC). By expanding the safety function to an order higher than its relative degree using Taylor's expansion with Lagrange remainder, rTLC ensures the safety constraint remains satisfied over the entire discretization interval. The method requires only a single hyper-parameter, making it more practical than existing approaches that need significantly more tuning. The paper introduces NICO, a learned 2-opt policy for routing problems that achieves size generalization by representing the incumbent solution as edge tokens without positional encodings, using scale-free features, and incorporating exact move gains into the logits. Trained on instances with at most 100 nodes, NICO reaches a 1.1% gap on 1000-node Euclidean TSP, compared to 10.7% for greedy 2-opt and 36% for the best prior learned policy. This work addresses a key limitation of neural routing solvers—poor generalization to larger instances—by identifying three specific failure points and providing a principled solution. It could significantly impact the design of learned local search methods for combinatorial optimization, enabling models trained on small problems to effectively solve much larger ones. A controlled factorial study shows that edge tokens outperform node tokens with positional encodings, exact gains are necessary for transfer, and scale-free features help only in conjunction with exact gains. NICO also improves tours from constructive and diffusion-based solvers and outperforms classical controls on CVRP and road-network costs.

The method outperforms strong distillation baselines across math, code, and instruction-following benchmarks. This work challenges the dominant trajectory-imitation paradigm in reasoning distillation, arguing that intermediate reasoning steps are locally under-specified and should not be rigidly copied. If validated, it could lead to more efficient and robust distillation of multi-step reasoning from large LLMs to smaller models, impacting how practitioners build efficient reasoning-capable models. The key mechanism is a context-dependent modulation of the distillation loss: instead of forcing the student to match every teacher token, the update strength is adjusted based on how locally valid the student's proposed action is relative to the teacher's under the same prefix. The abstract reports gains on math, code, and instruction-following benchmarks, but no specific numbers or model sizes are provided in the summary.

## [DUET: Dual-Controlled Token Allocation Boosts RLVR Efficiency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08441) ⭐️ 7.0/10

DUET introduces a dual-controlled token allocation layer over GRPO that jointly decides how many rollouts each prompt receives and when to stop them, using a lightweight pre-rollout surrogate of prompt informativeness and a marker-gated abort rule with importance reweighting. On Qwen3-1.7B trained on MATH, DUET outperforms full-budget GRPO and three budget-aware baselines, achieving a 1.62x wall-clock speedup, and with only 50% of the token budget it still beats all baselines at full budget with a 2.51x speedup. This work shows that jointly tuning prompt allocation and rollout length under a shared compute budget can improve both reasoning quality and training time, contrary to the usual trade-off where efficiency methods sacrifice quality as compute decreases. It offers a practical way to reduce the high computational cost of RLVR training, which generates hundreds of thousands of tokens per step, and the gap to baselines widens as budget tightens. DUET is a computationally efficient layer over GRPO that uses a pre-rollout surrogate to set rollout counts per prompt and a marker-gated abort rule with importance reweighting to stop rollouts early. It generalizes to other benchmarks across math and coding, is on par with the best baseline on scientific Q&A, and is verified on Qwen3-4B to 14B and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct.

A new arXiv paper shows that GPU power capping is largely ineffective for autoregressive LLM decode because decode kernels are memory-bound and underutilize power, drawing less than half of the H200's 700W rating. It also shows that once prefill is measured without prefix caching, recurrent architectures (Gated DeltaNet and Mamba2) pay no prefill penalty and their linear-time mixing undercuts quadratic attention on long prompts, lowering total request energy from the first output token at large batch.

## [Shared-weight recurrent Transformer develops distinct roles without modular partitioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17811) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces Asymmetric Input Recurrence (AIR), a minimal two-state reasoning architecture where the same Transformer model is reused for both L-updates and H-updates, with the only difference being that the encoded input is injected during L-updates but not H-updates. Experiments on Sudoku-Extreme and Maze show that the shared model develops emergent specialization: z_H behaves as a fully committed proposal state, while z_L retains local uncertainty and shifting intermediate structure. This work shows that a single shared-parameter recurrent Transformer can develop stable, related functional roles without explicit module partitioning, suggesting that architectural asymmetry in input injection may be sufficient to induce specialization. This could inform the design of more parameter-efficient reasoning architectures and deepen understanding of how recurrent models organize computation internally. Ablations reveal that to induce specialization, the shared model must be able to distinguish the two update types, either through input injection asymmetry or a separate level token. Attention analysis shows that L-updates are consistently more local than H-updates in both tasks, and freeze interventions provide evidence of dynamical dependence between the two states, with responses varying across tasks, intervention directions, and seeds.

## [QGF: Test-Time Gradient Guidance for Flow Policies in RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11087) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose QGF (Q-Guided Flow), an RL algorithm that performs policy optimization entirely at test time by pre-training a reference flow policy via behavioral cloning and a value function critic, then using the value gradient to guide the policy toward higher-value actions without additional policy learning. It outperforms prior test-time RL methods on single-task and goal-conditioned offline RL benchmarks with high-dimensional action spaces. This approach sidesteps the instability of backpropagating through denoising processes, which has hindered the integration of expressive diffusion and flow policies into RL pipelines. By leaving stable supervised policy training intact and moving policy improvement to test time, QGF offers a practical and scalable alternative that could make expressive policies more accessible for robot control and other continuous control domains. QGF is competitive with state-of-the-art training-time algorithms while being much cheaper to run, and it exhibits favorable scaling with model size by avoiding the instability of actor-critic training. Notably, a variant called QGF-Jacobian performs worse, showing that dropping the Jacobian in the gradient estimator improves performance.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Flow models and diffusion models are expressive generative models that have become popular for imitation learning in robotics, as they can represent complex, multimodal action distributions and scale stably in supervised settings. However, incorporating them into reinforcement learning for policy improvement is challenging because typical actor-critic methods require backpropagating gradients through the iterative denoising process, which is unstable and computationally expensive. Test-time optimization is an alternative paradigm where a pre-trained policy is adapted during deployment without retraining, potentially avoiding these issues.

## [ART fine-tunes multimodal LLMs by optimizing a single input image](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11854) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose Art-Based Reinforcement Training (ART), which optimizes a single auxiliary input image to specialize a frozen Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) for a specific task. At inference, this image is simply included in each standard multimodal prompt, requiring no changes to the serving engine. ART avoids adapter-aware serving infrastructure, making it easier to serve many task-specific adaptations at high throughput. It reaches accuracy close to LoRA and soft prompting while serving faster than LoRA, and its artifacts are plain images that are easy to store, distribute, and share. Across five reasoning benchmarks and four small MLLMs from three architectures, ART ranks first or second in 10 of 20 benchmark-MLLM pairs, with best results on GSM8k and SVAMP. In vLLM, ART reduces throughput by 6% to 14% relative to text-only requests, compared to LoRA's 13% to 93% slowdown.

## [First Study Evaluates Robustness of LLM Proof Autoformalization in Lean 4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14867) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper presents the first study on the robustness of LLM-based proof autoformalization in Lean 4, introducing global and local perturbations to test whether models remain faithful to altered informal proofs. It builds a benchmark on miniF2F and MATH-500 and evaluates seven recent models, finding that correctness varies under global perturbations and that models mostly fail to remain faithful under local perturbations. This work highlights a critical gap: autoformalizers that perform well on curated datasets may not be reliable when informal proofs are paraphrased or contain deliberate alterations, which is essential for real-world mathematical practice. It could motivate more robust training and evaluation methods for AI-assisted formal verification. Global perturbations paraphrase the entire theorem-proof pair in a different style, where formalization should remain consistent; local perturbations alter a value, symbol, or proof step, possibly counterfactually, and a robust formalizer should faithfully reflect the change rather than reverting to the original or inferring a different one. The benchmark automatically measures stability under global perturbations and faithfulness under local perturbations.

## [KumbhDoot: A Similarity-First, LLM-Bounded Assistant for Mass Gatherings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07520) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2608.07520v2) presents KumbhDoot, an agentic pilgrim assistant deployed for the Nashik Simhastha Kumbh Mela that inverts the usual LLM-first design by using an embedding-indexed semantic cache as its single retrieval primitive and invoking generative models only when similarity-based retrieval cannot produce a correct answer. The system uses a custom three-tier agent architecture that operates directly on this store, avoiding generic multi-agent frameworks that would trigger implicit per-step LLM calls. This work argues that for bounded, high-stakes, low-connectivity public-service domains, a similarity-first and LLM-bounded design is not merely cheaper but architecturally more appropriate than an LLM-default one, addressing cost, latency, hallucination, and offline usability at the scale of tens of millions of pilgrims. It offers a concrete, inspectable alternative to LLM-centric agent stacks for safety-critical deployments. The semantic cache handles intent routing, answer caching, offline lookups, and multi-agent retrieval in one store, and the paper includes an analytical cost model for per-query economics plus an honest account of where similarity suffices and where generative reasoning remains necessary. The authors explicitly avoid generic multi-agent frameworks because they would introduce implicit per-step LLM calls that undermine cost and inspectability.

## [Frozen LLMs Encode Geometric Relations but Fail to Act on Them](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.17843) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces a controlled auditing framework using parametric CAD to separate encoding, expression, and activation-level control failures in frozen LLMs. Testing eight pretrained models against matched randomly initialized controls, it finds that local geometric relations are linearly decodable but this decodability does not translate into zero-shot behavior, and simple activation steering cannot reliably control it. This work challenges the common assumption in mechanistic interpretability that if information is linearly decodable from a model's activations, it is functionally used by the model. The 'decodable but not actionable' finding suggests that probing results alone are insufficient evidence of usable internal knowledge, which has implications for how researchers evaluate and trust interpretability tools. Pretraining contributes substantially more to linear decoding of local relations than to global constraint status, which is already highly decodable even from random representations. Restoring clean internal activations can repair probe predictions, but simple activation steering does not provide reliable targeted control; however, low-rank fine-tuning with only 400 labeled relation pairs substantially improves generation on three representative models.

Activation steering attempts to control model behavior by adding direction vectors to activations during inference. ## [OptiFlow: One-step flow policies via value-weighted optimal transport for offline RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.15883) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers from Yonsei University propose OptiFlow, a framework that learns efficient one-step flow policies for offline reinforcement learning by jointly training a value-aware reference flow policy and a one-step policy, coupling their action samples through state-wise entropic optimal transport. The method avoids direct critic maximization, thereby preventing mode collapse and out-of-distribution exploitation while capturing multimodal action distributions. Offline RL agents often need to represent complex, multimodal behaviors from fixed datasets, but existing flow-based policies require many sampling steps and value-guided fine-tuning can collapse modes or exploit critic errors. OptiFlow's transport-based distillation offers a principled way to obtain fast, in-distribution one-step policies, which could improve the practicality of deploying offline RL in robotics and other real-world control settings. For each state, critic-estimated values define the priority of distillation target actions, while an action-distance cost ensures geometrically compatible pairings between the reference and one-step policies. The approach anchors the one-step policy to high-value, dataset-supported modes without risking out-of-distribution divergence, and code is available at https://github.com/Yonsei-DILLab/OptiFlow.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to learn a policy solely from a fixed dataset of previously collected transitions, without any online interaction with the environment. Flow policies, based on flow matching, are generative models that can naturally represent multimodal action distributions by transforming simple noise into complex actions through an ODE, but they typically require multiple sampling steps at inference time. One-step flow policies distill these models to generate actions in a single step, improving efficiency, but value-guided distillation in offline RL is challenging because maximizing the critic can push the policy toward out-of-distribution actions where the critic is inaccurate, leading to overestimation and mode collapse.

## [IterCaL Mitigates Teacher Bias in LLM Distillation Without Target Rewards](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17474) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes Iterative Calibration and Learning (IterCaL), which alternates source-reward teacher calibration via token-level branching with student learning on target prompts, and proves polynomial convergence in expected average KL to the oracle student. It also presents a separation result showing that regularized direct teacher matching retains positive oracle-KL error at its population optimum for every shared reference penalty, even when the teacher is stronger than every student. This work provides theoretical guarantees for mitigating teacher bias under covariate shift when target-domain reward feedback is unavailable, a realistic and under-addressed setting in LLM distillation. It offers researchers a principled alternative to direct teacher matching, which the separation result shows is fundamentally limited in this setting. IterCaL uses token-level branching to calibrate the teacher with source rewards while updating the student on target prompts, and a quantified source-to-target calibration discrepancy yields an explicit additive true-return term. The convergence guarantee is polynomial in expected average KL to the oracle student, defined as the reference-regularized target-reward maximizer within a potentially misspecified student class.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: LLM distillation trains a smaller student model to mimic a larger teacher model, but when the target domain differs from the source domain (covariate shift) and no target reward feedback is available, the student can inherit the teacher's biases. Token-level branching is a technique that lets calibration of the teacher and updates of the student interact at the token level rather than treating the teacher as a frozen label generator. The oracle student is a theoretical reference representing the best achievable student under the target reward and a reference penalty, and KL divergence measures how far the learned student's distribution is from this reference.

## [RL adaptively selects FOM/ROM per subdomain in Schwarz coupling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17837) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces a reinforcement learning approach that uses deep Q-networks (DQNs) to online-adapt the choice between full-order models (FOMs) and operator-inference reduced-order models (ROMs) for each subdomain in overlapping Schwarz alternating method (O-SAM) simulations. Trained offline with a reward balancing accuracy, cost, and switching frequency, the policies are deployed predictively on unseen problem instances without a reference FOM solution, and are demonstrated on a 1D advection-diffusion moving-front problem and a 3D linear elastic wave propagation problem in Norma.jl. This work addresses a key limitation of hybrid FOM-ROM domain decomposition—static model assignment—which is inadequate for transient problems where high-fidelity regions move over time. By enabling predictive online adaptation, it could improve efficiency and accuracy in multiphysics simulations, benefiting researchers in scientific computing and engineering who rely on Schwarz-based coupling. The reward function explicitly balances accuracy, computational cost, and model-switching frequency, and the DQN policies are trained offline then deployed without requiring a reference FOM solution. For the advection-diffusion benchmark, the learned policy outperforms static FOM/ROM assignments, but letting the agent also adapt the domain decomposition provides no further benefit; for the elastic wave benchmark, policies for two and three subdomains track the wave as expected.

## [JANUS: Post-hoc Jacobian Null Space Projection Mitigates Catastrophic Forgetting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19985) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces JANUS, a purely post-hoc and tuning-agnostic weight rectification framework that projects parameter updates into the Jacobian null space to achieve Parameter Space Orthogonality, the necessary and sufficient condition for preserving historical performance to first order. It further proposes a Multi-step Adaptive Rectification mechanism that uses the JANUS shift to dynamically verify the valid trust region and adjust step sizes, overcoming the local validity of the Jacobian approximation. JANUS offers a general, plug-and-play solution that can be applied after any fine-tuning method to recover compromised historical knowledge without interfering with downstream adaptation, directly addressing the stability-plasticity dilemma in continual learning. This could significantly improve the deployment of foundation models in sequential task settings where retaining prior capabilities is critical. ## [Blind Thermodynamic Ontology Discovery from Anonymous Experiments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.23387) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper formulates and solves the problem of discovering a hidden thermodynamic ontology—extensive/intensive scaling sectors, dual pairings, and admissible potentials—directly from anonymous controlled experiments. It presents an operational identifiability theory and a constructive polynomial-time algorithm that extracts scaling sectors from replication contrasts, recovers dual cotangent pairing from thermal contact and reciprocity, verifies a globally admissible concave potential via discrete cyclic concavity, and determines an invariant matroid of reservoir ensembles. The paper proves that the residual observational equivalence is strictly (x, λ) ~ (A x, a A^{-T} λ + β), establishing the sharp observational limit that no permitted experiment can break. Blind evaluations on van der Waals fluids and Curie-Weiss magnets confirm robust recovery under ill-conditioned mixing, correctly resolving anonymous Maxwell tie-lines while rejecting non-equilibrium continuations, and external validation across six real fluids from the NIST WebBook demonstrates transfer to real substances without coordinate leakage.

## [CRAFT traces medical VLM failures to distinct attention head populations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38810) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The CRAFT framework identifies two spatially disjoint attention head populations in medical vision-language models: 'arbitration heads' that let misleading text override correct images, and 'brake heads' that cause the model to commit without sufficient visual evidence. By excising these head sets, the authors causally verify that arbitration heads drive conflict-following while brake heads regulate abstention, with the interventions generalizing across multiple medical VQA benchmarks and VLM architectures without retraining. This work provides mechanistic, causally grounded explanations for two high-stakes safety failures in clinical VLM deployment, showing that targeted modulation of specific heads can correct them without retraining. It advances mechanistic interpretability beyond unimodal text models and offers a potential path toward safer, more trustworthy medical AI systems. Arbitration heads form a mid-to-deep wideband reflecting cross-layer evidence competition, while brake heads concentrate in a narrow middle-to-late layer band; CRAFT localizes each failure mode to a minimal causal head set using dual criteria and verifies necessity and sufficiency via temporal probes and Tuned Lens trajectory analysis. Excising arbitration heads sharply reduces conflict-following with negligible degradation on clean inputs, and excising brake heads restores appropriate abstention under degraded visual evidence.

## [OpenAttention: 1% KV Cache Read with Count-Aware Tail Proxies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30951) ⭐️ 7.0/10

OpenAttention introduces a count-aware mean proxy that folds the entire unread tail of the KV cache into a single virtual token, and shows this proxy yields lower output error than sampling at every read rate behind a practical selector. The full pipeline combines clustering, ErrorGate, and top-k selection, retaining 99% of dense accuracy on RULER-32K HARD with Llama-3.1-8B at a 1% read. This work addresses a core bottleneck in efficient LLM inference: sparse attention must decide how to handle the unread KV cache tail, and existing sampling methods fail at very low read rates. By enabling accurate attention with only 1% of the cache, OpenAttention could significantly reduce memory bandwidth and latency for long-context inference. The paper provides a closed-form analysis showing that at low read rates, sampling nearly doubles the weight error of discarding, while a single proxy stays below it. It also designs training-free Query-Geometry Clustering (QGC) and a Query-Geometry Selector (QGS) that compress keys while respecting query directions, and a custom kernel that runs decode attention 10× faster than dense attention at a 1% read.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Sparse attention reduces the cost of LLM inference by reading only a small subset of the key-value (KV) cache instead of the full cache. A key challenge is how to treat the unread tail: discarding it biases the output, while sampling it can miss important tokens (heavy hitters) at very low read rates. OpenAttention proposes approximating the dense attention distribution with a few proxies that target the tail, using a count-aware mean to preserve the total weight of the unread tokens.

## [Compact-Bench Measures How Context Compaction Damages Long-Horizon Coding Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31710) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces Compact-Bench, a benchmark that pairs full-history and summary-only continuations from a shared repository state to isolate the effect of context compaction on long-horizon coding agents. It evaluates 35 SWE-bench repairs, 146 agentic sessions, and 106 production chains across 14 summarizer backbones, finding that stable damage ranges from 5% to 64% of 22 full-history successes. This benchmark provides the first systematic isolation of compaction-induced state loss, showing that retaining relevant information alone does not ensure successful task continuation. It gives agent engineers concrete evidence that summarization-based context management can silently break long-horizon coding workflows, affecting anyone building or deploying coding agents that rely on compaction to exceed context windows. LLM summaries retain at most 16.0% of recurring details compared with 79.1% for mechanical extraction, and production summaries retain only 15.7% at the first boundary. Failures recur across methods: one repair is damaged by 13 of 14 backbones, and another by all 5 prompts, while Claude Opus 4.8 preserves the most repairs and DeepSeek-Flash damages the most.

## [Sampler mismatch causes sign-fixed entropy drift in RLVR, paper proves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34044) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.34044v2) proves that in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), sampler mismatch—rollouts drawn with top-k/top-p truncation or temperature that the learner does not apply—causes a constant advantage shift to change the entropy of a softmax policy at first order, with a sign fixed by the sampler. Positive shifts sharpen the policy under top-k, top-p, min-p, and temperatures below one, but flatten it under flatter samplers, explaining why masking or counting over-length responses as failures can push entropy in opposite directions. This result gives RLVR practitioners a concrete theoretical explanation for the notoriously unstable entropy dynamics in LLM reasoning training, showing that seemingly minor implementation choices like truncation and over-length handling can deterministically control whether entropy explodes or collapses. It directly affects anyone training reasoning models with group-based RLVR methods such as GRPO-style algorithms, and suggests simple corrections that improved held-out accuracy by 8.2–8.8 points on a 9B model. In group-based RLVR with token-level losses, the baseline-dependent part of the drift is set by the token-weighted net advantage, which masking and failing can push to opposite signs, while the rest comes from a covariance between advantages and the sampler's sharpness gap that feeds back on itself. Experiments show the entropy slope is linear in net-advantage shifts under truncated sampling but flat under exact sampling; token-level importance ratios leave 98% of the drift, four clipped minibatch updates per batch amplify it sevenfold, and on a 9B reasoning model zeroing the net advantage or renormalizing the learner raised held-out accuracy by 8.2 and 8.8 points after ten steps.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: RLVR (reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards) is a post-training method that fine-tunes LLMs using automatic, rule-based checks—such as verifying a math answer or passing unit tests—instead of a learned reward model. In practice, rollouts are often generated with sampling tricks like top-k/top-p truncation or temperature scaling, while the policy update assumes exact sampling from the model's softmax distribution; this discrepancy is what the paper calls sampler mismatch. Policy entropy—how spread out the model's next-token distribution is—is a key quantity in RLVR, since too little entropy causes collapse and too much causes instability, and prior work has observed unexplained entropy swings tied to implementation details.

## [Proactive Memory Recall Suffers False-Alarm Inflation at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34507) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.34507v2) shows that proactive memory recall in long-lived assistants is a multiple-testing problem: a similarity threshold tuned to 5% false alarms at N=8 reaches 84–100% false alarms at N=2048 on LongMemEval replays. The authors prove a theoretical bound that pins the hit rate to the far left of the single-comparison ROC curve and validate it empirically, with a finite-pool form predicting held-out hit rates within 6.1 points. This work reveals a fundamental scaling limitation for long-lived AI assistants that proactively surface memories: as the memory store grows, naive similarity thresholds become unusable due to exploding false alarms. It provides both a theoretical framework and a practical conformal-gating solution, which could shape how future memory systems for LLM agents are designed and evaluated. The paper introduces a cue-swap conformal gate that ranks the current cue among other cues on the same store, achieving a finite-sample false-alarm guarantee under exchangeability; with background from the user's unfiltered history, it keeps false alarms at 3–6% on LongMemEval at the hit rate of a label-tuned threshold, and in chronological replay it speaks on only 6–8% of session-opening turns versus 57% for the deployed gate at N=2048, at about 50 ms per decision on one CPU thread. A cross-encoder reranker pays the same price of scale, and on a prospective-memory benchmark, similarity gates recall at most 9% of constraints at controlled false alarms.

**Background**: Long-lived assistants that proactively recall memories must decide at each turn whether to interrupt the user, which involves testing many stored items for relevance. ## [Amortized Localized Posterior Inference for Model Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37731) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper proposes a method for model calibration that constructs localized posteriors by weighting observation likelihoods with Gaussian localization weights that incorporate context uncertainty, and uses a conditional normalizing flow to approximate the family of posteriors via amortized variational inference. It demonstrates on a twin experiment with the Branin-Hoo model and on an ocean turbulence closure (k-ε) in a single-column model that localization reduces predictive errors compared to global posterior calibration. This work addresses the common problem of model discrepancy where a single calibration parameter cannot capture varying physical responses across different contexts, which is particularly relevant for climate and ocean modeling where parameters may need to vary with environmental conditions. The amortized approach enables efficient inference of context-dependent posteriors, potentially improving the reliability of turbulence closures and other subgrid models in Earth system simulations. The localization weights are Gaussian and include covariance inflation to account for context uncertainty, with reflection at domain boundaries and an optional correction for uneven context sampling. The method is evaluated in twin experiments designed to admit local compensation, and the marginalized parameter distribution is obtained by integrating localized posteriors under a prescribed context measure.

GARDEN introduces a method where an LLM reward engineer autonomously navigates environment code, training records, and agent behavior to design a single reward program for a family of related cooperative multi-agent scenarios, then transfers it unchanged to unseen scenarios. On Overcooked and SMAX benchmarks, it improved task returns by 58.2% and 52.5% over default rewards on two kitchen layouts, and raised mean win rate in two combat scenarios from 51.0% to 89.9%. Reward design is a major bottleneck in cooperative MARL, and GARDEN shows that a single autonomously engineered reward can generalize across related scenarios, potentially reducing manual effort and enabling more reusable reward programs. This could benefit researchers and practitioners deploying multi-agent teams in robotics and autonomous vehicles. GARDEN holds the learning algorithm and final reward selection rule fixed during development, and under matched candidate and probe budgets it outperformed fixed diagnostic feedback (84.2%) and Eureka-inspired reward reflection (79.2%). The approach relies on autonomous evidence navigation, where the LLM selects which source code, training artifacts, and behavioral evidence to examine rather than using a fixed feedback report.

The paper introduces Governance-Aware Federated Learning (GAFL), a framework that adds runtime governance, independent evidence verification, fairness assessment, anomaly detection, and tamper-evident audit logging to standard federated learning. In a 10-participant cross-silo prototype on the Adult Income dataset, complete GAFL identified 100% of falsified-evidence participants and intervened on all affected participants across seven threat scenarios, while GAFL without verification caught none. GAFL shows that binding client-reported governance evidence to model updates and independently recomputing it can catch falsified evidence, though the added governance processing (173.67 ms vs. 3.82 ms per round) and fairness-utility trade-offs highlight costs that must be managed. It adapts modality-level weights using batch-averaged, temporally smoothed shifts in pseudo-label confidence as a reliability heuristic, and outperforms TTRV in 16 of 18 benchmark-model settings on adaptation instances and 17 of 18 on held-out instances across six benchmarks and three Qwen3-VL model scales. Timbre formulates consensus as a weighted χ²-barycenter problem whose unique minimizer is the normalized weighted harmonic aggregate, without requiring correct-answer invariance. The paper introduces a formal semantics for coordinated systems of parameterized transformations, abstracting from the Transformer architecture to a general framework with extensional and intensional interpretations. It defines 'transforming concepts' and applies the framework to attention heads and residual connections, showing that semantic explanations depend only on a shared algebraic-semantic core. This work offers a theoretical foundation for understanding how complex neural architectures can be decomposed into semantically coordinated subsystems, potentially enabling more principled design and analysis of models beyond the standard Transformer. It bridges formal logic and machine learning theory, which could impact how researchers reason about modularity and compositionality in neural networks. The framework distinguishes the common algebraic-semantic core of transformation systems from their architecture-specific functional organization, allowing different mathematical instantiations and mechanical realizations of the same abstract system type. The analyses of attention heads and residual connections are claimed to generalize beyond the standard Transformer, revealing modularity where complex architectures decompose into simpler semantically coordinated subsystems.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Extensional semantics defines meaning by reference to objects in the world, while intensional semantics captures meaning via properties or descriptions that determine those objects. In logic, intensional systems are needed to represent richer notions like necessity and belief. The Transformer architecture relies on attention heads, which are parallel projection mechanisms that focus on different parts of the input, and residual connections, which add a layer's input to its output to ease training of deep networks. This paper uses such concepts to build a general semantic framework.

## [Agent Social Re-entry: Finding, Returning, and Reconstructing Evaluated Separately](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39781) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.39781) introduces 'agent social re-entry' as a multi-dimensional evaluation problem for LLM agents in persistent social environments, distinguishing three capabilities: Finding, Returning, and Reconstructing. The authors propose a shared-snapshot evaluation framework that measures these dimensions independently, and evaluations across six LLM configurations show that conversational resurfacing improves target conversation identification while persistent memory increases autonomous target-directed replying, but neither yields consistent gains in contextual reconstruction. This work highlights that remembering a past interaction is not the same as knowing when to re-engage or how to reconstruct context, which matters for building agents that maintain coherent long-term social relationships. It provides a way to evaluate these capabilities separately rather than relying on memory retrieval or response quality alone, potentially influencing future benchmarks for persistent agent memory. The shared-snapshot framework isolates Finding, Returning, and Reconstructing so that improvements in one dimension are not conflated with others; results across six LLM configurations reveal a dissociation where resurfacing and persistent memory help identification and reply initiation but not contextual reconstruction. The paper is an early-stage arXiv preprint with no demonstrated downstream impact yet.

The paper introduces Assur-KB, a compositional representation of planar mechanisms built from irreducible modules, boundary interfaces, and solve dependencies, and reports a geometric-mean 1.8x advantage in sample efficiency over flattened adjacency and position inputs across training budgets of 50 to 10,000 mechanisms. This work shows that injecting physical constraint structure into the representation can substantially reduce data requirements for learning mechanism behavior, which could benefit data-scarce engineering design tasks and inform broader compositional representation learning research. Bridge-LP is a new framework that unifies graph and language representations for link prediction on text-attributed graphs (TAGs), built around three theoretically justified components: jumping connection of textual proximity, compressed embedding, and a cache embedding training strategy. The framework's three components address robust LM training (D1), learnable encoding of neighborhood information from classical heuristics (D2), and reduced computational complexity (D3). ## [Neighborhood Elites: Quality-Diversity Search for Uncertainty Quantification in QA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40278) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper recasts input perturbation for uncertainty quantification in question answering as a quality-diversity search problem and proposes Neighborhood Elites (NE), a neighborhood constructor that spreads answer-preserving rewrites across two axes: the kind of edit and the explicitness of support. Across five extractive-QA datasets and five instruction-tuned LLMs, NE improves failure detection against every other constructor in at least 24 of 25 dataset-model pairs, reaching 0.726 AUROC and 0.211 AUPRC lift over the base rate. This work addresses the critical problem of LLMs producing confidently wrong answers by making perturbation-based uncertainty quantification more principled and controllable. It could lead to more reliable QA systems and better failure detection in downstream applications, benefiting researchers and practitioners working on LLM reliability. NE outperforms semantic entropy computed over decoder samples by 0.074 AUROC and 0.062 AUPRC lift, and this advantage widens as the neighborhood grows. The comparison holds the editor, QA model, uncertainty measure, and search objective fixed, isolating the effect of the neighborhood constructor.

**Background**: Uncertainty quantification (UQ) for large language models aims to estimate how likely a model's answer is correct, which is crucial because LLMs often produce wrong answers that look as confident as correct ones. Perturbation-based UQ probes a model with multiple rewritten versions of the input and measures prediction variance, but traditional methods use generic rewrites that don't control what changes. Quality-diversity (QD) search is an optimization technique that seeks a diverse set of high-quality solutions across a predefined space, and this paper applies it to generate more informative perturbations for QA.

## [Cassette-Editor: A Video Editing Agent with Atomic Commits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37690) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Cassette-Editor is a video editing agent that constrains all edits through a single read tool and a single write tool, with every write passing through the same executor, rules, and commit service as manual edits, committing atomically or being rejected with located diagnostics. In a controlled experiment, a real model was shown 277 of its own committed edits after damaging them, and it corrected nearly every call with full or minimal feedback, while locating each problem cut the input tokens needed for a correction to less than half. This work shows that a minimal read/write tool interface with atomic commit semantics can keep a video timeline structurally valid without relying on critic agents or restricted output formats, leaving creative decisions to the model. It offers a clean pattern for language agents operating on persistent artifacts, where invalid edits can break the artifact and diagnostics must guide recovery. The experiment used 277 self-committed edits that the model had damaged; locating each problem reduced the input tokens a correction needed to less than half, and the model's corrections dropped other values it had written in one case rather than seven. Reads relate stored analysis of the footage to each use of it on the timeline, so knowledge about footage holds only for particular uses.

**Background**: Language agents increasingly work by calling tools on a persistent artifact, such as a code repository, where each call's result shapes the next step. A new arXiv paper presents an empirical fairness audit comparing classical and quantum classifiers (SVM, MLP, QSVM, QCNN) on two medical imaging datasets: dermatological lesions from DDI with Fitzpatrick skin type as the sensitive attribute, and chest X-rays from CheXpert-derived data with age group as the sensitive attribute. The study finds that quantum classifiers can achieve competitive aggregate performance while still exhibiting subgroup disparities, and that some mitigation strategies that reduce disparity do so by degrading the best-performing group rather than improving the worst. The audit uses ResNet-18 embeddings and tests three mitigation settings: differentiable Equalized Odds regularization, Gradient Reversal Learning, and their combination. A key finding is that a smaller subgroup AUC gap may stem from degrading the best group rather than improving the worst, so each mitigation is tested against a pre-specified non-inferiority margin; several configurations with the smallest disparity, notably QCNN with GRL on DDI, are not clinically acceptable due to loss of global discrimination. All quantum models run in classical simulation, and the authors claim no quantum advantage.

DeFT-RAG uses a QA table updated by rules and a fine-tuned lightweight decision model for yes/no decisions, and with a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, reducing LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy. ## [Learning Lotteries with Minimal Stakeholder Violations from Membership Queries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37828) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces a model for selecting a lottery over AI system versions to minimize the number of rejecting stakeholders when acceptance criteria are unknown halfspaces learned via membership queries. It proves APX-hardness even with known halfspaces and provides exact algorithms for constant m, quasi-polynomial time under a margin condition, and sampling-based guarantees when only some agents can be queried. This work addresses a practical challenge in AI deployment where conflicting stakeholder requirements (e.g., safety vs. helpfulness) may make universal acceptance impossible, providing theoretical foundations for balancing trade-offs via randomized version selection. It contributes to algorithmic game theory and ML by formalizing query-based learning of stakeholder preferences and deriving hardness and approximation results. The problem is APX-hard even when all halfspaces are known and utilities are binary, and for m≥3, any deterministic algorithm querying only K agents cannot guarantee fewer than n−K extra rejections, which is tight. A linear program gives a polynomial-time method for any m, and sampling a uniform subset of agents yields guarantees independent of n, with synthetic experiments suggesting worst-case bounds are conservative on random instances.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: In AI development, A/B testing often involves deploying a mixture of system versions, sending each request to a randomly chosen version. Stakeholders such as safety teams or regulators may accept a mixture only if its expected performance meets their standards, but these standards are typically unknown and can only be learned by asking binary membership queries (e.g., 'is this mixture acceptable?'). The paper builds on recent work by Choo et al. (ICML 2026) that sought a lottery acceptable to all agents, but here the goal is relaxed to minimizing rejections when no universally acceptable lottery exists. APX-hardness indicates that no polynomial-time approximation scheme exists unless P=NP, motivating the study of exact algorithms for restricted cases and sampling-based approximations.

## [More Planning Updates Can Hurt Learned Planners for World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37891) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper shows that increasing the number of planning updates in learned planners for world models can degrade performance, with a simple fixed action updater (1,505 parameters) solving 8 of 16 PushT scenes while a released LePlanner solved all 16 but at much lower cost. In a matched experiment, budgets of 4, 8, and 12 updates yielded 9, 8, and 7 successes respectively, and extra updates never rescued a failing task. This counterintuitive finding challenges the common assumption that more planning compute always improves decision quality, suggesting that learned planners can over-optimize toward inaccurate world-model predictions and that simpler updaters may be more robust in some settings. It has implications for designing efficient model-based RL systems where planning budget is a key hyperparameter. The fixed action updater did not satisfy the pre-evaluation task-cost criterion, and the performance differences were concentrated in one scene cluster where extra updates reduced the cost of selected latent world-model trajectories but turned previous successes into failures. The paper releases code, weights, evaluators, execution traces, and cost accounting.

**Background**: World models in reinforcement learning are learned simulators that let agents imagine future trajectories and plan without interacting with the real environment, improving sample efficiency. ## [TERRA: Task-Oriented Edge AI for Regional Fire Detection with Identity-Free Reporting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37909) ⭐️ 6.0/10

TERRA is an edge-AI framework that combines task-oriented local inference, identity-free region-tagged reporting, and permutation-invariant aggregation to detect fire regions without recovering device-specific measurements. Evaluated on the EN54 fire-alarm dataset, TERRA-Feature achieves mean AUPRC 0.990 with a 24-bit payload, while TERRA-Score achieves 0.987 with only 6 bits, both at an MDR of 1.81% for FAR ≤1%. This work shows that for regional fire detection, communicating only task-relevant information (a probability score or compact feature) can drastically reduce uplink payload while maintaining high accuracy, which is important for large-scale distributed sensing systems with many devices sharing a constrained uplink. TERRA supports two modes: TERRA-Score sends a quantized local fire probability (6 bits), and TERRA-Feature sends a compact learned representation (24 bits) aggregated via a DeepSets model. Under reliable message recovery, TERRA-Feature has slightly higher AUPRC, but TERRA-Score is more robust to false-message contamination; the study uses repetition-disjoint three-fold cross-validation on all 15 numerical sensing modalities of the EN54 dataset.

A dissertation case study applied TF-IDF with Logistic Regression and BERT to classify social media messages from the 2015 Nepal earthquake into nine humanitarian categories, mapping them to four routing priorities (P1–P4) within the ONE simulator using a modified Binary Spray and Wait router.
