## [SAG-Sep: Sparse Graph Neural Separator for Vehicle Routing Cuts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37952) ⭐️ 6.0/10

SAG-Sep introduces a sparse augmented graph encoder that scores node membership in rounded capacity cut (RCC) inducing subsets from a fractional LP solution in a single forward pass, avoiding the iterative predict-and-coarsen inference of NeuralSEP-style separators. It also proposes Onion-Sweep, a training-free decoder that ranks customers by score and evaluates all prefixes in one vectorized pass to emit the most violated nested RCC candidates. On the NeuralSEP benchmark with N=1000 customer instances, SAG-Sep with Onion-Sweep reduces the average root gap by 17.7% relative to the strongest NeuralSEP baseline while achieving roughly a 30-fold per-iteration neural separation speedup. This suggests that LP-aware sparse encoding and exploiting the nested structure of high-value cuts could broadly improve neural separation for combinatorial optimization. The Sparse Augmented Graph adds flow-informed multi-hop edges to expose long-range routing structure without densifying attention, and the Onion-Sweep decoder requires no tuned threshold or probing band. The approach is evaluated on the NeuralSEP benchmark for rounded capacity cut separation in capacitated vehicle-routing relaxations.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Rounded capacity cuts (RCCs) are among the most effective cutting planes for strengthening linear programming relaxations of the capacitated vehicle routing problem, but exact separation is computationally prohibitive at scale. NeuralSEP is a prior neural separation algorithm that uses a graph neural network to heuristically separate RCCs, but its iterative predict-and-coarsen inference can be slow and may yield too few effective cuts within practical budgets. SAG-Sep builds on this line by encoding the LP solution as a sparse augmented graph and exploiting the observation that high-value exact RCCs tend to be nested, forming onion-like subset families.

The paper introduces Merge and Branch (M&B), a tree-structured supervised fine-tuning method for LLM-based recommendation that compresses each historical item's semantic identifier (SID) and text into a few learned tokens (Merge) and then predicts multiple target SIDs from the compressed history (Branch). It also develops tree FlashAttention and a tree-structured key/value cache to efficiently process the shared history once while propagating gradients from all branches and to enable constrained decoding with history sharing. By enabling multiple targets per encoded history, M&B could significantly reduce training and decoding costs, making LLM-based recommenders more practical for large-scale deployment. M&B organizes each example as a shallow, wide tree to share history computation while keeping targets independent, and it uses tree FlashAttention to process the shared history once and propagate gradients from every branch end-to-end. A tree-structured KV cache extends history sharing to constrained decoding, and experiments on public benchmarks show improved training and decoding efficiency over strong baselines.

## [EARS-Info boosts multi-robot exploration with information-aware reallocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38040) ⭐️ 6.0/10

EARS-Info extends the Event-Driven Ant Reallocation Search (EARS) algorithm with information-aware components such as marginal sensing gain, feasible relocation, return-aware routing, sensing reservations, and cached shortest paths. In 168,000 simulated episodes across eight OpenStreetMap-derived city maps, it achieved the highest mean operational score in every evaluation panel, improving over EARS-Safe by 5.43% with eight robots and 3% communication dropout, raising weighted discovery from 88.88% to 98.46%, and reducing mean energy use by 2.62%. This work demonstrates that information-aware coordination can significantly improve exploration efficiency and energy use in multi-robot systems, which is relevant for applications like search and rescue, environmental monitoring, and autonomous mapping. The large-scale simulation study and statistically significant results suggest practical benefits for swarm robotics, though generalization to real-world scenarios remains to be tested. The improvements are consistent across all eight cities (p=0.0078125; 95% city-bootstrap interval [0.0159, 0.0694]), with no simulated incidents in 5,600 EARS-Info episodes. However, the authors acknowledge uncertainty about the individual contribution of each component, and generalization is limited by reused geography, a single training replicate, coarse maps, and adapted comparison methods.

## [Economic Theory Paper Analyzes Model Distillation's Market Impact](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38088) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.38088) uses an economic theory lens to model how model distillation by a competitor affects market outcomes and incumbent incentives in generative AI. It characterizes how the incumbent's model characteristics drive the competitor's distillation incentives and studies two regulatory settings: one where distillation attacks can be detected with a probability that grows with the extent of distillation, and one where they cannot be reliably detected. Distillation lets smaller firms train competitive models cheaply from outputs of proprietary closed-weight models, potentially eroding incumbents' returns and reshaping competition in the AI market. The paper's finding that penalty-based regulation can fully deter distillation but may harm competition and user surplus is directly relevant to ongoing policy debates over AI market regulation. The analysis shows that when detection is possible, penalty-based regulation can completely deter distillation but may have adverse effects on market competition and user surplus; when detection is unreliable, the incumbent can use self-distillation as a mitigation strategy, whose effectiveness depends on how cost-efficiently the incumbent can deploy a new self-distilled model. On the positive side, self-distillation can preserve market competition and thus protect user surplus to some extent.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Model distillation (or knowledge distillation) is a technique in which a smaller, cheaper model is trained to imitate the behavior of a larger, more capable model, retaining much of its performance at lower cost. In generative AI, firms can distill from transcripts of conversations with proprietary closed-weight models, whose trained parameters are not publicly released, raising both security concerns and questions about fair competition. This paper applies game-theoretic economic analysis, similar to prior work on the economics of AI foundation models, to study these market dynamics.

## [Paper Proposes Gettier-Inspired Framework for Trust in Generative AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38112) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.38112) argues that trust in generative AI outputs cannot rely on testimony or tool reliability, and proposes a three-step account of rational trust grounded in post-Gettier epistemology. The paper introduces the concept of a 'Gettier machine' and a criterion called 'justified true output' (JTO) with the everyday test: 'Had this been false, would I have noticed?' As generative AI becomes embedded in everyday inquiry, this paper offers a philosophically rigorous way to distinguish rational trust from mere fluency-based acceptance, which could inform AI ethics, user education, and the design of verification workflows. It is valuable for researchers in epistemology and AI ethics, though its practical impact remains uncertain as a preprint without community discussion. The paper argues that general-purpose generative models lack a type-stable process for reliabilist warrant, a practical form of the generality problem, and that stopping at obtaining an output turns AI into a Gettier machine where fluency-based justification is disconnected from truth. The proposed three-step structure—acquisition, understanding, independent verification—maps to the classical belief and justification conditions plus a post-Gettier sensitivity condition, yielding a stakes-indexed criterion of rational trust.

**Background**: The Gettier problem, introduced by Edmund Gettier in 1963, challenges the traditional definition of knowledge as justified true belief (JTB) by showing cases where a belief is justified and true but not knowledge due to luck. Post-Gettier epistemology seeks additional conditions, such as anti-luck or sensitivity, to rule out such cases. Reliabilism, which grounds justification in the reliability of belief-forming processes, faces the generality problem: it is unclear which level of process description is relevant for assessing reliability.

## [New Paper Defines Expected Log Density Ratio Estimation and Its Limits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38151) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces the concept of an expected log density ratio (ELDR), where log density ratios are integrated under a third, possibly distinct measure, and proves fundamental finite-sample limitations on ELDR estimation. It argues that standard density ratio estimation (DRE) methods are unsuitable for ELDR tasks and proposes a simple modification to some DRE methods that allows samples convergent to the integral distribution to appear in training data. This work clarifies that many problems with implicit densities where DRE is naively used are actually ELDR estimation tasks, which could affect applications from experimental design to generative modeling and reinforcement learning. By exposing the mismatch between standard DRE and ELDR, it motivates the development of bespoke ELDR estimators and provides a practical modification that improves estimation error in benchmarks. The paper proves fundamental limitations on finite-sample ELDR estimation and shows through benchmarks that including samples convergent to the integral distribution in training can improve ELDR estimation error. The proposed modification is simple and applies to some existing DRE methods, but the approach is foundational rather than a fully developed estimator.

**Background**: Density ratio estimation (DRE) directly estimates the ratio between two unknown probability densities from sample data, avoiding the hard problem of full density estimation. It is used for covariate shift adjustment, outlier detection, change-point detection, classification, and synthetic data evaluation. ## [CuraEval: Simple Length Baseline Rivals Complex Demo Scoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38221) ⭐️ 6.0/10

CuraEval introduces a controlled evaluation framework for demonstration curation on mixed-skill robot data, revealing that a PSD score depends almost entirely on episode length (ρ=0.999 on square) and that selecting the shortest 50% of demonstrations improves Diffusion Policy success from 70.7% to 76.5% on square. However, after rigorous statistical correction, no curated condition significantly outperforms full-data training. This work challenges the assumption that complex demonstration-scoring methods outperform simple baselines, urging the robot imitation learning community to adopt standardized, size-matched comparisons and proper statistical testing. It could lead to more reliable data curation practices and prevent overfitting to evaluation protocols. The adapted geometric-entropy LOO selector reduced success at 25% retention from 94.7% to 74.0% on can and achieved only 41.7% on square, below all random subsets (59.8–62.5%). Length-based selection at 75% retention improved success over full-data training from 76.7% to 86.7% under the original protocol but dropped to 79.5% from 80.5% after jointly changing checkpoint reporting, rollout count, and evaluation seed.

## [DecisionUnlearn-Bench: New Benchmark for Unlearning in Probabilistic Decision Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38431) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers introduced DecisionUnlearn-Bench, an empirical framework that evaluates machine unlearning in probabilistic decision models by comparing full, unlearned, and retain-only models across deletion granularities, label renderings, and candidate sets. Experiments on the BANKING77 dataset with 20 model configurations show that full-to-oracle displacement increases from example to association to class deletion, and that replacing semantic labels with opaque codes nearly eliminates the retrained oracle's recognition of deleted classes. This work highlights that unlearning evaluation for decision models must account for inference-time candidate sets and label schemas, not just training data removal, which could lead to more reliable and comparable unlearning benchmarks. It affects AI/ML researchers and practitioners deploying unlearning in intent detection and other classification systems where model behavior depends on the options presented at inference. SimNPO satisfied the screening criterion in 19 of 20 configurations, but its gains varied substantially across seeds and deletion targets, and development tuning on CLINC150 did not establish a positive pooled effect across 48 intents. At approximately matched suppression, methods can differ markedly in oracle fidelity, and recovery experiments distinguish initial forgetting from subsequent adaptation with conclusions depending on architecture and metric.

## [Decision models vs. LLMs on medical multiple-choice questions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38448) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper benchmarks 13 decision models against 15 generative LLM configurations, including different reasoning settings, on 1,273 four-option MedQA questions under text-only conditions. Generative LLMs achieved higher peak accuracy (up to 96.86%) compared to decision models (up to 89.08%), while decision models offered lower cost and latency but showed calibration and repeatability issues. This study provides empirical data on the trade-offs between decision models and LLMs for medical multiple-choice tasks, which is relevant for healthcare AI deployment where accuracy, cost, latency, and reliability all matter. It highlights that while LLMs achieve higher accuracy, decision models can be more resource-efficient but require careful consideration of probability quality and repeatability. Among the tested configurations, Mercury Decide had the lowest mean final-attempt cost (USD 0.0069 per 1,000 questions), and Clef Omni had the shortest median request duration (0.291 seconds). Decision-model probabilities distinguished correct from incorrect answers, but error rates among answers assigned probabilities of at least 0.90 ranged from 1.71% to 12.77%, and answer agreement across three runs ranged from 92.30% to 100%.

**Background**: MedQA is a benchmark dataset of multiple-choice questions from medical licensing exams, such as the United States Medical License Exams (USMLE), designed to evaluate medical knowledge and clinical decision-making. ## [SaiVLA-JEPA: Future Latent Prediction Adds No Gain to JEPA-Conditioned VLA Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38508) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces SaiVLA-JEPA, a JEPA-conditioned vision-language-action flow policy that combines a vision-language model with a diffusion transformer action expert and frozen V-JEPA features. Evaluated on 10,030 paired LIBERO-Plus episodes, current JEPA conditioning achieves about 82.5% success versus 71.6% without JEPA, but adding future latent prediction supervision yields no detectable aggregate gain at the tested training budget. This negative result challenges the assumption that adding future latent prediction objectives to JEPA-conditioned VLA policies automatically improves closed-loop control, suggesting that latent loss alone is an unreliable proxy for control performance. It motivates the use of paired closed-loop rollouts for evaluating representation-learning objectives in robot learning. Two lightweight auxiliary heads predict future representations during training and are omitted at inference, leaving the action sampler unchanged. The paper also evaluates SaiVLA-JEPA-TCA (latent context adaptation) and SaiVLA-JEPA-TPA (parameter adaptation), finding that context-retry gains are a system-level result under a larger attempt budget, while parameter adaptation shows no consistent advantage over the frozen policy and target controls.

## [PLF Learns Reusable Persona Adapters for Personalized AI Assistants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38561) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Persona Learning from Feedback (PLF), a framework that trains reusable, preference-grounded assistant personas as independent LoRA adapters on a shared frozen backbone. Training uses a frozen self-teacher that conditions on persona specifications and response-specific feedback to provide token-level supervision, with a feedback gate focusing updates on responses needing improvement, and a deployment-time supervised router selects or composes adapters without user-specific finetuning. PLF offers a modular alternative to persona prompting and persona distillation, potentially enabling adaptive personalization of AI assistants without degrading general capabilities. If validated, this approach could make it easier to deploy multiple user-specific behaviors efficiently in production systems. The method is evaluated on single-turn personalization with model-generated critiques and multi-turn tutoring with simulated students' reactions, showing improved model-judged preference fit over fixed-persona policies, persona prompting, and persona distillation. However, evaluation relies on model-judged preference fit and simulated users rather than real human feedback, and the approach requires training separate adapters per persona.

**Background**: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that injects small trainable low-rank matrices into a frozen model, drastically reducing compute and memory costs. Knowledge distillation typically uses a teacher model to guide a student, and self-teacher supervision extends this by having the model generate its own supervisory signals. LLM routers are trained models that direct queries to the most suitable model or adapter, and PLF combines these ideas for personalization.

A new arXiv paper proposes a two-step forensic strategy that uses partial C2PA Content Credentials to adapt image forensic detectors and mitigate distribution shifts. The method first reconstructs the operations applied by the last signer through structural analysis of the partial credentials, then uses that reconstruction to adapt the detector to the image's statistical characteristics. ## [Information-Theoretic Bounds on Reliability-Safety Trade-off in AI Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38651) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper proves a universal trade-off inequality between AI reliability and safety that is independent of model form, with its boundary determined solely by a parameter Kh quantifying the hidden layer's ability to distinguish benign from hazardous inputs. It then develops a Boltzmann-machine model to derive exact relations between reliability and safety, and uses a renormalization-group approach to characterize multigenerational knowledge distillation, yielding testable predictions for critical transitions. This work provides a theoretical foundation for understanding how safety properties transfer through knowledge distillation, which is widely used to compress large models into smaller ones. It could inform the design of distillation protocols that preserve both capability and safety, affecting practitioners deploying distilled models in safety-critical applications. The trade-off curve is determined by the hazard discrimination capacity K, while the overall answer tendency controls the operating point along the curve. For multigenerational distillation, the authors derive exact recursion relations and renormalization-group-like flows for two direct intergenerational distillation protocols at arbitrary teacher-student alignment strength, revealing fixed-point structures and critical behavior.

**Background**: Knowledge distillation is a technique for transferring knowledge from a large teacher model to a smaller student model, commonly used for model compression. Boltzmann machines are stochastic neural networks rooted in statistical physics, often used as theoretical models for learning and inference. Information theory provides tools like mutual information to quantify how much information one variable carries about another, and renormalization groups are physics methods for studying systems across scales, here adapted to analyze how distillation effects propagate across generations.

## [SatOps-Decision: Low-Latency Discriminative Models for Onboard Satellite Operations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38697) ⭐️ 6.0/10

SatOps-Decision introduces a locally adapted Laya encoder with a native decision head that selects among supplied operational answers in a single forward pass, achieving a median latency of 90.3 ms per decision versus 493.9 ms for Qwen3.5-0.8B generation and 388.4 ms for OneJev1.6-0.8B. The paper also presents the first dedicated benchmark for this approach, built from authored operational contracts, controlled state changes, and independently checked labels. This work shows that discriminative decision models can deliver roughly 5x lower latency than generative LLM baselines while achieving higher raw accuracy (85.3% vs. 40.7% for Qwen generation), which is critical for onboard satellite operations where decisions must be made quickly and reliably under constrained compute. It also establishes an auditable benchmark that could standardize evaluation for edge AI in space systems. The evaluation uses the same 1,024 held-out questions for all main accuracy comparisons, separate from training and development, and reports speedups of 5.47x and 4.30x based on median request times in measured FP32/MPS implementations. The local scorer's mean raw accuracy of 85.3% approaches cloud references Jev 1.14/1.13 at 87.4/81.9%, though the benchmark and results are specific to the satellite operations domain.

## [Unified Benchmark of GNNs for AC Power Flow Reveals Key Design Trade-offs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38985) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper presents a unified benchmark of representative graph neural network (GNN) architectures for AC power flow (ACPF) prediction, using identical preprocessing, training procedures, and comparable parameter budgets to isolate the effects of message-passing mechanisms and inductive biases. Evaluated on the IEEE 14-bus and 118-bus systems, the study finds that anisotropic message-passing architectures offer the best trade-off between predictive accuracy and physical consistency. As modern grids require more frequent system analyses, fast and accurate ACPF models are increasingly important, and this benchmark provides practical guidelines for designing graph-based power system models by clarifying which architectural choices actually help. It helps the ML-for-power-systems community move toward more reproducible and physically consistent GNN models. Explicit edge features encoding line impedances and global context aggregation are particularly important for voltage-angle predictions on the topologically bottlenecked IEEE-118 grid, and two or three message-passing layers generally provide the best balance between depth and representation width. Ablations also show that standard residual and root connections are not necessarily beneficial in shallow models, and that aggregation operators involve trade-offs between statistical accuracy and physical consistency.

The paper introduces 'weighted t-SNE,' a modification of t-SNE that incorporates feature importance scores to visualize and compare feature scorer results on high-dimensional datasets. The method modifies the relationship between data points in the embedded 2D space to reflect the importance of each original dimension as assessed by a feature scorer. ## [Certifying Sequential AI Agent Risk with Zero-Success Audits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39124) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.39124) models sequential AI agent tasks as chains of k milestones divided into checkpoint segments and derives how many zero-success audit responses are needed to certify, at level α, that the completion probability is at most ε. It provides an asymptotic formula for the minimum expected number of zero responses and shows that every asymptotically optimal evaluator must allocate its response budget equally among active milestones. This work gives dangerous-capability evaluators a formal basis for deciding how much evidence is enough when auditing agents that operate over multiple steps, which is directly relevant to AI safety and regulatory frameworks that require systematic risk assessment. It could influence how evaluation budgets are designed and how audit results are interpreted in deployment decisions. The certificate relies on a transport assumption—that adaptive deployment processes have success probabilities after every complete history capped by the corresponding audit success probabilities—which the audit itself does not test. The asymptotic result applies in rare-risk phase interiors where each segment is either rarely completed within the budget (active) or nearly always completed (free), and counting failed cycles can sharpen the certificate for segments with known or unqueried prefix steps.

## [LSTM-beta-VAE data augmentation boosts multi-output soft sensors for anaerobic digestion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39768) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper proposes a generative data augmentation framework using an LSTM-beta-Variational Autoencoder (LSTM-beta-VAE) coupled with a multi-output LSTM (MO-LSTM) soft sensor to simultaneously predict key stability indicators (pH, VOA/alkalinity ratio, biogas production) in industrial anaerobic co-digestion. Trained on synthetic sequences of transitions to unstable operations generated from one year of full-scale plant data, the MO-LSTM achieved robust simultaneous estimation across all targets, overcoming the sparsity and steady-state skew of industrial datasets. This work addresses a critical gap in data-driven monitoring of anaerobic digestion by enabling simultaneous prediction of stability indicators rather than just production yields, which could lead to earlier warning of process failure and more reliable operation of industrial biogas plants. It also demonstrates how generative augmentation can mitigate data scarcity in niche industrial bioprocesses, paving the way for hybrid mechanistic-data-driven models. Baseline evaluations showed that standard algorithms (Random Forest, XGBoost) and unaugmented LSTMs failed to recognize transitions to unstable operations due to data scarcity, resulting in poor estimation of stability indicators. The LSTM-beta-VAE synthesizes physically valid sequences to safely populate sparse regions of the feature space, and the approach provides a basis for early-warning soft sensors in industrial bioprocesses.

## [SHPRR: Sequential Halving variant for best-arm identification under regret budget](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39837) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces SHPRR (Sequential Halving with Proportional Regret Rationing), an algorithm that front-loads a regret budget to allow more exploration when many arms remain, improving best-arm identification under a fixed sampling horizon and regret budget. The authors theoretically show that the regret cost of exploration decreases across phases of Sequential Halving, yielding improved guarantees on the probability of identifying the best arm. This work extends best-arm identification to settings where exploration cost is measured relative to a trusted baseline, which is relevant for operational decision-making where regret matters as much as sample count. It provides a practical algorithm with theoretical guarantees that could influence how exploration budgets are allocated in real-world bandit applications. The algorithm builds on Sequential Halving and uses proportional regret rationing to allocate the budget non-uniformly across phases; experiments on synthetic and real-world instances show improved best-arm identification performance over uniform regret allocation and existing baselines. The theoretical analysis focuses on the structure of regret as a resource, where sampling better arms is less costly relative to the baseline.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Best-arm identification (BAI) is a pure-exploration problem in multi-armed bandits where the goal is to identify the arm with the highest mean reward, typically under a fixed sampling budget. Sequential Halving is a widely used algorithm that successively eliminates the worse half of arms to focus sampling on promising candidates. This paper considers a variant where the cost of exploration is measured as regret relative to a baseline policy already in place, rather than just the number of samples.

## [CovFedAvg: Local Low-Loss Curves and Federated Model Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39902) ⭐️ 6.0/10

CovFedAvg proposes retaining local models and low-loss curve controls on clients to select a compatible shared federated model without centralized calibration data. It provides exact selection guarantees that the chosen model has no higher evaluated training loss than the previous model and the current-round FedAvg candidate. This work addresses model selection in federated learning, where clients with heterogeneous data may learn locally equivalent but incompatible models. It offers a principled way to choose a shared model without sharing data, which could improve personalization and robustness in cross-device FL. The guarantees are limited to evaluated training loss and do not imply global optimality, stationarity, generalization, or differential privacy. Experiments on synthetic, activity-recognition, and gas-sensor tasks show modest gains over FedAvg (e.g., 89.84% vs. 88.88% macro balanced accuracy at width 16), but matched distributed fine-tuning reaches 91.65%, indicating no curve-specific advantage.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Federated learning trains a shared model across many clients without centralizing their data, and Federated Averaging (FedAvg) is the standard algorithm that aggregates locally trained models. However, when clients observe different parts of a prediction task, their local models may be incompatible outside their observed support. Mode connectivity research shows that independently trained models can often be connected by low-loss paths, which CovFedAvg leverages to find a common endpoint.

## [Prompting vs. token probabilities for assessing focus-sensitivity in language models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39923) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper tests language models of various sizes on semantic focus-sensitivity using text-based focus markers like boldface and italics, comparing explicit prompting with token-probability methods. It finds that token probabilities yield above-chance performance universally, but in some larger models prompting outperforms probabilities by a wide margin, likely because models are reluctant to produce out-of-the-blue focus marking. This work challenges the assumption that token-probability methods are always superior for linguistic evaluation and shows that prompting can be more robust for stylistically atypical data, which has important consequences for how we assess language models' linguistic competence. The authors replaced standard focus markers with randomly generated ones and found that token probabilities still beat chance but showed a significantly greater performance decrease compared to prompting, supporting the idea that models' reluctance to produce out-of-the-blue focus marking muddies probability-based results.

**Background**: Focus-sensitivity is a linguistic phenomenon where the placement of focus (e.g., which word is emphasized) changes the meaning or acceptability of a sentence, as in 'Lucy only SWAM yesterday' versus 'Lucy only swam YESTERDAY'. Token-probability methods evaluate language models by measuring the likelihood they assign to specific tokens in a given context, while prompting methods ask models to make explicit metalinguistic judgments. SIFR introduces a frequency-aware dual-stream framework that performs spectral-guided invariant fusion of frozen CLIP and DINOv2 features and adds a spectral decoder refinement module to suppress domain-sensitive interference in dense prediction. Experiments on synthetic-to-real, real-to-real, and adverse-weather DGSS benchmarks show consistent improvements over prior state-of-the-art methods. Domain generalized semantic segmentation is critical for deploying segmentation models in real-world scenarios like autonomous driving and medical imaging, where target-domain data is unavailable during training. SIFR's unified spectral principle for both feature fusion and decoder refinement offers a new way to balance domain robustness and fine-grained spatial accuracy, potentially benefiting foundation-model-based segmentation pipelines. SIFR filters out domain-sensitive responses during fusion while preserving complementary semantic and structural information, and its decoder refinement stabilizes multi-scale features via low-frequency statistics-based normalization and adaptive frequency selection. The approach is evaluated across multiple DGSS benchmarks, though the abstract does not report specific numerical gains or computational overhead.

FARE introduces a factor-aware retrieval method that ranks historical weeks for each target-week factor (e.g., promotions, calendar events) and merges them into a factor reference under a fixed budget. Two error-guided gates then fuse this reference with a shape reference and control correction of a backbone forecast, reducing WAPE by 11.46%, 4.06%, 14.63%, and 10.16% on Favorita, M5, Rossmann, and Rohlik across five backbones. Retail sales forecasting directly impacts inventory planning, and FARE's ability to leverage partial historical matches for rare factor combinations addresses a key challenge in demand forecasting. The method is model-agnostic and improves both conventional backbones and frozen foundation models like Chronos-2, making it broadly applicable in retail operations. The two gates are fixed during testing, meaning no test-time adaptation is required. FARE outperforms supervised residual correction and retrieval augmentation, and code is available on GitHub; however, evaluation is limited to four public retail datasets and the method assumes known target-week factors.

The paper proposes a response-aware patient dynamics model that explicitly represents physiological change during autoregressive state updating, decomposing predicted change into state-dependent baseline dynamics and respiratory-support-associated deviations, with room air as a reference. Across ICU cohorts from two independent institutions, it achieves comparable overall trajectory prediction to baselines, with more consistent improvements when physiological states are changing. This work offers a more interpretable way to model how individual ICU patients respond to respiratory support, which could help clinicians anticipate divergent trajectories among patients receiving the same intervention. It also advances clinical time-series forecasting by separating baseline physiology from treatment effects, a distinction relevant to broader healthcare AI applications. The model uses a response pathway that encodes predicted physiological change and updates the latent patient state across the forecast horizon, with formal analysis provided for the reference-anchored formulation. However, it is a specialized arXiv preprint with no community discussion, and its improvements are most consistent only when physiological states are changing.

## [Heavy-Tailed Memory Traces in Long-Horizon Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00010) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.00010v2) audits memory retrieval in long-horizon language agents, showing that repeated retrieval produces heavy-tailed memory usage where a few states are frequently accessed while many are rarely retrieved and more error-prone. The authors propose the Core-Tail Memory Controller (CTMC), a rank-based controller that allocates prompt budget with a single exponent τ, reducing prompt tokens by 24.48% on LongMemEval while maintaining accuracy. This work highlights that memory usage distribution, not just task success and token cost, is a measurable and actionable property of long-horizon agent memory, offering a practical signal for improving memory efficiency in LLM agents that rely on external memory for persistent interaction and planning. The tail audit shows that memory concentration is reproducible but strongly policy-dependent, ranging from log-normal-compatible patterns under random walks to truncated-power-law-compatible heavy tails under semantic LLM policies. CTMC preserves summarized information from the tail and was evaluated on Synthetic Graph World, ALFWorld, and LongMemEval.

## [MintFlow: Minimal Trajectory Intervention for Constrained Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02260) ⭐️ 6.0/10

MintFlow introduces a training-free constrained sampling framework for flow matching models that enforces constraints by minimally perturbing an intermediate flow state, keeping the pretrained flow field unchanged. An adjoint formulation yields a closed-form expression for the perturbation, eliminating iterative optimization, and the method adaptively selects the intervention time. This work addresses a key trade-off in constrained sampling: enforcing constraints often displaces samples from the learned data distribution. By minimizing distribution deviation while achieving competitive constraint satisfaction, MintFlow could benefit applications in generative vision and physical system modeling where both constraint adherence and sample fidelity are critical. MintFlow is training-free and keeps the pretrained flow field unchanged, perturbing only an intermediate state. The adjoint method provides a closed-form perturbation, avoiding expensive iterative optimization, and the intervention time is chosen adaptively to balance perturbation magnitude against its amplification by the remaining flow.

## [Clipped Barrier Policy Gradients with Convex Regularization for Budget-Constrained Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.19193) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces a clipped barrier policy gradient method for budget-constrained control, where the one-step reward is clipped from below at a level m to keep returns finite. It provides a theoretical decomposition of failure risk and proves exponential convergence of the population policy-gradient flow for convex regularizers. This work bridges safe reinforcement learning and policy optimization by offering near-optimality guarantees for risk-constrained policies, which could impact safety-critical applications like autonomous driving and industrial control. It extends mean-field analysis to practical regularizers like weight decay, making theoretical results more applicable to finite networks. The clip level m acts as a price of failure risk, and the clipped value decomposes exactly into utility before failure, margin cost, and m times geometric failure risk. The risk exceeds that of any comparison policy by at most order 1/m and can be certified from value or validation data; bounds are evaluated on benchmarks including a fuel-tank controller and a maintenance task.

Clipping the reward addresses this, and convex regularization (like relative entropy or weight decay) ensures convergence of policy gradient methods.

## [Brouwerian Assertibility Constraint Proposed for Responsible AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.03971) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces a Brouwer-inspired assertibility constraint for responsible AI, requiring systems in high-stakes domains to provide a publicly inspectable and contestable certificate of entitlement before making categorical assertions or denials; otherwise, they must output 'Undetermined'. This yields a three-status interface semantics (Asserted, Denied, Undetermined) and is operationalized through structured certificates, decision-layer gates, and a reason-coded output contract. This proposal addresses the risk of generative AI converting uncertainty into authoritative-seeming verdicts, which can displace democratic epistemic agency. By requiring contestable warrants rather than confidence alone, it aims to preserve human agency in public justification and could influence AI ethics and governance frameworks for high-stakes applications. The framework distinguishes internal entitlement from public standing, connecting them through the certificate as a boundary object. A design lemma shows that, under a refutation-soundness condition, certificate-sound binary totality presupposes witnessed decidability on the declared scope, and 'Undetermined' is a mandatory status rather than a tunable reject option.

**Background**: Brouwerian intuitionism is a philosophy of mathematics that rejects the law of excluded middle, holding that a mathematical statement is true only if there is a constructive proof of it. ## [Online Surrogate Repair Decouples High-Fidelity Feedback from Search Length](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07655) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces online surrogate repair (OSR), a closed-loop algorithm that uses sparse high-fidelity evaluations to update a surrogate model during longer agent searches conducted primarily with inexpensive surrogate feedback. An acquisition rule selects which of the agent's accumulated proposals receive high-fidelity evaluation, and the resulting labels update the surrogate for subsequent episodes. This work addresses a key bottleneck in closed-loop AI-driven scientific discovery, where reliable feedback from wet-lab synthesis or high-fidelity computation is costly while candidate generation is cheap. By reducing oracle queries by 84.3–90.3% for matching discovery counts, OSR could make autonomous discovery workflows far more practical in chemistry and materials science. Experiments across controlled synthetic environments show that improving global surrogate fit does not necessarily reduce maximum regret, whereas Q90-UCB and expected improvement (EI) substantially reduce regret by directing evaluations toward regions that determine the optimizer's decisions. Across LLM and Chemeleon workflows, Online EI reduces oracle queries by 84.3–90.3% for matching discovery counts and by 77.9–81.6% for matching the quality of the best material found.

It derives exact non-flip certificates, a minimum-variance (BLUE) replay gain, an ℓ∞ trust-region projection, and an analytic near-tie spacing law, and implements three compensation levels (L1–L3) in C++ with an open-source release. Rebuilding the kNN graph at every block boundary is a major cost in equivariant structure-prediction pipelines, so reducing this overhead without sacrificing accuracy could make such models more practical for large-scale protein or molecular structure prediction. The formal guarantees and open-source implementation also provide a reusable framework for optimizing dynamic graph construction in other equivariant architectures. The L2 compensation level exactly reproduces the per-boundary (PB) edge set (D = 0.0000 at every boundary), L1 stays within 0.6% error, and L3 interpolates monotonically between frozen and PB topology; the recorded trajectory yields a measured 1.5× Pass-1 and 1.76× epoch speed-up with no measurable loss gap. The approach is validated under a matched-conditions protocol (identical seed, MSA depth, and trajectory family, only topology mode differs), and the analytic near-tie spacing law E[m] ≈ r_k/(3k) matches measurements to 1%.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: SE(3)-equivariant neural networks are designed to respect 3D rotational and translational symmetries, making them well-suited for predicting molecular and protein structures. In these pipelines, coordinate updates alternate with the construction of a k-nearest-neighbour (kNN) graph whose membership changes discretely as coordinates move, and rebuilding this graph at every block boundary is expensive. Trust-region methods are a class of optimization techniques that constrain updates to a region where a local model is trusted, and damping (as in Levenberg–Marquardt) controls step size to ensure stable convergence.

## [PACE: Pareto-Adaptive Compression for Efficient Native MLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24005) ⭐️ 6.0/10

PACE introduces the first visual token compression framework tailored for ViT-free native multimodal LLMs with Multimodal-RoPE, using direction-aware importance estimation and Pareto optimization to jointly select compression depths and retention ratios. Experiments show near-lossless performance at only 25%-50% visual token retention, with over 2x FLOPs reduction and even improvements on several benchmarks. Native MLLMs that tokenize pixel patches directly suffer severe visual token redundancy, but existing compression methods target ViT-based architectures, leaving the models that stand to gain the most unexplored. PACE closes this gap, potentially enabling more efficient inference for a promising new class of multimodal models. The method decomposes attention into two orthogonal spatial saliency estimates along height and width, gated by a positional attention signal, and casts token budget allocation as Pareto optimization over performance preservation, inference efficiency, and spatial coverage. A pilot study confirms that ViT-free MLLMs tolerate aggressive compression with near-lossless or even improved performance, unlike ViT-based models that degrade.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Native multimodal LLMs (native MLLMs) jointly encode visual and linguistic sequences within a unified autoregressive Transformer, unlike conventional ViT-based MLLMs that rely on external vision encoders. By tokenizing pixel patches directly, they can generate thousands of visual tokens per input, causing a visual token explosion that bottlenecks inference. Visual token redundancy is a well-studied problem, but prior compression methods (pruning, merging, etc.) are designed for ViT-based settings. Multimodal-RoPE refers to rotary position embeddings extended to handle both spatial (height/width) and textual positions, whose dimensional decoupling enables direction-aware analysis.

## [BR-MoE adds differential privacy budget to traffic camera text summaries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.27026) ⭐️ 6.0/10

BR-MoE proposes budgeted semantic release, an extension of an existing reinforcement learning and mixture-of-experts framework that converts traffic camera scenes into text summaries. It adds a fixed privacy budget, a controller that selects which expert summaries to release, and calibrated noise so that the full release transcript satisfies an event-level differential privacy bound. Replacing images with text reduces direct visual exposure but does not formally bound disclosure, especially when summaries are released repeatedly. This work provides auditable privacy accounting for repeated traffic descriptions, which matters for city agencies and vendors deploying camera analytics under privacy regulations. The privacy guarantee holds only under explicit chunk isolation and bounded-event assumptions, and the paper's illustrative tables show the intended reporting format rather than empirical gains. The design also allows reuse of previous summaries without additional disclosure, and the evaluation protocol covers traffic utility, privacy attacks, release freshness, and computational cost.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Differential privacy is a formal framework that adds calibrated noise to outputs so that any single individual's data has limited influence, with a privacy budget (epsilon) capping total disclosure across queries. Mixture-of-experts models route inputs to specialized sub-models, and reinforcement learning can train a controller to select which expert outputs to use. Traffic cameras raise privacy concerns because their outputs can reveal individuals' locations and behaviors, and converting images to text is a common mitigation that lacks formal guarantees.

## [Topological Symmetry Index for Neural Network Loss Landscapes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28864) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces a topological symmetry index based on equivariant degree theory to systematically characterize symmetries and critical orbits in neural network loss landscapes across arbitrary architectures. It detects the isotropy of critical points and quantifies their net topological contributions, with examples including softplus MLPs, Transformers, and equivariant neural networks. This provides a general mathematical framework to analyze symmetries in loss landscapes beyond specific architectures, potentially unifying observations about critical points and their stability. It could impact theoretical deep learning research by offering tools to understand optimization and generalization through symmetry. The framework applies to arbitrary network architectures and includes methods for degenerate critical orbits, which are often difficult to handle. The index is computed using equivariant degree theory, and the paper demonstrates computations on softplus MLPs, Transformers, and equivariant neural networks.

This work extends such methods to provide a general index for critical orbits in neural networks.

## [Value-Rectified Distillation Tackles OOD Mode Averaging in Flow-Based Offline RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29075) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Value-Rectified Distillation (VRD), a framework that reformulates offline policy distillation as a value-guided generative trajectory alignment problem. It instantiates two algorithms, VRD-Q (value-quantile behavior distillation) and VRD-R (latent space reorganization), to decouple behavioral modes and avoid out-of-distribution action collapse when distilling flow-matching policies. This work addresses a critical failure mode in offline RL with multi-modal datasets, where standard distillation causes policies to average across modes and produce invalid actions. By cleanly isolating high-value behaviors, VRD could improve the reliability of generative policies in continuous control and planning tasks, impacting practitioners using D4RL, OGBench, and Minari benchmarks. VRD employs a dynamic coupling mechanism to rectify flow dynamics, with VRD-Q statistically filtering low-value behaviors via value quantiles and VRD-R geometrically isolating high-value trajectories in latent space. Empirical evaluations show improvements over generative baselines, especially on multi-modal, non-expert datasets.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Offline reinforcement learning trains policies from fixed datasets without environment interaction, but distribution shift can cause policies to select out-of-distribution actions with unreliable values. Flow matching is a generative modeling technique that learns continuous transformations from noise to data, and when used for behavior policies, distilling them can inadvertently interpolate across distinct behavioral modes, leading to invalid actions.

## [Absolute Fix and Anti-coherence Regularization Improve SCALE OOD Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32255) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper identifies that SCALE, a post-hoc OOD detection method, degenerates when negative activations are present because positive and negative contributions cancel in the percentile-based magnitude ratio. It proposes an Absolute Fix that computes the ratio over absolute-valued activations instead of discarding negatives via ReLU, and introduces Anti-coherence regularization that penalizes the scaling factor based on sign-mismatched max-logit contributions. This work fixes a specific flaw in an existing post-hoc OOD detection method, making it applicable to backbones like ViT that produce negative activations, and shows that the corrected method can match or outperform training-data-dependent activation-shaping methods without needing training data or labels. It contributes to AI safety by improving OOD detection in a data-efficient manner. The method requires no access to training data or training labels and achieves ties or improvements over training-data-dependent activation-shaping methods in AUROC and FPR@95 on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet under the OpenOOD v1.5 protocol. The anti-coherence regularization specifically targets unreliable evidence for the predicted class by penalizing sign-mismatched contributions to the max logit.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection aims to identify inputs that differ from the training distribution, which is crucial for deploying reliable AI systems. Activation shaping is a family of post-hoc methods that modify penultimate layer activations to improve the separation between in-distribution and OOD samples without retraining the model. SCALE is one such method that rescales activations using a percentile-based magnitude ratio, but it assumes non-negative activations, which is violated in architectures like Vision Transformers (ViT) that use GELU or other activations allowing negative values.

## [CrowdCC benchmark jointly evaluates corruption robustness and quantization for crowd counting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36340) ⭐️ 6.0/10

CrowdCC introduces a controlled benchmark that jointly evaluates corruption robustness and deployment quantization for crowd-counting models across 23 corruptions at three severity levels, four datasets, and 26 models. It evaluates TensorRT engines at FP32, FP16, and post-training INT8 precision on an A100 GPU, with throughput and energy measurements on Jetson Orin NX configurations. This work fills a gap by jointly studying two factors usually evaluated separately—corruption robustness and quantization—showing that clean accuracy does not reliably predict corrupted performance and that precision changes robustness rankings. It matters for practitioners deploying crowd-counting models on resource-constrained edge devices who need to consider accuracy, robustness, and cost together. The corruptions span six families, with head annotations adjusted when geometry or visibility changes. Results show capture-chain corruptions cause the largest degradation, INT8 changes corruption robustness more than FP16 without a consistent direction, and INT8 inference efficiency is strongly associated with reformat overhead in the compiled engine, with slowdowns also observed under limited INT8 coverage.

## [Expert lithological labels do not improve learning when used to predict marine sediment properties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36410) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A masked variational autoencoder trained on 236,963 ocean drilling observations from 296 boreholes shows that expert lithological labels are recoverable from logged properties and do not improve embedding quality when used as supervision. Increasing the weight on the labels degrades reconstruction while leaving classification unchanged. This counterintuitive finding suggests that in geoscience ML, adding expert labels as supervision may not always help and could even harm generative performance, prompting practitioners to reconsider label usage in self-supervised models. It also highlights the value of self-supervised embeddings for predicting missing physical properties in unseen boreholes. The model uses six routinely logged properties (bulk density, magnetic susceptibility, natural gamma radiation, and red, green, blue reflectance) and a heteroscedastic Gaussian decoder with learnable mask tokens. On held-out boreholes, depth alone achieves a median R² of -0.02, while the embedding reaches 0.20, showing that depth does not account for the predictive power.

**Background**: Scientific ocean drilling produces large archives of physical, chemical, and magnetic measurements, but these are often incomplete due to varying sampling intervals, partial recovery, and destructive analyses. ## [REGER: Explicitly Modeling Inter-Item Relations with Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37584) ⭐️ 6.0/10

REGER introduces a unified framework that explicitly incorporates inter-item semantic and collaborative relations into semantic pretraining, history encoding, and SID generation for generative recommendation. It pretrains the GR model via generative semantic retrieval to inherit semantic similarity, combines global and local attention aligned with SID boundaries, and distills a discriminative teacher's full conditional distributions over legal next tokens at ground-truth prefixes, jointly optimized with cross-entropy. This work addresses a key limitation in generative recommendation: randomly initialized SID token embeddings and models trained from scratch fail to inherit item semantic relations, while collaborative relations are learned only implicitly. By explicitly modeling these relations, REGER could lead to more accurate and semantically aware recommendations, benefiting researchers and practitioners working on GR systems. REGER develops a theoretical framework for hierarchical preference decomposition over the SID prefix tree, proving an exact factorization of collaborative preference distributions and a weighted decomposition of item-level KL divergence into prefix-conditional KL divergences. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show consistent improvements over existing GR baselines, supporting the effectiveness of preference distillation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 31, 04:00

**Background**: Generative recommendation (GR) is a paradigm that autoregressively generates discrete semantic IDs (SIDs) of items, which are compact codes derived from item content and often organized in a prefix tree. Unlike traditional recommenders that use unique item IDs, GR models generate SIDs token by token, similar to language models. However, standard GR training initializes SID embeddings randomly and learns collaborative relations only implicitly through attention and next-token prediction, which may not fully capture item semantics.
